title: Boring Linux
text:
Boring Linux
A detailed, progressive guide to understanding and operating Linux systems, from the first administered machine to advanced systems engineering.
The book begins with the machine, installation and boot. It develops single-host administration, storage, Linux networking and network services, security, application services, virtual machines and containers. Later parts bring those facilities together through observability, performance, automation, fleets, availability, recovery and kernel-level investigation.

title: Boring Linux
text:
Starting point
You should be comfortable opening a terminal, editing a text file and running a simple command. No prior systems-administration knowledge is assumed. New systems concepts are explained when they appear, and each practical task includes the command details needed to complete it.
Worked examples use Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as the reference environment. General Linux mechanisms are distinguished from distribution-specific packaging, policy and defaults. Other distribution behavior is explained where it changes the administrative task.

title: Boring Linux
text:
How to learn
Follow the parts in order on the first pass. Each subject connects its mechanism to configuration, observation, operation, diagnosis and recovery. Diagrams show relationships; worked examples explain input, output and the limits of an observation. Labs provide results you can verify, and recall cards support later reference.
The opening inspection examples can be studied before building the lab VM. Repeat them on that VM after completing the lab-building chapter. Configuration and recovery experiments belong in the designated disposable lab.

title: What Linux Consists Of
text:
A map of the system



An installed Linux system combines userspace programs, a kernel and the machine’s devices.


Think of an installed Linux system as three cooperating things:

A mechanism for running and protecting work: the kernel, its supported interfaces and its device support.
A collection of software: libraries, administrative tools, service managers and applications.
A particular configured installation: its identities, packages, settings, data and runtime state.

The kernel project’s introduction explicitly distinguishes the kernel from a complete distribution. That distinction becomes practical whenever the kernel version, operating-system release and application version tell different stories.

The kernel
The kernel is the central privileged software managing the machine’s resources. It schedules runnable work on processors, also called CPUs, manages memory, implements filesystem and networking facilities, and coordinates access to devices through drivers.
A driver is software that lets an operating system control a device or implement a device-facing interface. Some Linux drivers are built into the kernel image; others can be loaded as modules. You do not need to compile drivers to begin administration. You do need to recognize that a visible device, a loaded driver and a working application are different milestones.
The kernel is not your shell, graphical desktop, web server or package manager. Those programs can request its services, but each also has its own configuration and failure modes. A web server can have a syntax error while the kernel continues scheduling processes normally.


Userspace
Userspace is the environment in which ordinary application and system-service code runs. It includes shells, editors, databases, login programs and many administrative daemons. A daemon is a program intended to provide background service; a service is an operational role that can involve one or several processes.
Root-owned programs are still userspace programs. Being a privileged user does not turn a process into part of the kernel. Privilege changes which operations it may request, subject to the host’s other policies.
The separation provides a useful diagnostic question: did an application reject its own configuration, did a library fail to load, or did a kernel operation fail? All can prevent a command from completing, but they call for different investigations.


Libraries and system calls
A library supplies reusable functionality to programs. A program might use a library to format text, look up a name, handle encryption or interact with the operating system. Libraries can be shared by many installed programs or incorporated into a program when it is built.
A system call is an interface through which userspace asks the kernel to perform an operation such as opening a file or creating a socket, a communication endpoint. Programs commonly reach it through library wrappers. A library function is not necessarily one system call: it might do all its work in userspace, make several calls, or use a different call on different architectures. The Linux system-call reference describes this boundary.
For administration, the important idea is the contract. A program asks for an operation; the kernel applies the relevant mechanism and policy, then returns a result. A failed request is evidence. Reinstalling the requesting program does not necessarily change why the request was denied.


The distribution
A distribution assembles a usable operating system from the kernel and other software. Its maintainers choose package versions, build options, update policies, installation tools, integration and defaults.
Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora can all run Linux while differing in package management and security policy. Two Ubuntu machines can also differ because they were installed from different images, upgraded along different paths or configured for different roles.
The distribution supplies a starting point. It does not make every installation identical. When a runbook says “the default configuration,” ask which release, image and installation path the author actually observed.


The installation and its running state
An installed system is software and persistent state arranged on storage. A running system is the current execution of a kernel and its processes, with active mounts, interfaces and other live state.
Installing a new kernel package does not switch the running kernel to that version immediately. Editing a service configuration file does not guarantee the running service has read it. These are examples of a general distinction:







Persistent state
Related runtime state




Kernel and boot files on disk
Kernel selected for this boot


Service unit and configuration files
Loaded manager configuration and running processes


Network configuration files
Addresses and routes active now


Account database entries
Identity and group information held by existing sessions


Filesystem table
Filesystems actually mounted



Administration means understanding both sides and the operation that brings them into agreement.

title: What Linux Consists Of
text:
Follow one ordinary request
Suppose a shell runs:
cat /etc/os-release
The pathname names a file containing operating-system identification data. In an ordinary interactive session, the shell locates cat and arranges to run it. The resulting process opens the file, reads bytes and writes output to its standard output, which is connected to the terminal in this example.
That explanation crosses several ownership boundaries:







Component
Responsibility in this example




Shell
Interpret the command and arrange program execution


cat program
Implement the requested read-and-copy behavior


Loader and libraries, where applicable
Prepare the executable and provide supporting functions


Kernel
Perform the requested file and output operations under the applicable policy


Filesystem and backing storage
Supply the file’s content, possibly already cached in memory


Terminal environment
Present the output to the user



Not every read reaches a disk. The content can already be cached. Not every program needs the same shared libraries. The table identifies responsibilities without assuming one low-level implementation for every executable.
If the file is absent, the executable is missing, or the output destination has failed, the same command line can fail for different reasons. Learn to preserve the actual error rather than translating all failures into “command does not work.”

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: Worked example 1: identify the operating system and kernel separately
text:
Worked example 1: identify the operating system and kernel separately
The following inspection commands can be run in an existing Linux environment. If you do not yet have a lab host, study the examples now and repeat them after the VM-building chapter. No installation is required to understand the model.
Input:
cat /etc/os-release
uname -s
uname -r
uname -m
Illustrative output, with unrelated release fields omitted:
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="26.04"
ID=ubuntu

Linux
<running-kernel-release>
x86_64
Read the answers as four different facts. The release file describes the operating-system userspace in the filesystem view you are inspecting. uname -s identifies the kernel name. uname -r identifies the running kernel release. uname -m reports a machine architecture identifier for this execution environment.
The os-release specification defines the release fields. Do not edit them to “upgrade” a system. Changing its label changes neither its packages nor the running kernel.
An application package can have yet another version. There is no expectation that an Ubuntu release number, Linux kernel release and web-server version should match numerically.
What this does not prove: which kernel will boot next, whether the installation is fully updated, or whether this filesystem view is the physical host’s root. Record those as unanswered questions.

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: Worked example 2: separate a command from the kernel it queries
text:
Worked example 2: separate a command from the kernel it queries
Input in a Bash session:
command -v uname
uname --version
cat /proc/sys/kernel/osrelease
uname -r
Possible observations:
/usr/bin/uname
<the installed implementation's version banner>
<running-kernel-release>
<running-kernel-release>
Why: uname is itself an installed userspace program. Its --version banner describes its implementation; its -r result describes the running kernel. An implementation without --version can reject that option while still providing the kernel query. Use the local manual rather than treating one vendor’s options as universal.
The /proc/sys/kernel/osrelease interface supplies a second route to the kernel release. /proc is a kernel-provided filesystem view, not an ordinary directory of files copied onto a disk. Reading it is observation; writing to other writable kernel interfaces can change runtime behavior. Here we use only the documented read operation.
On a Debian-family installation, you can additionally ask who owns a known installed pathname:
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/uname
This queries the local package database. The recorded path and package can differ with the installation’s layout or implementation. A “no path found” result needs investigation; it is not proof that the kernel has disappeared. File ownership, runtime kernel identity and package availability answer different questions.

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: Worked example 3: distinguish program, process and manager
text:
Worked example 3: distinguish program, process and manager
A program is executable code and associated files. A process is an instance executing with a process ID, credentials, memory and open resources. Starting the same program twice usually produces distinct processes.
In Bash, input:
printf 'This shell PID: %s\n' "$$"
ps -p "$$" -o pid=,ppid=,comm=
ps -p 1 -o pid=,comm=,args=
Illustrative output:
This shell PID: 1842
1842 1799 bash
1 systemd /sbin/init
Your shell is one process. PID 1 identifies the initial process in the PID namespace visible to you. On the reference system’s ordinary host environment, it is normally the system manager. In a container, PID 1 can instead be the container’s application or a small init program.
This is why finding a systemctl executable does not prove a systemd manager is running in the environment. Likewise, finding a server executable on disk does not prove the server has a running process or an active listening socket.
You will learn namespace details later. For now, record the boundary: a process listing describes the process view available to that command.

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: Worked example 4: inspect one system call boundary
text:
Worked example 4: inspect one system call boundary
This is an optional observation exercise if strace is already available. It does not require writing a program or installing packages now. The strace manual documents tracing a child command and selecting system calls.
strace -e trace=openat,read,write,close cat /etc/os-release
A successful trace might include lines with this shape:
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/os-release", O_RDONLY) = 3
read(3, "NAME=...", 131072) = <positive-byte-count>
write(1, "NAME=...", <byte-count>) = <byte-count>
close(3) = 0
These lines are schematic, not a byte-for-byte transcript. You can also see executable startup, libraries and locale files. The numeric file descriptor 3 is a handle chosen in this process, not a permanent identifier for the release file. Descriptor 1 is standard output by convention.
Now predict the result for a pathname you know does not exist. The open should fail, and there can be no successful read of that nonexistent file through the failed open. A trace is useful when it tests a prediction; a long trace alone is not an explanation.
Some restricted environments do not permit tracing even your own child process. Preserve that error as an observation about the environment. Do not alter host security policy merely to complete this optional first exercise.

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: The same Linux label can describe different boundaries
text:
The same Linux label can describe different boundaries
You may encounter a physical installation, a full VM, a container, a live image or an offline filesystem exposed through a repair environment. Each can contain familiar Linux paths.
Ask two questions together:

Which kernel is answering? Kernel queries describe the running execution environment.
Whose files am I reading? A mounted installation or isolated filesystem view can supply userspace files from a different environment.

Consider an offline installation accessed from rescue media. Its release file belongs to the installed userspace. The rescue environment’s running kernel still answers kernel queries. There is no inconsistency to fix simply because those versions differ.
This habit prevents a common repair mistake: building an installed artifact for the recovery kernel because a command returned the recovery environment’s release. The full recovery procedure comes later, but the reasoning starts here.

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: Break/fix: a package upgrade did not change the running kernel
text:
Break/fix: a package upgrade did not change the running kernel
Symptom. An administrator installs an updated kernel package, then reports that the update failed because uname -r still shows the previous release.
Hypotheses. The package could have failed to install; it could be installed but not selected by a boot entry; or no new boot has happened yet. These are different conditions.
Diagnosis. Record the running release, inspect the installed package result and identify which boot artifacts and entries exist. At this point in the book, the important observation is that package installation changes stored files, while uname queries current execution. Do not delete old kernels to force the two observations to agree.
Resolution. If installation and boot configuration are correct, the new kernel takes effect through a planned boot into that entry. Check its release afterward. If the host already rebooted into the old release, investigate selection and fallback rather than repeating the same install blindly. Later boot and update chapters provide the exact workflow.
Success criterion. You can explain both the installed state and the running state, including any intentional difference.

title: What Linux Consists Of
section: Practice: build a component evidence table
text:
Practice: build a component evidence table
Make the following table in your notes using the read-only examples above. If an interface is absent or a command is restricted, record that exact result.









Question
Evidence source
Your observation
Remaining uncertainty




Which userspace release is visible?
/etc/os-release

Is this the host, a guest or another filesystem view?


Which kernel is running?
uname -r

Which kernel will boot next?


What architecture is reported?
uname -m

Which hardware/virtualization layer exposes it?


What program is PID 1 here?
ps -p 1

What is outside this process view?


Where is the query command?
command -v uname

Which package or installation method supplied it?



Then classify these statements:

“The package manager installed a new executable.” This is a claim about persistent software state.
“A process is still running the previous executable.” This is a claim about runtime state.
“The command exists, so its corresponding service must be healthy.” This conclusion is unsupported.
“The release file and kernel release have different numbering.” This can be normal; they identify different components.

The exercise is complete when you can explain the component behind each answer and one thing the answer does not establish. No configuration cleanup is needed because the inspection did not change system settings.

title: What Linux Consists Of
text:
Recall card

Linux’s kernel manages resources and supplies interfaces to userspace.
Shells, service managers, libraries and applications are separate software components.
A distribution integrates software, packages, policy and update practices.
A program on disk and a running process are different objects.
Installed files and current runtime state can intentionally differ.
os-release, kernel queries and package queries identify different things.
Record which environment supplied an answer before interpreting it.
Diagnose the responsible component, then verify the specific claim you made.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Map: a machine can be physical or presented by another system
text:
Map: a machine can be physical or presented by another system



A physical Linux installation and a Linux VM have similar internal responsibilities but different resource providers.


Hardware is the physical equipment: processors, memory, controllers, storage media, network interfaces and supporting components. Firmware is software associated with hardware or platform startup. A virtual machine is a presented machine model capable of running its own guest operating system.
The host provides the VM’s execution environment. The guest runs inside the VM. A hypervisor implements or coordinates virtualization so guest execution and resources can be managed. These words identify relationships; they do not imply that every virtualization implementation is organized as the same software stack.
In our reference example, Linux’s Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) supplies virtualization facilities, QEMU supplies a machine/device model, and management software can coordinate VM definitions and lifecycle. The guest runs its own kernel. The QEMU system introduction explains its machine model and virtualization accelerators.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: What firmware does before Linux is usable
text:
What firmware does before Linux is usable
On a typical general-purpose machine, platform firmware initializes enough of the machine to select and start a boot path. The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) is used on many current systems; older PC environments can use a legacy Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) path. Other architectures and devices can have different startup arrangements.
For the first mental model, separate these jobs:








Stage
Responsibility
An example failure




Platform startup
Initialize the platform sufficiently to proceed
No usable console or memory initialization failure


Boot selection
Choose media or an executable boot entry
Wrong disk or installation image selected


Loader/kernel launch
Make the intended kernel and startup inputs available
Referenced kernel file is missing


Kernel initialization
Discover devices and establish core OS facilities
Required storage support is unavailable


Userspace startup
Reach the installed root and start its services
A required filesystem or service fails



Some arrangements combine stages. A firmware entry can launch a kernel-containing artifact directly. The table is a model of responsibilities, not a promise that every machine executes five separate programs.
An administrator can therefore ask a more precise question than “will it boot?”: which stage produced the last reliable evidence? A boot menu proves something different from a successful login.

Platform firmware and device firmware are related but distinct
A network card, SSD or other device can also have firmware of its own. Updating a platform’s firmware does not necessarily update every device. Updating the Linux kernel is another separate operation.
Record which component an update targets, its version, compatibility requirements, activation procedure and recovery route. For a VM, there can also be virtual platform firmware files supplied by the host. Updating a package in the guest does not automatically update those host-provided files.
Detailed firmware updates and Secure Boot policy come later. At this stage, identify ownership before planning a change.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: What a virtual machine actually receives
text:
What a virtual machine actually receives
A guest is presented with a set of resources and devices. These need not map one-to-one to physical parts.








Guest-visible resource
Possible host-side implementation
Operational consequence




Virtual CPU, or vCPU
A schedulable guest execution context
The host can delay its execution while serving other work


Guest physical memory
Memory backed by host resources under virtualization policy
Guest and host memory pressure need separate evidence


Virtual disk
Image file, logical volume, physical device or remote storage
Free space and failure can exist at several layers


Virtual NIC
A virtual device attached to a host networking path
Guest link state alone cannot prove external connectivity


Console
A virtual display or serial channel
It can remain available when guest networking fails


Firmware and boot variables
Virtual firmware and persistent per-guest state
Firmware mode and saved settings are part of the guest definition



The guest’s view is real and useful: its kernel really schedules processes and mounts filesystems. It is simply not the complete view of the infrastructure underneath it.

A disk image illustrates layered ownership
Imagine that guest lab-01 sees /dev/vda, and that its host uses an image file called lab-01.qcow2 as backing storage.
Inside the guest, an administrator might investigate partitions and filesystems on /dev/vda. On the host, another administrator might investigate the image, its backing chain and the filesystem storing it. The guest pathname does not name the host image file. The host file’s size does not directly describe the guest filesystem’s available space.
If the host filesystem becomes full, guest writes can fail even when the guest reports free filesystem space. If the guest filesystem becomes full, adding space to the host filesystem does not automatically enlarge the guest’s virtual disk, partition and filesystem.
Write the complete path when troubleshooting: application → guest filesystem → guest block device → virtual disk backend → host storage. Each boundary has its own state and evidence.


Virtual CPUs are not physical-core reservations
Giving a guest four vCPUs makes four guest CPU contexts available. It does not, by itself, reserve four physical cores exclusively for it. Host scheduling, placement, limits and competing workloads affect the resources delivered.
The guest may also see a synthetic CPU topology. Treat lscpu inside the guest as information about the presented environment; physical topology requires evidence from the host. Guest-visible instructions and features can be selected for compatibility or migration needs.
The advanced virtualization part will develop allocation and tuning policy. For now, avoid explaining poor performance solely by the number written in the VM settings dialog.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
text:
Virtualization, emulation and containers
These terms solve different problems:








Environment
Kernel used by the workload
What is presented or isolated?




Physical installation
The kernel booted on the physical system
Physical platform resources


Full VM
A guest kernel
A machine environment with guest CPUs, memory and devices


Container
The containing system’s kernel
Selected filesystem, process, network and resource views


Software machine emulation
A guest kernel
Machine behavior implemented in software, possibly for another CPU architecture



The rows can be combined. A container can run inside a VM. A VM can run on a host that is itself a VM. A virtual machine manager can use hardware-assisted execution or software CPU emulation where supported.
For the first lab, a full VM is valuable because you can practice the guest’s own kernel startup, bootloader, storage and recovery without changing your personal system. A container alone does not provide an independent guest kernel boot sequence.
This explains why a container image’s release file can name one distribution while uname -r reports the containing kernel’s release. Neither observation needs to be falsified to make the labels agree.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Worked example 1: establish what virtualization is detected
text:
Worked example 1: establish what virtualization is detected
If these tools are available in your current Linux environment, input:
systemd-detect-virt
systemd-detect-virt --vm
systemd-detect-virt --container
Possible outputs from separate commands in one environment:
kvm
kvm
none
The first query asks for a detected virtualization environment. The next two constrain detection to a VM or container. A detection command returns nonzero when it does not detect the requested type; that is a meaningful result, not necessarily a broken command. Do not run a simple collection script with unconditional exit-on-error and lose the rest of the inventory on this result.
The detection manual documents the identifiers and return behavior. Detection is bounded by available signals. A none result does not establish exclusive physical access, and a nested environment can have layers the current query does not fully describe.
Record the command’s exact result and its execution location: “inside lab-01,” “on its hypervisor,” or “inside this container.” Without that location, a correct observation can still lead to the wrong conclusion.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Worked example 2: inspect the guest-visible machine
text:
Worked example 2: inspect the guest-visible machine
Input:
uname -m
lscpu
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,MODEL,MOUNTPOINTS
ip -brief link show
Illustrative findings on a small VM:
Architecture:           x86_64
CPU(s):                2
Hypervisor vendor:     KVM

NAME   TYPE SIZE MODEL        MOUNTPOINTS
vda    disk  24G Virtio Block
├─vda1 part   1G              /boot/efi
└─vda2 part  23G              /

lo      UNKNOWN ...
enp1s0  UP      ...
The output combines selected fields from several commands. It is not a required installation layout or a promise that a tool will print these exact model strings. Your VM may use SCSI-style virtual disks, different network names and a separate /boot.
Why: each tool interrogates a different presented resource. Together they establish what the guest can see, not the physical machine’s total capacity. Use the lscpu documentation to distinguish presented CPU topology from host hardware.
Do not add or remove devices during this inventory. Device lifecycle operations belong to later controlled labs.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Worked example 3: observe the firmware interface available here
text:
Worked example 3: observe the firmware interface available here
Input:
if test -d /sys/firmware/efi; then
    printf 'An EFI firmware interface is visible here.\n'
else
    printf 'No EFI firmware interface is visible here.\n'
fi
Why: the result is an observation about the current kernel’s exported view. On an ordinary Linux host, the interface is useful evidence about EFI startup. In a container, restricted environment or specialized boot setup, an absent directory is insufficient to describe every underlying firmware layer.
Suppose you are inside a VM with UEFI firmware. Its interface belongs to the guest’s virtual platform. It says nothing by itself about whether the physical host booted with UEFI, or which physical firmware version the host uses.
The safe conclusion is narrow: this execution environment exposes this interface. Detailed boot verification later combines it with selected entries, artifacts and command-line evidence.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Worked example 4: understand the KVM boundary without creating a VM
text:
Worked example 4: understand the KVM boundary without creating a VM
On a Linux host intended to provide KVM-based virtualization, input:
if test -e /dev/kvm; then
    ls -l /dev/kvm
else
    printf '/dev/kvm is not present in this device view.\n'
fi
The device node is an interface through which a virtual machine monitor can use KVM. The KVM API documentation distinguishes operations for the subsystem, VMs, virtual CPUs and devices.
Presence alone does not prove that your user can open it, that the needed capabilities are available, or that the proposed VM configuration will work. Absence inside a guest does not mean that guest is malfunctioning: nested virtualization may not be exposed or required at all.
Do not change device permissions or firmware settings for this observation exercise. During lab construction, the chosen host’s prerequisites and authorized access are checked deliberately.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Keep configuration, execution and saved state separate
text:
Keep configuration, execution and saved state separate
A VM definition can describe its next boot while a running VM uses settings established when it started. Some virtualization tools support live changes; others require shutdown. Know whether an edit changed persistent configuration, active state or both.
The libvirt domain format is one example of a definition that describes CPUs, memory, firmware and devices. The existence of a field in that format is not proof that a running guest already uses the edited value.
Also distinguish three useful but different recovery objects:

An installation image supplies software for installing or booting a recovery environment.
A VM checkpoint or snapshot records selected VM state under a particular storage/management implementation.
An independent backup provides recoverable material outside the failure dependency being protected against.

A checkpoint that depends on the original image and host storage can be convenient for a lab experiment. It does not become independent merely because you gave it a reassuring name. Later backup chapters make independence and restore verification explicit.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
section: Break/fix: the guest returns to the installer after installation
text:
Break/fix: the guest returns to the installer after installation
Symptom. A VM’s installation completes. After restart, the installation screen appears again instead of the installed system.
First hypothesis. The VM may still be booting its attached installation image. That is a boot-selection question, not yet evidence that the installation failed.
Diagnosis path. Use the VM console. Check the selected boot device and whether installation media remains attached. Confirm the intended virtual disk exists and that the firmware mode is the one used for installation. A disk installed for one firmware arrangement may not boot under an arbitrarily changed arrangement.
Fix. Select the installed disk or detach the installer as appropriate for the VM manager. Preserve the firmware configuration unless evidence requires a change. Do not reinstall or repartition merely because the installer appeared.
Verification. Boot the installed system, identify its mounted root and confirm the expected installed files. Keep the console available. Only then proceed to ordinary guest administration.
Alternative result. If selecting the disk produces a loader error, the investigation has advanced to a different boundary. Record that new error; it changes the next question.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
text:
Practice: draw the ownership boundary
Choose a Linux environment you can inspect or use the illustrative VM above. Draw five boxes and fill them with facts or explicit unknowns:

The machine on which your current commands execute.
The kernel answering those commands.
Its firmware interface and presented devices.
The provider of its CPU, memory, disk and networking.
The console and recovery route available if networking stops.

For a VM, annotate at least one disk path twice: once as the guest sees it and once as the host or management system identifies its backing resource. If you lack host access, write “host backing unknown”; do not infer a host pathname from /dev/vda.
Then answer:







Statement
Supported conclusion




“The guest has two vCPUs.”
It has two presented execution contexts, with allocation details still to establish


“The guest’s disk has free space.”
This guest filesystem has reported capacity; host backing capacity remains a separate question


“Virtualization detection printed none.”
This query did not identify the requested virtualization type


“The guest has a console.”
There may be an access route independent of guest networking; test the actual management path



The exercise succeeds when you can locate an observation and a proposed change on the correct side of the host/guest boundary. No VM changes are required in this chapter.

title: Hardware, Firmware and Virtual Machines
text:
Recall card

Firmware, kernel startup and userspace startup are separate responsibilities.
A VM has its own guest kernel and presented hardware resources.
Host and guest inventories describe different administrative boundaries.
Guest vCPUs and disks do not imply exclusive physical resources.
Containers share their containing kernel; a full VM can practice independent boot.
Detection results are evidence with limits, especially in nested environments.
Configuration, active execution and saved/checkpoint state can differ.
Keep a console and an independently understood recovery route for experiments.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
text:
Map: four resources, one workload



CPU, RAM, storage and network devices cooperate under the Linux kernel.


Use this first model:








Resource
What it supplies
Typical question




CPU
Execution of instructions
Can the work get execution time when it needs it?


RAM
Fast working storage for active state
Can required data remain available without excessive reclaim or waiting?


Persistent storage
Durable space and read/write service
Is there capacity, and can the stack complete I/O in time?


Networking
Communication between endpoints
Can the intended path carry useful traffic with acceptable delay and loss?



Capacity, demand and delivered service are different quantities. A 24-GiB disk describes a size. Twenty milliseconds describes a delay. A thousand operations per second describes a rate. None is a substitute for the others.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: CPU: execution capacity and the need to wait
text:
CPU: execution capacity and the need to wait
A central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions. A CPU core is a hardware execution resource. A logical CPU is an execution context exposed to the operating system. A core can expose more than one logical CPU through simultaneous multithreading; a VM can expose virtual CPUs supplied by its host.
A thread is an execution stream that the scheduler can arrange to run. A multithreaded process can have several such streams. A runnable thread needs a turn on an eligible CPU. A thread waiting for a timer, disk result or remote reply may not be runnable at all.
The scheduler is the kernel mechanism that selects runnable work for execution. You do not need its implementation details yet. You do need to distinguish running, ready to run, and waiting for something else.

Two logical CPUs do not make every operation twice as fast
Suppose one request needs 20 milliseconds of CPU work and cannot execute that work in parallel. An otherwise idle second CPU does not halve that request’s CPU time. The extra context may allow another independent request to execute concurrently, subject to actual hardware and allocation.
For a simple capacity estimate, 100 requests per second at 20 milliseconds of CPU work each require:
100 requests/s × 0.020 CPU-seconds/request = 2 CPU-seconds/s
That already consumes the nominal two-CPU execution budget of a two-vCPU guest, before overhead and other processes. It is a starting model, not a benchmark result. Shared host capacity, affinity, quotas, cache behavior and simultaneous multithreading can change delivered work.
This is why adding a service without considering its workload can overload a host whose installation requirements looked small.


Worked example 1: inventory CPU topology
Input:
lscpu
lscpu -e=CPU,ONLINE,SOCKET,CORE,NODE
Illustrative table:
CPU ONLINE SOCKET CORE NODE
  0    yes      0    0    0
  1    yes      0    1    0
Here, two logical CPUs are online in the presented topology. A socket is a processor-package grouping in this view; a NUMA node groups memory/CPU locality information. On a VM these can be virtual arrangements. On another architecture some columns can be absent or unavailable. The lscpu manual describes the inventory sources and output options.
Record the environment with the table. Do not multiply a count twice because both a summary and a per-CPU table display the same resources. Also distinguish “online” from “available to this particular workload”: affinity, resource policy and host scheduling can impose additional limits.


Worked example 2: elapsed time is not CPU time
In Bash, input:
time sleep 1
One possible result:
real    0m1.002s
user    0m0.001s
sys     0m0.001s
Why: approximately one second passed, but the command spent very little time executing. It was mostly waiting for its timer. user accounts for execution in userspace; sys accounts for kernel execution charged to the command. Exact timing varies.
A slow network request or a blocked disk read can exhibit the same broad pattern: long elapsed time with little CPU execution. The correct question is then “what was it waiting for?” rather than “why is the CPU not busy?”


Load average is a demand clue
Input:
cat /proc/loadavg
The first three values describe load averages over different time windows. Linux includes runnable work and tasks in uninterruptible sleep in this accounting; it is not simply a percentage of CPU time. The load-average interface documents the fields.
A rising load with idle CPU can lead you toward waiting tasks and I/O. A low average does not prove a latency-sensitive request never waited. Time windows and sampling can hide short events. Treat this as a lead to investigate, not a verdict about the bottleneck.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: Memory: active state, cache and limits
text:
Memory: active state, cache and limits
Random-access memory (RAM) holds active program state, kernel data and caches. It is usually volatile: a power loss removes its contents. Persistent storage supplies durability through a different path.
A process normally accesses a virtual address space, an arrangement of addresses mapped and protected by the kernel and processor. The amount of address space described for a process is not automatically the amount of physical RAM it occupies. Some regions may not have been touched; some mappings refer to files; some pages are shared.
The kernel’s memory concepts overview introduces virtual memory, protection and controlled sharing. Our practical task is to ask which memory is actively needed, what can be reclaimed, and which limits govern the workload.

Used RAM can be useful cache
Linux can retain file data in RAM so later reads avoid slower storage. This page cache uses memory, but some cached pages can be reclaimed for other work. Dirty pages, which contain changes not yet written back as required, have different constraints from clean cache pages.
Therefore, “almost no completely unused RAM” does not by itself mean the machine is out of memory. Conversely, a large cache is not a guarantee that a particular workload will fit: active demand, writeback and configured limits matter.
Swap supplies backing storage for some memory that can be moved out of RAM. It is not equivalent to additional RAM with the same access cost. A little swap use alone does not prove current thrashing. Sustained pressure and the workload’s waiting behavior provide stronger evidence.


Worked example 3: read a small set of memory facts
Input:
free -h
awk '/^(MemTotal|MemFree|MemAvailable|Cached|SwapTotal|SwapFree):/ {print}' \
    /proc/meminfo
Illustrative selected fields:
MemTotal:        4096000 kB
MemFree:          180000 kB
MemAvailable:    2400000 kB
Cached:          2100000 kB
SwapTotal:       1048576 kB
SwapFree:        1048576 kB
Why: this machine has little entirely free RAM but a much larger estimate of memory available for new work. The estimate accounts for more than simply adding two fields. Do not independently sum overlapping accounting categories and present the sum as additional capacity.
MemTotal is usable memory reported by the kernel, so it need not match the exact number entered in a VM configuration or printed on a RAM module. The meminfo reference defines these fields, and free presents a summary of them.
In a container or other constrained workload, host-style totals may not express the limit governing that process. A cgroup is a kernel grouping used to account for and control resources; a workload can hit its group limit while the whole host still has available memory. The cgroup v2 documentation provides the underlying hierarchy and controller model. We will configure it in the resource-administration part.
What this snapshot cannot show: how long pressure lasted, which allocation failed, whether swap traffic is currently intense, or whether a service’s own internal limit was reached. Keep the scope of the measurement with its value.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: Storage: a device, a filesystem and a path are different objects
text:
Storage: a device, a filesystem and a path are different objects
A block device exposes addressable storage blocks. A partition describes a region of a partitioned device. A filesystem organizes data and metadata. A mount attaches a filesystem view at a location in the directory tree.
The relationships can be simple:
virtual disk → partition → ext4 filesystem → mounted at /
Or layered:
physical storage → encryption mapping → logical volume → filesystem → /srv/data
Those are examples, not universal ordering rules. An installation may use RAID, several devices, datasets, network storage or a different arrangement of layers. Always inspect the actual stack.
A pathname such as /srv/data/report.txt names an object through the current filesystem view. It does not tell you which physical disk supplies the data. A mount can change which filesystem serves that same pathname.

Worked example 4: connect a path to mounted storage
Input:
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
findmnt --target / -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
df -h /
df -i /
An illustrative device tree:
NAME   TYPE SIZE FSTYPE MOUNTPOINTS
vda    disk  24G
├─vda1 part   1G vfat   /boot/efi
└─vda2 part  23G ext4   /
lsblk describes visible block devices and related filesystem information. findmnt identifies the mounted filesystem serving a path. df asks about that filesystem’s space or inode accounting. An inode holds a filesystem object’s metadata; inode exhaustion can prevent new files even when byte capacity remains.
The lsblk manual explains why explicit output columns and many-to-many storage relationships matter. The findmnt manual distinguishes asking about a path from asking whether the path itself is a mountpoint.
If this is a container, / might be an overlay filesystem with backing storage outside your current view. Its source need not appear as a simple partition in lsblk. Record the visible relationship without inventing an unseen physical device.


File size and allocated storage can differ
A sparse file can represent a logical range without allocating blocks for every byte in that range. Compressed filesystems, snapshots and shared extents introduce other differences between logical size and physical allocation.
Optional experiment in an ordinary writable lab filesystem:
workdir=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'Experiment directory: %s\n' "$workdir"
truncate -s 64M "$workdir/sparse.bin"
ls -lh "$workdir/sparse.bin"
du -h "$workdir/sparse.bin"
On a filesystem supporting the expected sparse-file behavior, the listed logical size is 64 MiB while the allocated space reported by du can be much smaller. This does not mean that storing 64 MiB of actual new data is free. Allocation occurs as data is written, subject to the filesystem’s behavior. The du documentation distinguishes allocated storage from apparent size.
Cleanup only the file created for this experiment:
rm -- "$workdir/sparse.bin"
rmdir -- "$workdir"
No partitioning, formatting or privileged disk operation is needed. Avoid carrying a pathname from this example into unrelated cleanup commands.


Capacity and I/O performance are separate
A device can have ample space but poor response time. A fast device can still be full. Workloads also differ: many small random reads stress a different path from a large sequential write.
Useful dimensions include:

Latency: time for an operation or request to complete.
Throughput: amount of useful data or work completed per unit time.
IOPS: storage operations completed per second, meaningful alongside operation size and workload.
Queue depth: operations outstanding at a particular point in the stack.

A queue can absorb short bursts. Sustained arrival faster than completion causes waiting and eventually pressure or failure. More queueing is not automatically more performance, particularly when the user cares about response time.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: Networking: an interface is one part of a service path
text:
Networking: an interface is one part of a service path
A Linux network interface is an object through which traffic can enter or leave a network stack. It can correspond to a physical network interface controller (NIC), virtual NIC, bridge, tunnel or another software interface. The loopback interface supports communication within the local network stack.
An IP address belongs to an interface or networking context under configuration policy. A route selects a next path for a destination. A socket is an operating-system communication endpoint used by a program. A server listening on a socket still depends on routing, filtering and the remote client path.
Later chapters will configure these facilities and their services. For now, keep four questions distinct:

Is the interface present and usable at the link layer?
Is addressing and routing suitable for the intended destination?
Is the service listening at the address and port the client uses?
Does the end-to-end application operation succeed?


Worked example 5: inventory interfaces and listening endpoints
Input:
ip -brief link show
ip -brief address show
ip route show
ss -lnt
Illustrative observations:
lo      UNKNOWN ...
enp1s0  UP      ...

LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:*
Why: the interface exists and appears up, while the example TCP listener is bound to loopback. A remote client cannot reach that loopback-only listener by using the server’s LAN address. That is an endpoint configuration issue to investigate before blaming a physical cable.
ss -lnt lists listening TCP sockets with numeric addresses. Other transport types need the corresponding query. See the socket inspection manual. The output reflects the network namespace in which the command runs; another container or VM can have a different view.


Worked example 6: look at counters without overinterpreting them
First choose an interface name from your inventory. For an interface named enp1s0:
ip -s link show dev enp1s0
This is an example name; replace it if the host uses another. The counters describe traffic and selected errors or drops at this reporting interface. The kernel’s interface-statistics documentation explains the available reporting paths.
One cumulative counter cannot establish the current rate. If received bytes increase by 10,000,000 over 10 seconds, the observed average is:
10,000,000 bytes ÷ 10 seconds = 1,000,000 bytes/s = 8,000,000 bits/s
Use consistent units. A nominal 1-Gbit/s link corresponds to 125 million bytes per second before protocol and implementation overhead. It is not 1 gigabyte per second, and it does not guarantee that rate for an application.
Counter interpretation also needs timing, reset/wrap awareness and the relevant interface. Traffic can pass through several virtual interfaces; summing every counter along the same path can count the same work repeatedly.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: Follow a request through all four resources
text:
Follow a request through all four resources



A request can alternate between CPU execution and waiting on other resources.


Imagine a small catalog service returning a file-backed record:

Traffic reaches the host’s network stack and the appropriate socket.
The service becomes runnable and receives CPU time.
It parses the request and accesses in-memory state.
It needs record data. A cached result may be available in RAM; otherwise the path can require storage I/O.
While waiting for necessary I/O, the thread need not consume CPU execution time.
The service becomes runnable again, constructs its response and submits output.
Networking carries the result toward the client.

The exact implementation might be asynchronous or use several threads, but the resource questions remain. End-to-end delay can include several waits. A snapshot showing idle CPU cannot identify which wait occurred.
For an invented request, suppose total elapsed time is 100 milliseconds, with 8 milliseconds of CPU execution. There are approximately 92 milliseconds left to explain in that accounting model. Possible contributors include scheduling delay, storage, locks, a connection pool or a remote dependency. The missing time is a question, not evidence for whichever subsystem you happen to know best.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: Break/fix: “the VM has resources, but the service is slow”
text:
Break/fix: “the VM has resources, but the service is slow”
Symptom. A two-vCPU VM has free disk capacity and some available memory. Requests still slow down badly during a scheduled backup.
Initial claim to reject. “There is unused CPU, so the guest must need a kernel tuning change.” The evidence does not support that conclusion.
Investigation. Compare a baseline period and the backup period. Record request latency and rate, CPU execution, memory pressure, storage completion behavior, interface traffic and the backup schedule. Keep guest and host evidence separate. The backup may compete for guest I/O, host storage, network capacity or another shared dependency.
Bounded action. If evidence identifies backup contention, change its schedule or resource policy in the lab and repeat the same workload. If the cause is elsewhere, the prediction should fail and the hypothesis should change. Do not disable backups permanently as a performance fix.
Success criterion. The service meets its measured objective and the backup still completes within its required window. A lower utilization percentage alone is not the goal.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
section: Practice: inventory and explain before tuning
text:
Practice: inventory and explain before tuning
Build a small worksheet from the examples:









Resource
Inventory
Current observation
What remains unknown?




CPU
Online logical CPUs and topology
Load and a small timing observation
Workload eligibility, quotas and host contention


Memory
Usable RAM and swap
Available estimate and current state
Demand over time and workload-specific limits


Storage
Device → filesystem → mount
Byte/inode capacity
Latency, backing layers and failure behavior


Network
Interfaces, addresses and routes
Listener bindings and counters
Remote path and application success



Do not change configuration to make your worksheet match the illustrative output. Different values and device names are expected. If you are reading before building the VM, complete the worksheet from the examples and mark the values as illustrative, then repeat on the lab host later.
Finally, explain these cases in a sentence each:

A command took one second but used almost no CPU. It can spend elapsed time waiting.
Free memory is small but available memory is much larger. Some current uses can potentially be reclaimed; inspect pressure and limits before declaring exhaustion.
lsblk shows 24 GiB but a filesystem is smaller. Devices, partitions and filesystem capacity are different layers.
The interface is up but a service listens only on loopback. Link availability does not establish the desired remote endpoint.
A guest has free space but its host storage is full. The write path contains several independent capacity boundaries.

The exercise is complete when each conclusion identifies both its evidence and its limits. Clean up the optional sparse-file experiment if you ran it; all other commands in this chapter inspect state.

title: CPU, Memory, Storage and Network Resources
text:
Recall card

Separate capacity, utilization, pressure, latency and throughput.
CPU execution, runnable demand and waiting are different states.
Virtual CPU counts and topology describe the presented environment.
Available memory, caches and workload limits need separate interpretation.
A device, filesystem, mount and pathname describe different storage objects.
Interface state, routes, listeners and client success are separate networking observations.
A request crosses resources and can spend most of its time waiting.
Measure a baseline, form a testable hypothesis, and verify an operational result.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
text:
One tree, several sources
An absolute pathname begins at /, the root of the pathname tree. A relative pathname is interpreted from a process’s current working directory. /etc/hosts and etc/hosts can therefore identify different objects. The account called root, its home directory /root, and the root directory / are three separate concepts.
A directory associates names with filesystem objects. A filesystem supplies the rules and structures used to represent files, directories and their metadata. Some filesystems store data on disks. Others expose information maintained by the kernel or keep their contents in memory.
A mount attaches a filesystem, or another view of existing filesystem content, at a location in the visible tree. That location is the mount point. Walking from / into /home does not tell you whether you crossed into a separate filesystem. The directory names alone cannot answer that question.



A pathname tree joins storage, volatile state and kernel interfaces.


Imagine a machine with one filesystem for / and another mounted at /srv/archive. Before the second filesystem is mounted, /srv/archive is an ordinary directory in the root filesystem. Once mounted, looking inside that path shows the mounted filesystem’s contents. Existing files in the underlying directory are hidden by the mount; mounting does not automatically copy or delete them.
This explains a common storage incident. A backup job writes into /srv/archive while its intended storage is absent. The files consume space on /. When the expected storage is mounted later, those files seem to vanish. The correct investigation starts with the mount, not with a claim that the backup application deleted data. Later storage chapters develop guarded mounts and recovery procedures; do not unmount a working service’s storage just to explore this behavior.

Worked example: identify the backing filesystem
Run:
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
findmnt --target /etc --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
findmnt --target /run --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
findmnt --target /proc --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
Illustrative results for the last two commands:
TARGET SOURCE FSTYPE
/run   tmpfs  tmpfs

TARGET SOURCE FSTYPE
/proc  proc   proc
--target locates the filesystem containing the requested path. It also works when that path is not itself a mount point. A result with TARGET equal to / for /etc means that /etc is on the root mount in this view. It does not mean /etc is missing. The findmnt manual documents the distinction between a containing target and an exact mount point.
tmpfs is memory-backed storage that can use swap; it is not a promise that every byte stays in physical RAM. proc exposes process and kernel information. Reading /proc/meminfo retrieves a kernel-generated view rather than a report saved by someone into a disk file.
These results belong to the environment where you ran the command. A container can see a different mount arrangement from its host. A service can also run with a restricted filesystem view. For now, record whether you inspected the VM, its host, or a container; later isolation chapters explain why those views differ.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
text:
Directories express responsibility
The following map is a starting guide to conventional Linux layouts. An installed application may use additional paths, and distribution policy can refine them.








Path
Usual responsibility
Question to ask




/usr
Installed system programs, libraries and shared resources
Which package or image supplies this?


/etc
Host configuration
Who owns the intended setting?


/var/lib
Persistent application and service state
How is this backed up and restored?


/var/log
Logs stored as files
What is the retention policy?


/var/cache
Data intended to be reconstructible
Can this application actually regenerate it?


/run
State used during the current boot
Which process recreates it?


/tmp
Temporary working files
When can cleanup remove them?


/home
Ordinary users’ home directories
Is this local, mounted or managed elsewhere?


/dev
Device interfaces
What kernel device does this represent?


/proc, /sys
Kernel-maintained interfaces
Am I reading information or changing a kernel setting?


/boot
Boot-related artifacts
Which boot tooling owns these files?



The Linux filesystem hierarchy specification describes these roles in more detail. Use the table to choose an investigation, not as permission to remove an unfamiliar directory.
For example, a database beneath /var/lib is not disposable merely because the path begins with var. “Variable” describes data that changes, not data you can discard. Similarly, a cache may be reconstructible in principle but expensive or impossible to rebuild while its upstream source is unavailable.
On merged-/usr installations, names such as /bin can be symbolic links into /usr. A symbolic link is a filesystem object that points to another pathname. Inspect the machine instead of assuming two visible names imply two independent copies:
ls -ld /bin /sbin /lib
readlink -f /bin
An illustrative result for the second command is /usr/bin. That is pathname resolution, not evidence that a program was moved while you were looking. Package ownership, links and compatibility names matter when interpreting installation instructions.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
section: Persistence is a property to verify
text:
Persistence is a property to verify
Persistent state is intended to survive the relevant lifecycle boundary, often a reboot. Runtime state describes a live instance: processes, open connections, current locks and similar working information. Some runtime information is represented by files, but the presence of a file does not make it durable.
Consider a fictional service called catalog:








Object
Example
Intended lifecycle




Program
/usr/bin/catalogd
Replaced by software installation or upgrade


Configuration
/etc/catalog/catalog.conf
Retained until an authorized configuration change


Business data
/var/lib/catalog/items.db
Preserved across process restarts and host reboots


Runtime socket
/run/catalog/control.sock
Created for a live service instance


Working cache
/var/cache/catalog/
Reconstructed according to application behavior



These are explanatory paths, not a package to install. A socket is an endpoint through which processes can communicate; its pathname is not the database it serves.
Reboot is only one boundary. A file can survive a guest reboot yet disappear when that VM is deleted. A file in a container’s writable layer can survive a process restart but disappear when the container is replaced. A VM snapshot can return storage to an earlier state without providing an independent backup. Always complete the sentence: “This survives which event?”
Do not use /tmp or /run for the only copy of important data. Cleanup schedules and mount choices vary. Conversely, do not assume everything under /var/log is recorded forever: retention, rotation, storage limits and logging configuration determine what remains available.
Persistence also does not guarantee durability at every instant. A successful application write can still be buffered before reaching persistent storage. Databases coordinate writes and recovery using their own mechanisms. Backup and storage chapters will separate application consistency, filesystem behavior and device durability; at this stage, recognize that copying a live database file is not automatically a valid backup.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
section: Configuration has an owner and an activation path
text:
Configuration has an owner and an activation path
A configuration source expresses intended behavior. Effective configuration is what the running component actually uses. Between them may sit include files, defaults, generators, environment variables, command-line arguments and activation steps.
Use four questions whenever you find a promising file:

Is it an input owned by an administrator, or an output generated by another tool?
What other sources can override or supplement it?
How does the application validate the combined configuration?
When does the running application read it?

Suppose catalog.conf specifies listen_port=8080, but the running process still listens on its old port. Several explanations remain possible: the process has not reread the file, it uses a different file, an override takes precedence, or the edit failed validation. Repeatedly editing the same line does not distinguish these hypotheses.
The useful evidence chain is:
intended setting → authoritative input → validation
                 → activation → observation of live behavior
A reload asks a component to reread supported settings without a full stop/start. A restart replaces its running instance. Neither is a generic guarantee that every intended change becomes effective. Some settings require restart, and some applications cannot reload at all. Read that application’s instructions before choosing an operation.
Generated files deserve special attention. If a network tool writes a runtime resolver file, manually editing that output may appear to work and then be overwritten. The durable fix belongs in the tool’s input configuration. The ownership question prevents a cycle of repeatedly “repairing” the generated result.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
section: Worked experiment: a file changes before its consumer does
text:
Worked experiment: a file changes before its consumer does
This experiment models an application that reads a setting once. It does not edit system configuration. Run the commands in one Bash terminal:
state_lab_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/boring-state.XXXXXX")
printf 'blue\n' > "$state_lab_dir/setting"
read -r loaded_setting < "$state_lab_dir/setting"
printf 'green\n' > "$state_lab_dir/setting"
printf 'Loaded value: %s\n' "$loaded_setting"
printf 'File value: '
cat "$state_lab_dir/setting"
Expected result:
Loaded value: blue
File value: green
mktemp -d creates a uniquely named directory; the variable holds its actual path. read copies one line into the shell’s memory. Replacing the file does not change that already loaded variable. This deliberately small model reproduces the distinction between stored configuration and a running consumer’s state without touching a service.
Now simulate rereading:
read -r loaded_setting < "$state_lab_dir/setting"
printf 'Loaded after reread: %s\n' "$loaded_setting"
The result should be green. This is not an implementation of a service reload protocol. It illustrates why an activation step exists at all.
Clean up only the file and directory created above:
rm -- "$state_lab_dir/setting"
rmdir -- "$state_lab_dir"
unset state_lab_dir loaded_setting
If you closed the terminal, do not guess the variable’s old value. Locate your named experiment directory and inspect it before removing anything.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
section: Diagnosis: three failures that look like missing files
text:
Diagnosis: three failures that look like missing files

The directory exists, but the data is wrong
A path can exist on the wrong filesystem. Inspect its backing mount and compare it with the expected storage before creating more data there. Preserve observations of the path, mount source and service error. Creating an empty replacement database can make recovery harder by mixing new state with the incident.


The data returns after reboot, but access fails
The file may be persistent while the runtime directory or socket through which a client reaches it has not been recreated. Investigate the service that owns that runtime object. Copying yesterday’s socket pathname from a backup does not recreate a listening process.


The administrator can read it, but the service cannot
The service may run under a different identity or see a restricted filesystem tree. “It exists in my shell” establishes only one observer’s view. Capture the service identity and its error before changing permissions. Making a file readable by everyone can expose data while leaving the real view or path problem unresolved.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
text:
Practice: classify before changing
On your lab VM, select /etc/hosts, /var/lib, /run, /proc/meminfo and your home directory. For each, record the intended role, the backing filesystem reported by findmnt, the likely owner, and the lifecycle event that could remove its contents. You do not need to read other users’ files or list service secrets.
Then answer these scenarios:

A service stores its only customer records in /run. What failure should you expect after reboot?
A mounted archive is absent and a job writes to the mount-point directory. Which filesystem receives the writes?
A file contains the new value but the running application behaves as before. What evidence is missing?

Success means you can explain the answers in terms of lifecycle, mount attachment and activation. The first design loses its intended persistence; the second uses the containing filesystem; the third needs the actual configuration sources and live consumer state checked.

title: System Paths, Configuration and State
text:
Recall card

A pathname identifies an object through a visible tree; it does not identify the backing storage by itself.
A mount can hide a directory’s previous contents without deleting them.
Classify data by responsibility and lifecycle before editing, deleting or backing it up.
Persistent across reboot does not mean protected from replacement, corruption or loss.
A configuration change is complete only after validation, activation and a behavior check.
Identify who generates a file before treating it as the authoritative input.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
section: Program, process, service: three different objects
text:
Program, process, service: three different objects
A program is executable code. Its file can exist while no instance of it is running. A process is a running instance with an identity, execution state, memory and references to resources such as open files. Multiple processes can execute the same program. A program can also create workers, so one application’s activity need not fit into one process.
A process identifier, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. A namespace is a mechanism that gives a group of processes a particular view of a resource; for this chapter, the practical consequence is that a container’s process numbering may differ from the host’s. A parent PID, or PPID, identifies the parent in that view. Parentage helps explain how work was started, but it is not a complete inventory of responsibility.
A service is an operational function managed across a lifecycle: start, readiness, ongoing work, failure and stop. A service manager can start the program, track its processes, collect exit results and apply a restart policy. Some services perform a short task and exit. Others keep several worker processes running.



Process ancestry, service ownership and login sessions answer different questions.


The system manager is the system-wide manager. On the reference VM, systemd runs as PID 1. A user manager can separately manage services for an individual user. The fact that both are controlled with systemctl does not make them the same manager: systemctl --user selects the user manager instead of the system manager.
A container or a minimal recovery environment may have another program at PID 1. If systemctl reports that systemd is not running as the system manager, first identify where you are. Installing more service files does not change the identity of the already running PID 1.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
section: Inspect a process without guessing from its name
text:
Inspect a process without guessing from its name
Start with a small, explicit view:
ps -p 1 -o pid,ppid,user,stat,comm
ps -p "$$" -o pid,ppid,user,stat,etime,args
In Bash, $$ expands to the shell’s PID. ps selects that process and displays the requested columns. ETIME is elapsed time since process start. ARGS presents command arguments, while COMM is a shorter command-name view. Neither name alone proves which package supplied the executable or what the process is doing.
An illustrative shell row is:
    PID    PPID USER     STAT     ELAPSED COMMAND
   2410    2409 learner  Ss         08:14 -bash
Treat PIDs and times in examples as placeholders for observations, never as values to paste into a later termination command. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number written in an old incident note might identify unrelated work now.
The first letter of STAT describes a scheduling or lifecycle state. Common letters are R for running or runnable, S for interruptible sleep, D for uninterruptible sleep, T for stopped and Z for a zombie. Additional letters describe other properties; the lowercase s above indicates a session leader. A zombie has exited but still has exit information awaiting collection by its parent. It is not doing useful computation that can be stopped again. The ps manual defines the fields and state codes.
Most healthy idle processes spend time sleeping. A sleeping process is not necessarily broken; it may be waiting for a timer or request. Conversely, a runnable process is not proof that useful work is completing. Combine state with elapsed behavior and the task the process is meant to perform.
Command arguments can contain sensitive information. Do not paste an unrestricted process listing into a public bug report without reviewing it. For a first inventory, select the processes and columns that answer your question.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
section: Worked experiment: create, observe and finish one process
text:
Worked experiment: create, observe and finish one process
Run this in one interactive Bash terminal. It creates only a short-lived timer process:
sleep 300 &
observed_pid=$!
printf 'Child PID: %s\n' "$observed_pid"
ps -p "$observed_pid" -o pid,ppid,user,stat,etime,args
jobs -l
& asks the shell to run the command in the background. $! is the PID of its most recently started background job. jobs shows work tracked by this shell, not every process on the host.
A typical ps row looks like:
    PID    PPID USER     STAT     ELAPSED COMMAND
   2581    2410 learner  S          00:03 sleep 300
The parent is the shell observed earlier. The process is sleeping because its job is to wait for a timer. It is still a real process with an owner and lifecycle.
Finish the experiment promptly, while this terminal and job are still present:
kill -TERM "$observed_pid"
wait "$observed_pid"
printf 'Wait status: %s\n' "$?"
unset observed_pid
TERM requests termination. In this example, Bash commonly reports status 143, meaning termination by signal 15. If the timer had already finished, the result differs; do not interpret a missing process as a failure to create it. The shell’s wait collects the child’s completion result. This exercise is for an interactive shell without a strict set -e policy, which could stop a script at a nonzero wait result.
Do not repeat the kill command later using a copied PID. Also do not generalize the example into killing any process whose name looks similar. For a managed service, operate on the service through its manager; a policy may otherwise start a replacement process immediately.
A signal is a notification delivered to a process. Some signals can be handled by the application; SIGKILL cannot. Immediate forced termination gives an application no opportunity to finish its own shutdown work. The right response to a stuck service begins with evidence and its documented lifecycle, not an automatic escalation to force.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
section: Services give processes an operational boundary
text:
Services give processes an operational boundary
Systemd represents managed objects using units. A .service unit describes a service, but units also describe sockets, timers, mounts and other objects. This is why a list of all units is not just a list of daemons. The systemd.unit reference describes their types and common configuration.
Inspect the manager without changing its state:
systemctl list-units --type=service --all --no-pager
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --no-pager
systemctl --failed --no-pager
The first view concerns service units loaded in the manager. The second concerns installed unit files and their enablement state. A machine can have many installed definitions that are not currently running. --failed narrows attention to recorded failed units; it is not a complete application-health test.
On the reference VM, inspect the journal service:
systemctl status systemd-journald.service --no-pager
systemctl show systemd-journald.service \
  -p LoadState -p ActiveState -p SubState -p MainPID -p FragmentPath
status is a human-oriented summary. show selects named properties. FragmentPath identifies the unit’s main definition file; it is not necessarily the whole configuration because additional settings may exist. A denied or partial log view can reflect your account’s access rights.
For these inspection commands and the loaded-versus-installed distinction, consult the systemctl manual. This chapter uses long-established operations; the installed manual remains the reference for your specific version.

Running now and starting later are independent questions
Active state concerns the current lifecycle. Enablement concerns installation of activation relationships, commonly used to arrange startup through a target. A target groups related units or marks a system state. An enabled service is not automatically healthy, and a disabled service is not automatically stopped.
A service might have been started manually or activated by a dependency. A socket can trigger service activation when traffic arrives. A timer can activate work on a schedule. Units marked static generally lack installation instructions for direct enablement but can still be activated by other units.
Keep two columns in your notes: “what it is doing now” and “how it is intended to be activated.” Conflating them leads to repairs that work until reboot, or changes that affect future boots while leaving today’s incident untouched.


Active does not always mean a process is still running
An active (running) service usually has continuing work. An active (exited) service can represent a completed setup action whose unit remains active. For example, a one-shot task may establish state and then exit; RemainAfterExit=yes allows its unit to retain an active state after successful completion. There may then be no main process to inspect. Service type and configuration explain the state, as described in systemd.service.
The main PID is useful but not the entire workload. A service can have workers. Systemd uses control groups, or cgroups, to group processes for management and resource accounting. Parent ancestry and cgroup membership are different relationships: one explains creation, the other helps express management membership. Resource-control chapters develop those mechanisms later.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
section: A session is a user’s access context
text:
A session is a user’s access context
A login session represents an authenticated interaction such as a local console login, graphical login or remote login. It can contain several processes. The login session is not identical to the shell, and a shell is not required to be an interactive login shell.
On a VM with systemd-logind, use:
loginctl list-sessions
loginctl session-status
The first command lists sessions known to the login manager. With no ID, the second asks about the caller’s session. Some environments, including terminals launched outside a registered login session, have no suitable session to report. That is a limitation of the context, not evidence that your shell has no process. See the loginctl manual.
A shell job, a login session and a user service have different owners of their lifecycle. Closing a terminal can affect jobs through hangup handling and session policy. A user service can have another lifecycle, with details depending on the user manager and system policy. Merely adding & is not a reliable way to create an unattended server that must survive logout and reboot.
