Suppose an administrator starts a development server from an SSH terminal. It responds during the demonstration but disappears after logout. Before looking for a network fault, ask who was responsible for maintaining that process. Was it a shell job, a user service or a system service? The permanent design needs an explicit lifecycle, logging and restart behavior. Later service chapters build that design rather than relying on a terminal remaining connected.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
section: Observe from the client back toward the process
text:
Observe from the client back toward the process
For a fictional inventory service, the useful chain is:
package present → unit definition present → process started
                → application ready → endpoint reachable
                → intended operation succeeds
Each arrow requires evidence. The chain is a diagnostic model, not a guarantee that every service has a network endpoint. A scheduled backup job, for example, is verified by its completion result and a usable restore rather than by a listening port.
Consider three reports:








Report
What it establishes
Next question




“The package is installed.”
Software files were installed
What starts the intended function?


“The service is active.”
The manager reports an active unit
What does active mean for this unit type?


“A TCP connection succeeds.”
A network endpoint accepted a connection
Can an authorized client complete the real operation?



A process can remain alive while its database is unavailable. A network path can work while authentication fails. A manager’s restart policy can replace a crashing process often enough that one snapshot catches it running. Repeated observations, logs and a meaningful client operation make these cases distinguishable.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
text:
First failure investigation
When a service does not behave as expected, write the symptom as an operation: “the local client cannot obtain the inventory list,” rather than “Linux is broken.” Then identify the service and record the time and environment.
For the journal service used above, a bounded log inspection is:
journalctl -b -u systemd-journald.service -n 30 --no-pager
-b selects the current boot, -u selects a unit and -n 30 limits the tail. Missing records may reflect access, retention or the absence of messages. Do not treat an empty log view as proof of successful operation.
For another service, substitute its verified unit name. Capture the manager state, error and recent relevant records before restarting. A restart can restore service while discarding evidence about the original failure. After an authorized repair, repeat the client operation that originally failed; a new PID alone is insufficient.
Do not stop the journal service, login manager or remote-access service as a beginner exercise. The timer experiment already provides a process lifecycle you can observe safely. Later disposable-VM labs introduce deliberately broken services with defined recovery steps.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
text:
Practice: build an evidence table
Record your shell PID, its parent, the owner and one observed state. Run the timer exercise and explain why its state is consistent with its purpose. Then select one service already present on your VM and record its active state, enablement state, main PID if any, and the useful operation it provides.
Answer these questions:

If a PID changes after a service failure, does that prove the application recovered?
Can a disabled unit still be active?
Can a healthy service have no continuing process?
Does jobs show work started by another user’s shell?

The answers are no, yes, yes and no. Explain the reason for each: process identity differs from behavior; activation has multiple paths; completed one-shot work can retain active state; job control belongs to a particular shell.

title: Processes, Services and Sessions
text:
Recall card

Program files, process instances and managed services are different objects.
A PID is temporary evidence, not a permanent identity.
Process ancestry, service membership and login sessions describe different relationships.
Check both current activity and intended activation.
Interpret service state using the unit’s purpose and lifecycle.
Verify the useful operation after a repair, not just the existence of a process.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: A distribution is an integration and maintenance boundary
text:
A distribution is an integration and maintenance boundary
A distribution combines the kernel, libraries, system tools and applications into an installable system. Its maintainers decide how software is built, which defaults are supplied, how dependencies fit together, how updates are delivered and which releases remain supported.
The upstream project develops a component such as a web server. The distribution package integrates a particular build into an operating-system release. The installed system adds local configuration and workload data. A cloud image or appliance vendor may add another layer. Each layer can make decisions that affect your machine.



Software passes through several owners before it becomes a running service.


Suppose an upstream guide places a server’s example configuration in /usr/local/etc, while your package reads /etc/example. Neither path should be chosen by familiarity alone. Inspect the installed package and service. Your responsibility is to find the configuration actually used by this instance.
The same distinction applies to service names, optional modules and startup defaults. A distribution may split software into several packages or ship a separate integration unit. Knowing the upstream product name is useful; it is not a complete installation inventory.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: Release models create different change schedules
text:
Release models create different change schedules
A release is a named, coordinated version of a distribution. A fixed-release model groups substantial changes into releases, with maintenance updates during each release’s supported life. A rolling-release model delivers an evolving collection of packages without requiring the same kind of major-version transition.
Neither model eliminates operational work. Fixed releases require planned release upgrades and continued maintenance between them. Rolling systems require regular attention to package transitions and compatibility. Both need backups, recovery access and testing appropriate to the workload.
Long-term support, or LTS, describes a maintenance commitment for a particular product and scope. It does not mean every program installed on the machine receives identical coverage. A separately installed vendor application, container image or manually built tool can have its own lifecycle.
Ubuntu’s official release-cycle page distinguishes LTS, interim releases and support offerings. The book uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its reference release. For deployment decisions, check the current coverage of the exact release and packages rather than copying a date from a tutorial. Record the check date alongside the result, since an operational plan must remain meaningful after time passes.
A practical support record includes:







Field
Why it matters




Distribution and release
Identifies the base maintenance stream


Architecture
Determines available builds and installation media


Package and source
Identifies who supplied the software


Coverage and conditions
Establishes which updates are actually available


Maintenance deadline
Gives a date by which action must be planned


Application compatibility
Identifies what needs testing before an upgrade


Recovery route
Explains how service will be restored if a change fails



“Supported operating system” is a useful starting statement, but the record must become specific enough to guide action. Conversely, an unsupported component does not become supported merely because it runs on an LTS host.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: Worked example: separate distribution identity from kernel identity
text:
Worked example: separate distribution identity from kernel identity
On the machine being investigated, run:
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
uname -m
/etc/os-release describes the operating-system identity. uname -r reports the running kernel release, and uname -m reports the machine architecture as exposed to the running environment.
Fields you may see include ID, VERSION_ID, PRETTY_NAME and ID_LIKE. Use ID and VERSION_ID to record the distribution and version; PRETTY_NAME is intended for display. ID_LIKE can suggest relationships but is not a guarantee that instructions for another distribution are compatible. The os-release specification defines these fields and identifies /etc/os-release as the preferred location, with /usr/lib/os-release as fallback.
Do not edit release-identification fields to make an installer accept the host. That changes the reported identity without providing the software compatibility the installer expected.
A container offers an instructive case: its distribution identity can describe the container’s userspace, while uname reports the kernel it shares with the host. A VM normally has its own guest kernel. Two identity commands can therefore report different layers without either being wrong.
Likewise, installing a kernel package does not by itself change the kernel already running. An update inventory and a runtime inventory answer different questions. Later maintenance chapters explain activation and reboot planning; here, preserve both observations rather than forcing them into one “Linux version” field.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
text:
Packages, repositories and origins
A package is a managed software artifact with metadata such as name, version, architecture and dependencies. A repository publishes packages and metadata for tools that select and retrieve them. A repository is a software supply relationship, not merely a convenient download address.
On Ubuntu and Debian, dpkg tracks installed Debian packages, while APT uses available-package metadata and dependency rules to plan operations. Ubuntu’s package-management documentation explains the responsibilities and workflows. Other distributions use different tools; the questions about installed versions and origin remain the same.
A mirror provides a delivery location for repository content. Its proximity does not by itself establish trust. Package-management trust involves the authenticated metadata, configured authorities and repository policy. A third-party source can introduce packages and dependency choices outside the base distribution’s maintenance process. Adding one is an administrative decision that needs an owner and removal plan.
This chapter does not ask you to add a repository. Before considering one, ask: What software is missing? Who signs and maintains this source? Which distribution releases and architectures are covered? Which installed packages could it replace? How will updates and retirement work? A copied command containing a signing key and a repository URL does not answer those questions.

Installed version and candidate version
On the reference VM, inspect the APT package itself:
dpkg-query -W -f='${binary:Package}\t${Version}\t${Architecture}\n' apt
apt-cache policy apt
The first command asks the installed-package database for selected fields. Single quotes keep the shell from expanding the field expressions before dpkg-query reads them. The dpkg-query manual defines the query format.
apt-cache policy distinguishes the installed version from the candidate selected using current local metadata and policy. Its version table helps identify the available origins and priorities. The candidate is not necessarily a newer version and is not necessarily the highest version published anywhere. Repository selection and policy constrain what this host considers.
The apt-cache manual also explains an important limitation: metadata is cached locally and can be stale. These inspection commands do not refresh it. If the cache is old or absent, label that limitation in the inventory rather than concluding that no updates exist.
For a beginner’s observation sheet, record the installed value, candidate value and listed source. If they differ, explain the difference before proposing an upgrade. If the candidate is absent, investigate metadata and source configuration; do not immediately substitute a package from an unrelated release.


Which package owns a file?
A pathname can be supplied by a package, a local installation, an application at runtime or a configuration generator. On the reference VM, inspect a known packaged file:
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/apt
An expected result is a package ownership record naming apt. This establishes the package database’s ownership claim for that path. It does not verify that the current file’s contents are unchanged, and it does not identify every possible manually installed program on the machine.
This distinction is useful when a guide says to overwrite an executable or edit a vendor-supplied file. First identify ownership. A local replacement may be overwritten by an upgrade, while a package-managed file may have a supported override mechanism that survives updates. Later chapters cover verification and configuration-file handling in detail.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: Versions are evidence, not complete security verdicts
text:
Versions are evidence, not complete security verdicts
A distribution can apply a selected correction to an older software series without adopting all features of a newer upstream release. This is called backporting. Consequently, comparing only the upstream version prefix can misclassify a distribution package. Debian’s security FAQ explains why its security maintenance uses backported fixes and why version-only checks can be misleading.
The opposite shortcut is also wrong: do not assume that an old-looking package is patched merely because backports exist. Identify the advisory, distribution release and exact package revision. Then compare the installed package with the advisory’s affected and fixed builds.
For an Ubuntu-managed component, Ubuntu Security Notices are an authoritative place to begin that lookup. A component installed from another vendor needs that vendor’s advisory path. Container images require attention to the packages inside the image as well as the host.
A useful security investigation record is:
Reported issue:
Affected component and source:
Distribution release and architecture:
Installed package revision:
Applicable vendor advisory:
Fixed revision or other required action:
Runtime activation needed:
Verification result and time:
This record separates discovery, installation and activation. Even after a corrected library is installed, a long-running process may still use previously mapped code until it is restarted. The appropriate action depends on the component; checking only the package database can leave the runtime question unanswered.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: Find documentation that belongs to the installed system
text:
Find documentation that belongs to the installed system
Use several kinds of evidence together:








Source
Best use
Limitation




Installed manual and --help
Syntax and features shipped with installed tools
Manuals may be absent or incomplete


Distribution documentation
Packaging, integration and supported workflows
Check release applicability


Upstream manual for the matching version
Component behavior and configuration semantics
Distribution defaults or patches can differ


Release notes and advisories
Changes, known issues and required actions
Match the affected product and build


Local change records
What administrators intentionally changed
Records can be incomplete or stale



For example, man 1 ps asks for the user-command manual named ps. Manual section numbers distinguish categories: section 1 commonly describes commands, section 5 file formats, and section 8 administration tools. man -k searches manual descriptions, provided a suitable local index is available. The man manual documents lookup and section selection.
On the reference VM, try:
man 1 ps
man 5 os-release
man 8 apt-cache
Press q to leave the usual manual pager. If man or the pages are absent on a minimal image, use the distribution’s versioned manual site and record that you used an external source. Missing local documentation is not a reason to run an unrelated installer from a search result.
Upstream pages marked “latest” can describe options added after your installed release. Before adopting an unfamiliar option, inspect the installed version, its local manual and the option’s version notes. A failed option does not necessarily indicate a damaged installation; it may be a feature mismatch.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: Worked investigation: a guide does not match the machine
text:
Worked investigation: a guide does not match the machine
Suppose a guide instructs you to enable a new configuration directive, but the service’s validator reports “unknown directive.” A productive investigation proceeds as follows:

Identify the actual executable and service instance that produced the error.
Record its package, installed revision and source.
Check the installed manual for the directive and its valid location.
Check the guide’s target version and distribution assumptions.
Decide whether an older supported equivalent meets the requirement, or whether a planned upgrade is necessary.

Do not remove validation just to make startup proceed. Do not install a foreign release’s library to satisfy one command without evaluating the rest of the system. The service may depend on an integrated collection of libraries and plugins. A narrow documentation mismatch can become a broad recovery incident if treated as a package-download problem.
This is also where local records matter. If the executable came from /usr/local and the unit was written locally, distribution instructions may be only part of the answer. Ownership must be traced to the actual installation path.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
section: Practice: write a documentation and support card
text:
Practice: write a documentation and support card
For your lab VM, record distribution identity, running kernel, architecture, the installed APT package version and its candidate. Add the source of your metadata and whether its freshness is known. Then locate one installed manual, one relevant distribution page and one upstream reference for a component you inspected.
Write one sentence explaining which source answers each question:

Where does this distribution put the component’s configuration?
Does this installed version implement a particular option?
Which package revision fixes a reported vulnerability?
What local change was made before the failure?

Finally, choose a maintenance deadline from the official lifecycle information applicable to the reference installation and record its scope and your access date. Do not silently include third-party software under that deadline.
Success means another reader could identify your environment and find the same class of documentation without guessing from a screenshot or a marketing name. Keep machine-specific values out of the book itself; they belong in your lab notes.

title: Distributions, Releases and Documentation
text:
Recall card

Distribution identity, running kernel and installed package versions describe different layers.
Support belongs to a defined product, release, source and scope.
Repository configuration establishes a software supply relationship.
Installed and candidate versions are different observations; cached metadata has an age.
Backported fixes require package-specific advisory checks, not version-prefix guesses.
Match documentation to the installed component, then verify local behavior.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
section: Define the lab before opening the installer
text:
Define the lab before opening the installer
Use the following identifiers consistently. The hypervisor’s VM name and the guest’s hostname are separate settings, even when both initially say bl01.







Item
First-lab choice




VM name
bl01


Guest hostname
bl01


Guest login
learner, with a unique lab password


CPU
2 vCPUs


Guest memory
4096 MiB


System disk
One new 32-GiB qcow2 disk


Firmware
UEFI, selected before installation


Initial network
A libvirt NAT network for installation and updates


Practice network
blpractice, isolated, with host address 192.168.231.1/24


Console
Virtual Machine Manager’s graphical display


Baseline
Powered-off full clone bl01-baseline


Recovery rehearsal
Another clone, bl01-recovered, started alone



These are a teaching budget, not a minimum specification for every Linux workload. Leave several GiB of RAM and adequate CPU capacity for the host. Budget roughly 100 GiB of free host storage for the guest, two full-size copies, installation media and headroom. Sparse images initially consume less than their virtual capacity; that is not a guarantee they will stay small. If the host cannot accommodate the budget, reduce the scope or use another lab host before running out of space during a copy.
A qcow2 image is a QEMU disk-image format with metadata and optional features such as backing files. Our first disk is a standalone image with no backing file. Do not attach a physical disk, personal home directory, shared clipboard secrets, USB security key or host filesystem share to this lab. They are unnecessary dependencies for the opening exercises.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
text:
Understand the two network phases



The same lab guest uses NAT during setup and an isolated network during practice.


Network address translation, or NAT, allows guest traffic to use a host-side outbound path. It is convenient for downloading packages. It is not complete isolation: the guest may reach services on the host, the local network and the Internet according to routing and policy. Do not run intentionally vulnerable network services during this setup phase.
An isolated libvirt network lacks an external forwarding configuration. It can still connect the host and guests on that virtual network. It is therefore suitable for controlled beginner practice, not a sandbox for hostile code. Avoid attaching a second NIC that silently provides another route out. Do not bridge the practice network to the physical LAN or configure the host to route it elsewhere.
A subnet describes a group of IP addresses sharing a network prefix. Here /24 corresponds to the mask 255.255.255.0. Our chosen prefix must not conflict with the host’s LAN, VPN or existing virtual networks. DHCP automatically supplies addresses and related network information; the first guest does not need a manually assigned static address.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
text:
Prepare and validate the host
On an Ubuntu host, install the supported tools:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system libvirt-clients \
  virt-manager virt-install ovmf
ovmf supplies virtual UEFI firmware on this x86-64 path. The management tools coordinate the guest definition, storage and networking. The Ubuntu libvirt guide explains the base host setup and authorization. These commands change the host, not the guest.
Validate before allocating a disk:
virt-host-validate qemu
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system list --all
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system net-list --all
qemu:///system explicitly selects the system libvirt connection. A per-user connection is a different inventory; checking one and creating the VM in the other produces confusing “missing VM” reports. The sudo prefix makes the scope of host management explicit. Virtual Machine Manager can use the desktop’s authorization prompt for the same system connection.
Read validation failures individually. Lack of usable hardware virtualization is relevant to this lab; an unavailable optional passthrough facility may not be. If /dev/kvm is unavailable, check host capability and firmware settings. If the host is itself a VM, its provider must expose nested virtualization. Installing more guest packages will not supply a missing host capability.
Open Virtual Machine Manager from the desktop. Confirm that its connection is QEMU/KVM, system, and that it connects successfully. Do not run the graphical application through sudo merely to bypass a connection problem; use the intended desktop authorization or the distribution’s documented group setup. VM-management privileges grant considerable control over the host.

Inspect the setup network
Many libvirt installations define a network named default. Its presence, activation and subnet are observations, not assumptions:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system net-info default
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system net-dumpxml default
Check that its XML contains a NAT forwarding mode and a subnet that does not conflict with the host’s networks. If that existing network is suitable but inactive, start it:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system net-start default
If it is absent, create a NAT virtual network through the connection’s Virtual Networks settings in Virtual Machine Manager. Give it a distinct name such as blsetup, select an unused IPv4 subnet, enable DHCP and select NAT forwarding. Start it and record its actual name and subnet. Use that name wherever the walkthrough asks for the setup network. Do not replace another workload’s network to make a screenshot match.
This book uses the graphical creation flow for that optional setup network because existing host networking varies. The isolated network below has an exact definition you can inspect and reproduce.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
section: Obtain the installer and verify what you downloaded
text:
Obtain the installer and verify what you downloaded
Use the official Ubuntu Server download page to select the 26.04 LTS server image for amd64, meaning the x86-64 architecture. A newer point release within the 26.04 series is appropriate. Record the actual filename and download date; do not substitute an interim release just because it appears first on a page.
Download the matching SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.gpg files from the same release directory. A checksum detects a mismatch; a verified signature connects the checksum list to a trusted signing key. Keep the ISO and those files in a dedicated download directory.
On the host, obtain the Ubuntu image-signing key according to the current official verification instructions, and compare its full fingerprint with Ubuntu’s published fingerprint through a trusted channel. A key’s display name alone is insufficient. Then, from the directory containing the downloaded files:
gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.gpg SHA256SUMS
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
Proceed only when the signature is valid for the expected signing key and the exact ISO you downloaded reports OK. Do not hide failures by filtering the output to successful lines. --ignore-missing permits other images named in the checksum list to be absent; it does not excuse a mismatch for your image. The Ubuntu verification procedure supplies the key-distribution and fingerprint details. Part 02 develops this trust chain further.
The installer ISO is bootable virtual optical media. You do not need to write it onto the host’s physical disk or a USB drive for this lab.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
text:
Create the virtual hardware
In Virtual Machine Manager, select Create a new virtual machine on the system connection. Choose local installation media and browse to the verified ISO. Confirm a suitable Ubuntu operating-system profile. If automatic detection fails, select an appropriate Ubuntu Linux profile rather than changing the guest architecture.
Set 4096 MiB memory, 2 CPUs and one new 32-GiB disk. Name the VM bl01. Select the inspected NAT setup network. Before finishing, choose the option to customize the configuration before installation.
Review the hardware details:

Select UEFI firmware before the first installation. Record the selected variant. Do not enable TPM-backed disk encryption for this initial lab; it introduces additional state that the simple clone exercise does not cover.
Confirm the disk is a new qcow2 image in the intended libvirt storage pool. Record its host pathname and virtual capacity. Use the VirtIO disk bus where available.
Confirm there is exactly one NIC, using the selected setup network and a VirtIO model where available.
Confirm a graphical display and video device are present. Open that display to interact with firmware and the installer.
Confirm that the bootable ISO is attached as optical media. Check the boot order if the installer does not start.

Labels vary slightly between application versions. The invariant is the resulting hardware: one guest disk, one NIC, a known firmware mode and a usable console. A storage pool is libvirt’s managed location for storage volumes; a pool name is not a guest filesystem mount point.
If libvirt cannot read an ISO inside a private host home directory, use its storage browser to place the verified file in a libvirt-accessible media location. Do not make your whole home directory world-readable. The error concerns host-side file access, not an installer driver.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
section: Install the guest through its console
text:
Install the guest through its console
Start installation from the graphical display. This is a deliberately simple first installation; Part 02 revisits partitioning, encryption, authentication choices and reproducible provisioning.
Select the keyboard layout you actually use, Ubuntu Server, automatic networking on the one NIC, no proxy unless your environment requires one, and a reachable distribution mirror. For storage, choose guided use of the new 32-GiB virtual disk. Leave optional disk encryption off for this disposable introductory guest. Read the final storage summary and confirm its target before accepting it.
Create hostname bl01 and account learner. Use a unique password and record it in your password manager. Skip optional software bundles and optional remote-access installation for now. Complete installation, reboot when prompted and detach the ISO when the installer requests it. Ubuntu’s basic installation tutorial describes the installer flow.
If the VM returns to the installer, inspect optical-media attachment and boot order. Do not immediately reinstall over the disk. If you see a login prompt, log in through the graphical console and establish which environment you reached:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
The root source should be installed storage rather than the live installer environment. Device and logical-volume names depend on the selected storage layout. A firmware check is:
test -d /sys/firmware/efi && printf 'Guest booted with UEFI\n'
No output means the test did not find that directory; investigate the firmware mode rather than claiming UEFI was used merely because the host has it.
While still on the setup network, update the fresh guest:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo reboot
Read the package plan before accepting it. A failed metadata refresh must be resolved before treating the package inventory as current. After reboot, log in through the graphical console again. This demonstrates that your access route survives guest shutdown and startup.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
Building the First Virtual Machine
section: Establish a baseline you can actually use
text:
Establish a baseline you can actually use
A checkpoint is a known state you intend to return to. A snapshot is one implementation mechanism, often dependent on other images and the same host storage. For this first lab, use a full powered-off clone rather than relying on a snapshot feature whose support depends on disk, firmware and manager versions.
In the guest, create a harmless baseline marker:
printf 'baseline-v1\n' > "$HOME/lab-baseline.txt"
sudo poweroff
On the host, confirm the VM is shut off, not paused or saved with suspended memory:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl01
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl01 --details
The following clone recipe assumes the single writable disk created above, no shared writable disks, no backing chain and no TPM state. The destination filenames and VM names must be new. Check free space before copying, then run:
sudo virt-clone --connect qemu:///system \
  --original bl01 --name bl01-baseline \
  --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/bl01-baseline.qcow2
The clone receives a distinct libvirt identity and network MAC address. For a UEFI guest, verify that its definition also references a distinct NVRAM file, which holds persistent firmware variables:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system dumpxml bl01
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system dumpxml bl01-baseline
Compare disk source paths and the <nvram> entries. Keep the baseline shut off, with no autostart enabled. The virt-clone manual documents disk-copy behavior and generated NVRAM paths. Do not use --preserve-data or --skip-copy: those options do not create the independent disk copy intended here.
The guest’s own hostname, machine ID, credentials and application identity are copied too. The clone is a recovery artifact, not yet a prepared second server. Keep only one copy running during this exercise. Later provisioning chapters handle identity changes for concurrently deployed clones.



The untouched baseline supplies a separate recovery copy.



Prove recovery with a visible change
Start the original bl01. In its guest console, replace the marker:
printf 'after-baseline\n' > "$HOME/lab-baseline.txt"
cat "$HOME/lab-baseline.txt"
sudo poweroff
Leave both original and baseline shut off. On the host, create a working recovery copy from the untouched baseline:
sudo virt-clone --connect qemu:///system \
  --original bl01-baseline --name bl01-recovered \
  --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/bl01-recovered.qcow2
Inspect its disk, NVRAM and NIC source as before. Start only bl01-recovered and open its graphical console. The guest hostname can still be bl01; the console window’s VM identity tells you which copy you are testing. Read the marker:
cat "$HOME/lab-baseline.txt"
Success is baseline-v1, a successful login, and an expected isolated-network configuration. This proves that the baseline’s earlier filesystem state can boot as a separate recovery copy. It does not prove that every future workload, multi-disk database or external service can be recovered by the same procedure.
Shut down the recovery copy after the test and resume the original bl01 for normal work. Keep the baseline unchanged. The recovery copy can be retained shut off or removed later through the manager after verifying its unique disk path. Do not select shared media or the original VM’s disk for deletion.


A local clone is not an independent backup
All three copies can disappear if their host storage fails. A backup plan needs independent storage, an inventory of required state, retention and a demonstrated restore. Firmware variables, VM configuration, disk dependencies, encryption material and application consistency can all matter. Never copy or modify a live image with an offline image utility; QEMU’s image-tool documentation explains that restriction.
The baseline is valuable for returning from an experiment. It is not protection against losing the entire lab host. Keep your lab notes outside the guest so they remain available when a guest cannot boot.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
text:
Diagnose the layer that failed








Symptom
First evidence
Likely investigation boundary




VM cannot start
Host manager error and available resources
Host virtualization or storage


Firmware says no boot device
Attached ISO/disk and boot order
Presented hardware and firmware


Installer cannot reach a mirror
NIC source, guest address and route
Setup-network path


Installed VM reopens installer
Optical media and boot selection
Boot configuration


Console works but package downloads fail in practice
NIC source is blpractice
Expected isolated-network behavior


Clone does not contain the marker
Exact source VM, disk paths and shutdown sequence
Baseline selection or copying



Do not solve a console issue by exposing SSH to the physical LAN. Recover the management path you designed first. Do not solve a full host filesystem by deleting an unfamiliar qcow2 image; it may be another VM’s only disk or a backing dependency.

title: Building the First Virtual Machine
text:
Completion record and recall card
Before moving on, write down the VM and guest names, firmware mode, CPU/RAM allocation, image path, NIC source, guest address, installer filename and verification result. Record how to open the console while networking is unavailable. Record the baseline creation time and recovery-test result.
You are ready for the next chapter when you can shut down and start the guest, log in without SSH, explain its current network boundary, and show the earlier marker in the separate recovery copy.

Host commands manage virtual hardware; guest commands administer the installed Linux system.
NAT is a setup convenience, not complete isolation.
A console independent of guest networking is part of the recovery design.
A powered-off clone has a limited, explicit consistency boundary.
Cloning hardware identities does not automatically regenerate identities inside the guest.
A baseline becomes useful evidence only after a recovery rehearsal.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
text:
Start with an operational question
“The server is broken” does not identify a test. “After today’s change, the console user cannot read the report that was available yesterday” gives an operation, observer and time boundary. A good symptom statement includes:

The intended operation and the result that would count as success.
Who or what attempted it, from which environment.
The actual result, including the exact error when available.
The first known failure time and last known success.
The scope: one user, one service, one VM or several machines.

Avoid turning a hypothesis into the symptom. “The firewall is blocking the application” already assumes a cause. “The client times out when connecting to the configured endpoint” leaves routing, filtering, listener and application behavior open for investigation.



An investigation moves from a precise symptom through evidence to a tested change.


A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that evidence can support or contradict. A discriminating check is one whose possible outcomes separate competing explanations. A command is useful because of the question it answers, not because it appears in a long troubleshooting checklist.
For example, if a service reports that it cannot open /srv/report/current.txt, checking the configured pathname and mount can separate “wrong path” from “missing storage.” Rebooting may change both the process and mount state without explaining either.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
section: Build an inventory with purpose and scope
text:
Build an inventory with purpose and scope
Create a lab record outside the guest, alongside the baseline and console instructions from the VM chapter. Record the following categories. Some values come from the host manager; others come from the guest. Label that boundary explicitly.








Category
Useful fields
Why it belongs




Purpose
Lab role, owner, expected operations
Defines what healthy means


Host-side identity
VM name, connection, disk paths, firmware
Locates the managed machine and its dependencies


Guest identity
Hostname, distribution, kernel, architecture
Matches instructions and runtime evidence


Resources
vCPUs, RAM, disks and filesystem capacity
Establishes expected limits


Network
NIC source, address, route, resolver context
Explains intended reachability


Access
Console route, login method, privilege boundary
Makes recovery possible


Service state
Expected services and known failures
Distinguishes baseline from regression


Recovery
Baseline date, scope, test result
States what can actually be restored


Maintenance
Update/source status and outstanding actions
Prevents a stale baseline from appearing current



Do not record passwords, private keys or authentication tokens in this document. A recovery record can identify the password-manager entry without copying its contents.
The inventory is not frozen truth. Include collection time and the environment from which each observation was made. An IP address can change after DHCP renewal; a kernel version can change after reboot; a disk image can move while the guest filesystem remains the same.

Worked inventory: identity, time and boot
In the guest, run:
date --iso-8601=seconds
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
uname -m
uptime
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
The boot ID identifies this kernel boot and helps distinguish records separated by a reboot. A PID alone cannot do that. The wall-clock time needs context too: a disconnected VM can have a different clock from the host. Record the offset or uncertainty rather than silently aligning events by an inaccurate timestamp.
For an event timeline within one boot, monotonic timestamps can be useful because they describe elapsed time from a boot-related origin rather than calendar time. For events spanning machines, synchronized wall clocks and timezone information matter. Later time-service chapters explain synchronization; for now, do not claim second-by-second ordering across unsynchronized machines.


Worked inventory: resources and storage
lscpu
free -h
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
df -h /
df -i /
lsblk describes block devices and their relationships; findmnt locates mounts. Their explicit columns make the intended observation clearer than relying on changing default displays. The lsblk manual describes its device information and column selection.
df -h / asks about filesystem space for /; df -i / asks about inode usage where the filesystem reports it. An inode represents filesystem metadata for an object. On filesystems with a finite inode supply, many small files can exhaust object capacity while data blocks remain available. The df manual distinguishes these reports.
Illustrative interpretation:
Filesystem     Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/vda2       30G  5.0G   23G  18% /
This describes a guest filesystem at one instant. It does not show the host filesystem’s free space or prove that a database can write under its own account. Filesystem reservation, quotas, permissions and a read-only mount can produce different application results. Record this evidence as “root filesystem reported available blocks,” not “storage is healthy.”
On the host, separately record the free capacity of the filesystem containing the VM images and baseline copies. A guest’s free-space report cannot detect every host-side capacity problem.


Worked inventory: networking and listeners
ip -brief address
ip route
ss -lnt
A listener is an endpoint prepared to accept incoming communication. ss -lnt selects listening TCP sockets, using numeric addresses and ports. It does not cover UDP services, outbound-only applications or all communication mechanisms. The ss manual describes these filters.
An address of 127.0.0.1 belongs to IPv4 loopback, usable inside the same network namespace. A listener bound only there is not automatically reachable through the guest’s external NIC. An unspecified address such as 0.0.0.0 has a wider local binding scope, but does not prove that a route or firewall permits a client connection.
On our isolated practice network, failure to fetch Internet packages is expected. Do not switch to the NAT network simply because a generic checklist says an external ping must work. Compare the observation with the documented role and phase of the lab.
If you need to understand which route Linux would select for an address, ip route get ADDRESS performs a route lookup; it is not a packet-delivery test. Replace ADDRESS with the actual destination under investigation. The ip-route manual explains this distinction.


Worked inventory: service state and bounded logs
systemctl --failed --no-pager
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager
journalctl --list-boots --no-pager
journalctl -b -p warning -n 30 --no-pager
A failed-unit list is a starting clue. A healthy application can have dependencies not represented there, and a failed optional unit might not explain the reported operation. Similarly, selecting warning-priority records can omit the informational event that caused the incident.
The journal commands show retained boots and a bounded view of current-boot warnings. Retention and your account’s access rights limit what is available. The journalctl reference documents boot, priority, unit and time filters. If a query reports insufficient access, record that limitation before deciding whether a privileged read is warranted.
Do not dump all logs into a public issue. Logs can contain usernames, addresses, request details and credentials accidentally emitted by software. Retain original evidence privately, and create a separately reviewed excerpt when sharing.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
text:
Save a small evidence bundle
For this exercise, create a private directory in the guest and collect a few explicitly selected reports. Run the commands in one Bash terminal:
umask 077
evidence_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/bl-evidence.XXXXXX")
date --iso-8601=seconds > "$evidence_dir/collected-at.txt"
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id > "$evidence_dir/boot-id.txt"
cat /etc/os-release > "$evidence_dir/os-release.txt"
uname -r > "$evidence_dir/kernel.txt"
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS \
  > "$evidence_dir/root-mount.txt" 2>&1
ip -brief address > "$evidence_dir/addresses.txt" 2>&1
systemctl --failed --no-pager > "$evidence_dir/failed-units.txt" 2>&1
printf 'Evidence directory: %s\n' "$evidence_dir"
umask 077 restricts permissions for newly created files and remains in effect for this shell. mktemp -d avoids overwriting an older evidence set. 2>&1 saves error output with ordinary output, so an unavailable command or denied query does not look like an empty successful report.
Read the saved files. The existence of a file is not proof that the command succeeded. Keep the directory path in your notes, and copy reviewed evidence to storage outside the VM when it matters for recovery. An evidence bundle only inside the guest can be lost when you revert that guest.
This small bundle is not a backup. It does not contain the VM disk, service databases or every configuration input. Its purpose is to preserve the context for a bounded investigation.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
text:
Separate facts, interpretations and actions
Use a table like this while investigating:







Kind
Example




Observation
Unit log says /home/learner/.../expected.txt cannot be opened


Interpretation
The configured input may not exist at that path


Alternative
The parent directory may be inaccessible to the service user


Discriminating check
Inspect the exact configured path and parent directory as the same user


Planned change
Place the intended file at that path, if the evidence confirms a naming mismatch


Verification
Repeat the same unit invocation and inspect its result



An observation can still be incomplete or stale. Its value comes from a recorded source, time and scope. An interpretation should be revisable when new evidence appears.
Change one relevant variable at a time when practical. If you change the pathname, account, permissions and startup command together, a successful retry will not tell you which change mattered. In a real outage, restoring service may take priority over a perfect experiment, but record that uncertainty rather than inventing a definitive root cause afterward.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
section: Worked failure: a service reads the wrong pathname
text:
Worked failure: a service reads the wrong pathname
This experiment uses a transient user service: a unit created through the manager for this session of work rather than installed as a persistent system configuration file. It runs under your ordinary account. No sudo is needed.
Check that the user manager is reachable:
systemctl --user list-units --type=service --no-pager
If it reports that it cannot connect, use a normal local login in the reference VM’s console. Do not change system authentication or the login manager just to run the exercise. A shell in an unrelated container or recovery environment may not have a user manager.
Use the unit name bl-reading-probe.service only if it is not already in use. An old attempt should be inspected and cleaned up before reusing the name. Create the input directory and the deliberately differently named file:
probe_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/bl-reading-probe.XXXXXX")
printf 'inventory-ready\n' > "$probe_dir/actual.txt"
printf 'Experiment directory: %s\n' "$probe_dir"
systemd-run --user --unit=bl-reading-probe \
  --property=Type=oneshot --property=RemainAfterExit=yes \
  /usr/bin/cat "$probe_dir/expected.txt"
Run interactively; do not wrap this expected failure in a script that exits immediately on any nonzero result. Type=oneshot makes this a finite task. RemainAfterExit=yes keeps the successful unit active after its process exits, making the final state easy to inspect. Do not add --wait: combining waiting for deactivation with a unit intentionally left active is inappropriate here. The systemd-run manual describes transient-unit creation and its execution options.
The command requests a file that you did not create. It should fail. Record the symptom precisely: “the user unit cannot read its configured input.” Do not call this a disk failure or a permission failure yet.

Observe without repairing
systemctl --user status bl-reading-probe.service --no-pager
systemctl --user show bl-reading-probe.service \
  -p ActiveState -p SubState -p Result -p ExecMainStatus
systemctl --user cat bl-reading-probe.service
journalctl --user -b -u bl-reading-probe.service -n 20 --no-pager
ls -ld "$probe_dir"
ls -l "$probe_dir"
The unit’s executed command should contain the exact expected.txt pathname. The directory listing should contain actual.txt instead. The log normally reports a missing file; wording depends on locale and software version. A nonzero status from a status-query command can reflect the failed unit being observed, rather than a broken query tool.
There are now several mutually supporting observations: the requested name, the actual name, and the failure at that path. Permissions remain worth understanding, but broad permission changes would not create the missing name. The isolated network is irrelevant because this command reads a local file.


Make the smallest supported correction
Move the intended input to the requested name, then start the same unit again:
mv -- "$probe_dir/actual.txt" "$probe_dir/expected.txt"
systemctl --user start bl-reading-probe.service
systemctl --user show bl-reading-probe.service \
  -p ActiveState -p SubState -p Result -p ExecMainStatus
journalctl --user -b -u bl-reading-probe.service -n 20 --no-pager
Expected properties include ActiveState=active, SubState=exited, Result=success and ExecMainStatus=0. The journal should include inventory-ready from the successful read. It may still contain the earlier failure; logs preserve history rather than becoming uniformly successful after a repair. Compare the timestamps and invocation order.
This is a direct example of an active service without a continuing main process. The useful operation was the file read, and its evidence is successful completion plus the expected content. Do not diagnose the absence of a running cat process as a new failure.


Clean up the experiment
Save the relevant output in your notes first. Then stop the transient unit and remove only the file and directory you created:
systemctl --user stop bl-reading-probe.service
rm -- "$probe_dir/expected.txt"
rmdir -- "$probe_dir"
unset probe_dir
A stopped transient unit can be unloaded by the manager. A later status query may report that it is not found; that is expected after cleanup. If an interrupted attempt remains failed, inspect it and use systemctl --user reset-failed bl-reading-probe.service before creating a new attempt. Do not reset all failed units and erase unrelated failure state.
The journal can retain the experiment’s records after cleanup. Removing the input directory is not a request to erase that historical evidence.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
section: Write the change note before forgetting the reason
text:
Write the change note before forgetting the reason
A compact note for this experiment might read:
Purpose: restore the user probe's expected file read.
Environment: bl01 guest, local console, learner user manager.
Baseline: probe input directory contains actual.txt only.
Symptom: bl-reading-probe.service exits unsuccessfully.
Evidence: ExecStart requests expected.txt; listing shows actual.txt.
Hypothesis: the intended input has the wrong pathname.
Change: rename actual.txt to expected.txt in the experiment directory.
Rollback: rename it back while the probe is stopped.
Verification: same unit starts successfully; result=success;
              journal contains inventory-ready.
Cleanup: stop transient unit; remove experiment input and directory.
Limit: proves this local read, not general storage or service health.
Add actual timestamps and the boot ID to your real note. For a production change, also record the authorized scope, affected users, maintenance constraints and recovery decision. The shape is the same: purpose, evidence, bounded action, verification and limits.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
section: A second investigation: connectivity changed as designed
text:
A second investigation: connectivity changed as designed
After moving bl01 from NAT to blpractice, an update attempt cannot contact its repositories. List three hypotheses before changing anything:

The guest has no usable NIC or address.
The guest is deliberately attached to a network without an external path.
The package configuration refers to an unavailable repository.

A discriminating sequence is to inspect the guest address, check the host-side NIC source, and compare it with the lab’s documented phase. If the guest has a practice address and the source is blpractice, external download failure agrees with the intended design. Replacing repository URLs would change an unrelated component.
If a later exercise needs updates, plan a brief return to the setup network while the guest is shut down, perform the maintenance, and return to the isolated network. Record both attachment changes and verify the final state. Do not silently leave an extra NAT NIC attached after the task.
This example matters because successful troubleshooting sometimes concludes that the system is behaving correctly and the expectation must change. Every failure message is evidence about an attempted operation; not every failed operation indicates a defect.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
text:
Practice: produce an evidence-led handoff
Give another learner a short handoff containing the VM inventory, the last known healthy state, the probe failure’s evidence, the repair and verification, and the recovery route. They should be able to identify the correct VM without guessing from its hostname alone.
Answer these questions in the handoff:

What did the successful probe prove, and what did it leave untested?
Which evidence would be lost if you reverted the guest before copying your notes out?
Why would changing permissions on the input directory not have fixed the original naming mismatch?
Why is an external ping failure insufficient proof that a VM is isolated?
How would you distinguish an old failure in the journal from the latest invocation’s result?

Success means you can trace each conclusion to a specific observation. The probe proved one read under one account and manager context; it did not validate an entire storage stack. Guest-local notes can vanish on rollback. Missing names and permissions are different causes. Network probes have several failure modes. Invocation timing and current result properties separate historical errors from a completed repair.

title: Inventory, Evidence and First Troubleshooting
text:
Recall card

Define the failed operation before selecting commands.
Record time, boot and observer context with evidence.
Distinguish observations from explanations and proposed actions.
Choose checks that separate plausible causes.
Preserve evidence before a restart or rollback changes it.
Verify the original operation and relevant side effects after a bounded change.
A useful handoff includes what remains uncertain.

You now have a working lab and an investigative method. Part 02 returns to installation choices in depth: media trust, firmware and storage planning, manual layouts, first-boot verification and reproducible provisioning.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
section: Choose the kind of artifact before its filename
text:
Choose the kind of artifact before its filename
An installation image supplies an environment that installs an operating system onto target storage. A preinstalled disk image supplies storage that already contains an operating system, usually expecting further initialization. A container image supplies a userspace filesystem and metadata for a container runtime; it does not by itself provide the independent guest kernel and firmware path used in our VM lab.








Artifact
Typical use
Question before downloading




Server installer ISO
Interactive or automated installation onto new storage
Does it support this architecture and boot environment?


Desktop live/installer ISO
Try or install a graphical workstation
Is its package and interface selection appropriate?


Cloud disk image
Provision an instance from a prepared disk
What initializes credentials, networking and instance identity?


Network-boot artifacts
Start an installer through network infrastructure
Where will the remaining installer and package data come from?


Container image
Start isolated userspace on a host kernel
Which runtime and image trust policy apply?



An ISO is a disk-image format commonly used for virtual optical media. The suffix alone does not establish its operating system, architecture or trustworthiness. Likewise, a .qcow2 file identifies a storage format, not a guarantee of a bootable, authenticated or correctly configured guest.
The official Ubuntu release directory distinguishes server and desktop installation media and publishes checksum files. The separate Ubuntu Cloud Images site distributes images tailored for cloud and virtualization environments. Downloading a cloud image and then expecting the interactive server installer is a mismatch of workflow, not a failed bootloader.

Architecture names describe compatibility
For this lab, the host and presented guest machine are x86-64. Ubuntu names this architecture amd64; the name also applies to compatible Intel CPUs. It does not mean that only AMD-branded processors work. arm64 describes a different instruction-set family.
A VM manager can present different machine types and device models, but hardware-assisted execution normally depends on a compatible host/guest architecture. Software emulation can bridge some architecture differences at another performance cost. Select the intended architecture deliberately rather than assuming that the largest or newest image is suitable.
Also distinguish the release series from the image build. Two artifacts can both belong to Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and contain different package revisions or installer updates. Record the exact filename and digest, not just “Ubuntu LTS.” A URL that always points to the newest build is convenient for acquisition but insufficient as a permanent identifier.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
section: Four separate claims about a download
text:
Four separate claims about a download
Integrity asks whether the bytes match an expected value. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 computes a fixed-size digest from the complete file. A changed byte will, for practical verification purposes, produce a different digest.
Authenticity asks whether the expected value or artifact came from the authority you intended to trust. A signature can authenticate a checksum manifest to a signing key. You still have to establish that the key belongs to the intended publisher.
Suitability asks whether the authentic artifact is appropriate for this machine and task. A valid signature on an ARM image does not make it the right image for our x86-64 installation.
Freshness asks whether the artifact and its maintenance state are acceptable now. A correctly signed older image remains an older image. Its signature does not install later security fixes or promise that its release is still supported.



Verification joins trusted publisher identity to a manifest and then to the selected image.


These checks are complementary. HTTPS protects communication with the site you reached, subject to its certificate trust. A signed manifest can remain verifiable after copying through a mirror or offline storage. Neither eliminates the need to know which publisher and artifact you intended to use.
A checksum copied from the same untrusted page as a malicious image can match perfectly. The attacker could replace both. The hash calculation would be correct, but the trust decision would be unsupported.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
text:
Collect a matched verification set
Create a new host directory for one release/build verification. Keeping each set separate prevents a checksum file from one release being confused with another:
umask 077
media_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/bl-install-media.XXXXXX")
printf 'Media directory: %s\n' "$media_dir"
Download the selected server ISO, SHA256SUMS, and SHA256SUMS.gpg into this directory from the same official release listing. Use the browser’s save location or move the three completed downloads there. Avoid using an incomplete .part download or an automatically renamed duplicate without checking which file you selected.
SHA256SUMS is the manifest: a list of filenames and expected hashes. SHA256SUMS.gpg is a detached signature over that manifest. “Detached” means the signature is stored separately from the signed content.
Enter the directory and inspect the manifest:
cd "$media_dir"
ls -lh
cat SHA256SUMS
Identify the exact server ISO entry for the intended architecture. A different filename may be legitimate after a point release, but it must correspond to your downloaded image. Do not edit the manifest to force a match; that would change the signed object.
If a moving release directory changes during your download, the ISO and manifest may legitimately belong to different publication states. A mismatch remains a reason to stop. Acquire a consistent set from the publisher instead of assuming the signature or checksum tool is being overly strict.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
text:
Establish the signing key’s identity
A public signing key can be distributed widely. Its availability on a keyserver does not by itself prove whose key it is. A fingerprint is a compact identifier derived from the key material. Compare the full expected fingerprint using the publisher’s authenticated documentation or another trusted organizational distribution channel.
Ubuntu’s download-verification instructions publish its image-signing key information. The documented 2012 image-signing key has this fingerprint:
8439 38DF 228D 22F7 B374 2BC0 D94A A3F0 EFE2 1092
Verify that Ubuntu still identifies the relevant key for your selected image when you perform the exercise. A future key rotation should lead you to verify the new publisher guidance, not accept an arbitrary key just because it makes an error disappear.
Use a dedicated verification key directory so this experiment is separate from your normal keyring:
verify_key_dir=$(mktemp -d "$media_dir/keys.XXXXXX")
expected_fingerprint=843938DF228D22F7B3742BC0D94AA3F0EFE21092
gpg --homedir "$verify_key_dir" \
  --keyserver hkps://keyserver.ubuntu.com \
  --recv-keys "$expected_fingerprint"
gpg --homedir "$verify_key_dir" \
  --fingerprint "$expected_fingerprint"
Compare the displayed full fingerprint with the trusted publisher record. hkps requests a TLS-protected keyserver connection. The requested fingerprint narrows the key retrieval; a matching user-ID name or email address alone is not enough. The GnuPG manual documents key retrieval, fingerprints and verification operations.
These commands import public verification material. They do not create a private signing key or require you to certify the publisher’s key as universally trusted. Keep the scope of the decision narrow: this is the key authorized to verify the selected distribution’s manifest.
If key retrieval fails because the host cannot reach the keyserver, diagnose that acquisition failure. An approved offline copy of the public key can be imported and checked against the same trusted fingerprint. Do not disable artifact verification to compensate for a network problem.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
section: Verify the manifest, then verify the image
text:
Verify the manifest, then verify the image
First check the detached signature against the manifest:
gpg --homedir "$verify_key_dir" \
  --verify SHA256SUMS.gpg SHA256SUMS
Read the complete result. You need successful cryptographic verification using the expected publisher key. A message about an unknown local trust level can occur when a newly imported key has not been certified in your personal trust database. That is a different question from a bad signature. Resolve key ownership through the fingerprint check; do not treat every warning as equivalent or blindly suppress warnings.
A valid signature binds the manifest bytes to the signing key. It does not yet say that your ISO matches an entry. Perform that second check:
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
Require the exact downloaded ISO filename to report OK, and check that the command reports no failed verification for it. --ignore-missing permits other files listed in the release manifest to be absent locally. It does not prove that the file you meant to test was present. A successful check of a desktop ISO in the same directory does not validate a server ISO that was never downloaded.
The GNU Coreutils manual documents checksum-checking behavior. For this exercise, use a directory containing only the intended artifact set and read the output without filtering it. In particular, do not pipe the result to a search for OK and mistake the search command’s success for the verifier’s complete result.
A completed record should now connect these facts:
Trusted publisher fingerprint
    → valid signature on this manifest
    → matching digest for this exact ISO
    → intended release, architecture and installation role
If any link is missing, label the artifact unverified and do not attach it as trusted installation media.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
section: Worked experiment: matching bytes are not trusted bytes
text:
Worked experiment: matching bytes are not trusted bytes
This small exercise uses ordinary text, not an installer. It demonstrates why a checksum must come from a trusted source. Run it in one Bash terminal:
hash_demo_dir=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/bl-hash-demo.XXXXXX")
printf 'approved-content\n' > "$hash_demo_dir/sample.txt"
(
  cd "$hash_demo_dir" || exit
  sha256sum sample.txt > checksums.txt
  sha256sum --check checksums.txt
)
The result should include sample.txt: OK. Now alter the data but retain the old manifest:
printf 'changed-content\n' > "$hash_demo_dir/sample.txt"
(
  cd "$hash_demo_dir" || exit
  sha256sum --check checksums.txt
)
Expect FAILED and a nonzero result. Run this interactively; a shell configured to exit on any nonzero command could stop at this expected failure. The mismatch means the data no longer agrees with the saved digest. It does not identify whether the cause was malicious, accidental or an intentional edit.
Now replace the manifest too:
(
  cd "$hash_demo_dir" || exit
  sha256sum sample.txt > checksums.txt
  sha256sum --check checksums.txt
)
The changed content reports OK. Nothing about the hash algorithm was defeated: you simply changed the expected value. A publisher signature prevents you from silently treating a modified manifest as the publisher’s original statement, provided the verification key itself is trusted.
Remove only this exercise’s files:
rm -- "$hash_demo_dir/sample.txt" "$hash_demo_dir/checksums.txt"
rmdir -- "$hash_demo_dir"
unset hash_demo_dir
Keep the real installer verification set and its record for the installation lab. They serve a different purpose from these temporary files.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
section: Carry the verification across the copy boundary
text:
Carry the verification across the copy boundary
The verified file must be the file the VM actually boots. If you copy the ISO to a libvirt-accessible media directory, compare its SHA-256 digest with the verified source or verify the destination against the authenticated manifest. Record the destination path in the VM’s installation plan.
A recognizable basename is not sufficient: two directories can contain different files with the same name. The VM manager’s optical-media path establishes which one is attached. If an administrator downloads a replacement into that path later, your old record no longer proves the attached bytes are unchanged.
For this VM exercise, attach the ISO as read-only virtual optical media. Writing it onto a physical USB device is a separate operation with a destructive target-selection step. There is no reason to use a raw disk-writing command on the host’s physical drives to create this guest.
Store these fields outside the guest:







Field
Purpose




Official source and retrieval time
Identifies the publication context


Exact filename, size and SHA-256
Identifies the verified bytes


Manifest and detached signature
Preserves the publisher’s signed statement


Expected signing-key fingerprint and its trusted source
Records the trust decision


Verification outcome
Records both signature and image checks


Attached-media path
Connects verification to the installer actually booted


Release/architecture and intended role
Records suitability



This record can reproduce an acquisition decision, but it is not a claim that the resulting host is permanently secure. Package updates, installer refreshes, later configuration and workload software all add new state.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
text:
Diagnose verification failures precisely








Observation
What it establishes
Next action




Public key unavailable
Verification cannot yet identify a usable key
Acquire the intended key and check its fingerprint


Bad signature
Manifest/signature pair does not verify
Stop; reacquire a matching official set


Valid signature from an unexpected key
A signature exists, but publisher authorization is unresolved
Check the publisher’s current signing policy


ISO hash mismatch
Downloaded bytes differ from the authenticated manifest entry
Check build pairing and reacquire the image


No exact ISO entry checked
The intended artifact has not been validated
Check filenames, directory and manifest coverage


Valid image for the wrong architecture
Authenticity does not solve suitability
Obtain the correct artifact



Retain diagnostic output before deleting a failed download if you need to investigate the cause. Repeated mismatches after clean downloads warrant examination of storage, transfer paths and publication state; they do not justify bypassing the check.

title: Installation Media, Authenticity and Integrity
text:
Practice and recall
Verify the server image you will use for bl02, then have another learner trace your record from the trusted fingerprint to the optical-media path. They should not need to infer which of several downloads was used. Complete the text-file experiment and explain why replacing both file and unsigned manifest produces a successful checksum result.
You are ready to proceed when the signature, exact ISO digest, architecture, release series and attached path are all accounted for.

Integrity compares bytes with an expected value; authenticity establishes who supplied that value.
A keyserver distributes keys; it does not replace the publisher-identity check.
Verify the manifest before using its digest as trusted evidence.
Require the exact intended artifact to be checked.
A valid signature does not establish suitability, freshness or a secure final configuration.
Preserve enough evidence to identify the bytes actually booted.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Write the purpose before choosing the layout
text:
Write the purpose before choosing the layout
For this pass, use this purpose statement:

Install a second disposable Ubuntu Server VM, inspect the guided LVM storage layout, and compare its installed state with the original lab VM. Preserve the original VM and all baseline copies. Use graphical console access and isolated networking after setup.

This purpose rules out several unnecessary choices. There is no production database to migrate, no need for shared host files, and no requirement for remote login during installation. It also defines a useful comparison: the distribution, virtual resources and network phase can be held similar while the storage plan is examined deliberately.
Provisioning is the broader process of making a usable machine ready for its role. Operating-system installation is one part. Identity, credentials, networking, updates, services, monitoring and recovery also belong to provisioning. A successful installer does not automatically satisfy all of those responsibilities.



An installation plan passes through decisions that must remain connected.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Separate the host, virtual machine and guest identities
text:
Separate the host, virtual machine and guest identities
The host is the physical Linux system that runs libvirt. The VM definition describes presented hardware. The installed guest has its own operating-system identity. Keep all three in the plan:








Layer
Example identifier
What it identifies




Host
Your lab workstation’s actual name
The resource and management provider


Libvirt connection
qemu:///system
The VM inventory and management scope


VM definition
bl02
The new presented machine


Guest hostname
bl02
The installed operating system’s chosen name


Guest user
learner
An account inside the new guest


System disk
New 32-GiB image, recorded host path
The storage that may be overwritten



A familiar hostname in a console prompt is not enough to identify a destructive target. A clone can retain the original guest hostname. Check the VM manager’s selected guest and the attached disk inventory before proceeding.
For our comparison, create bl02 from new installation media and a new disk. Do not clone bl01 as a substitute for performing the installation: that would reproduce its existing layout and identity rather than show the installer’s decisions.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
text:
Choose firmware before installing
UEFI is the selected virtual firmware interface for this lab. The installed system will need a compatible boot path, including an EFI System Partition, or ESP, for firmware-readable boot artifacts. The partition table and the firmware mode are related choices, but they are not the same object.
A partition table divides a block device into named ranges of sectors. GPT, the GUID Partition Table, is the partition-table format used for this guided UEFI example. GPT does not mean that the guest definitely booted through UEFI; confirm the actual mode from the installer and installed guest.
An ESP is typically formatted using a FAT filesystem and mounted at /boot/efi in the installed system. A separate /boot filesystem, if the installer creates one, serves a different role. It can hold kernels and initial boot files without being the firmware-readable ESP. The next part examines the complete boot chain; here, distinguish these locations so you can review the installer’s proposed layout.
Secure Boot adds signature-based policy to the boot path. It is not the same as checking the ISO signature, and it is not disk encryption. These mechanisms address different boundaries:







Mechanism
Main question




Installer-image verification
Are these the installation bytes authorized by the publisher?


Secure Boot policy
Are boot components accepted by the platform’s configured trust policy?


Disk encryption
Is stored data protected when the required unlock material is unavailable?


Login authentication
Is this user allowed to access the running system?



For bl02, select UEFI before the first boot, retain the manager’s supported Ubuntu-compatible firmware settings, and record whether Secure Boot is enabled. Do not switch between legacy BIOS and UEFI mid-install to work around an unexplained error. Such a switch can change which boot artifacts and entries are required.
Also record the guest’s persistent firmware-variable storage. A UEFI VM can have a host-side NVRAM file as well as a disk image. A recovery plan that saves only the disk should explain how firmware state will be reconstructed or restored.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Plan capacity at more than one layer
text:
Plan capacity at more than one layer
Use the same basic teaching allocation as bl01: two vCPUs, 4096 MiB of RAM and a 32-GiB virtual system disk. These numbers make comparison straightforward. They are not sizing advice for a production application.
The new VM consumes additional host resources. Keep bl01-baseline and recovery copies shut off, and avoid running more guests than the host can support comfortably. If you run bl01 and bl02 together, their nominal RAM allocation alone totals 8 GiB, before host and virtualization overhead.
Storage requires a separate budget. A 32-GiB virtual disk is a limit presented to the guest. A sparse host image may consume less space now and more later. A future baseline copy adds another allocation. Host free space must cover the anticipated combined growth rather than just today’s image-file size.
Inside the guest, the full disk is also not identical to usable root-filesystem space. Space can belong to partition metadata, the ESP, /boot, volume-manager metadata, unallocated volume-group capacity and filesystem overhead. The next chapter measures those layers instead of expecting df / to equal the VM manager’s disk capacity.
A practical capacity note might say:
Guest: 2 vCPUs, 4096 MiB RAM, one 32-GiB system disk.
Host: enough free space for the new disk and one future full copy.
Concurrency: run only the guests needed for the current exercise.
