Growth review: before adding data services or storage experiments.
Use your measured host free-space value in the real record. Do not copy a fictional number into a capacity decision.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Choose a storage policy, not just a checkbox
text:
Choose a storage policy, not just a checkbox
For the guided installation exercise, use the entire new guest disk, enable LVM if offered, and leave encryption off. This is a controlled disposable lab choice. It keeps the first inspection focused on the relationship between disk, partitions, volumes and filesystems.
Logical Volume Manager, or LVM, groups storage into allocatable volumes. Its introductory vocabulary is:

A physical volume is a block device prepared for LVM use, often a partition.
A volume group is a pool built from one or more physical volumes.
A logical volume is an allocated block device drawn from that pool.
A filesystem can be created on a logical volume and mounted at a path such as /.

These layers let storage allocation change without treating each filesystem as permanently tied to a fixed disk partition. They also introduce additional state to inspect. LVM by itself does not provide independent backup or guarantee tolerance of a disk failure.
The Subiquity storage guide describes guided use of a disk and the storage objects the installer can create. “Use an entire disk” authorizes replacing that disk’s previous layout; it does not mean every byte must become part of the root filesystem.

Reserved growth space can be intentional
The installer may leave free capacity in the volume group. That capacity can support later allocations or extension. It is different from free blocks inside an existing filesystem. A root filesystem can be nearly full while the volume group still has unallocated capacity; using that capacity requires an explicit allocation and filesystem-growth operation.
For the first guided pass, retain the proposed allocation after reviewing it, and record what was left free. Do not enlarge everything simply to make two displayed numbers agree. The goal is to understand the layout before changing it.


Encryption requires an access and recovery decision
On a real portable or sensitive system, leaving storage unencrypted can expose data if the device is lost. Encryption policy belongs in the installation decision because introducing it later may require migration or reinstallation.
An encrypted installation also needs an unlock method. Ask who supplies it after an unattended reboot, whether a console is available, where recovery material is stored, and what happens when relevant hardware or firmware changes. Hardware-backed unlock and a typed passphrase have different operational dependencies.
Do not put an encryption passphrase into the installation worksheet. Record the responsible person and the protected location of the recovery material. A backup of encrypted bytes is unusable without the necessary keys; a running unlocked machine still needs access controls. The next installation chapter on manual choices will treat encryption and swap directly, and later storage/security parts deepen those mechanisms.


Separate filesystems express separate policies
A separate filesystem for application data can make capacity limits, mount options and recovery procedures clearer. It also creates another mount whose absence or failure can affect boot and services. A separate /home is useful in some workstation workflows but is not a universal requirement for servers.
For bl02, do not invent separate filesystems for every directory. Use the guided layout as a measured baseline. Later exercises add a spare disk and explicit data mounts with a clear reason. Keep that future spare disk detached during this installation, reducing the number of possible destructive targets.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Plan account access before the first reboot
text:
Plan account access before the first reboot
Create the guest account learner with a unique lab password. The same username on bl01 and bl02 does not imply that the accounts share identity state or credentials. A local numeric user ID also has meaning within its account database; matching numbers across machines do not automatically establish a shared identity service.
For this pass, the graphical console is the primary access path. Do not enable remote login merely because an installer offers it. Remote access later requires its own authentication and exposure decisions.
After installation, acceptance will include logging in through that console and checking the account’s administrative authorization. A privilege check is more useful than assuming the first account must be configured exactly as expected. Preserve recovery access until the intended login path has been tested after reboot.
Choose a hostname that reflects the lab role and is not easily confused with the host workstation. Record the difference between a hostname and a DNS record: setting bl02 inside the guest does not automatically make every other machine resolve that name.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
text:
Make networking assumptions explicit
During installation, attach bl02 to the already inspected setup NAT network from Part 01. Use one NIC and DHCP for this initial pass. Later, while shut down, move that NIC to blpractice and verify the change. Do not attach both networks as a shortcut.
The plan should distinguish four functions:








Function
What it supplies
Evidence to collect




Address configuration
An address and prefix on the guest interface
Guest interface report


Routing
A next-hop/path choice for nonlocal traffic
Route table and intended destination


Name resolution
Names mapped to usable addresses
Resolver configuration and a relevant lookup


Software source access
Actual access to installer/package services
Installer mirror test or package operation



Success in one row does not prove success in the next. A DHCP lease does not prove that a mirror is reachable. A mirror failure can come from DNS, routing, proxy requirements, clock problems or the remote service.
Record whether the environment requires a proxy. A proxy is an intermediary for selected network requests, not another name for the default gateway. Do not enter a router address into the proxy field unless that router actually runs the required proxy service. If the network requires authentication or inspection that the lab cannot satisfy, resolve the host/network prerequisites before committing an installation dependent on remote sources.
For an offline installation, record exactly which installation and package artifacts are available locally and which setup actions must wait. Do not promise that a full update will complete while the VM is deliberately isolated from its repositories.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Decide what may change during installation
text:
Decide what may change during installation
An installer can offer to refresh itself. Package repositories also change over time. Two installations from the same ISO can therefore produce different final versions if one refreshes the installer or retrieves newer packages.
For this lab, accept supported installer updates when connectivity allows, and record the choice. Then record installed versions after boot. Reproducibility here means you can explain and repeat the essential design choices, not that two disks must be byte-for-byte identical.
The distinction becomes important in automation. Repeating “use the latest image and all updates” repeats a policy but may not reproduce the same artifacts. Exact reconstruction needs retained artifacts or controlled repositories, together with configuration and secrets management. Later provisioning chapters introduce those controls after you understand an interactive installation.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
text:
Review the destructive boundary
Before accepting storage changes, compare the installer’s proposed target with the host-side record. The authorized destructive scope is one new disk attached only to bl02.
Use at least two independent identifiers where available: the guest-visible size and device/model/serial information, and the host manager’s disk source associated with the selected VM. If the installer unexpectedly lists several writable disks, stop and inspect attachments. Do not infer that the smallest one is safe or that /dev/vda always names the intended target.
The installer may show device names such as /dev/vda, /dev/sda or /dev/nvme0n1 according to the presented controller. These names describe an observed enumeration. They are not labels saying “this disk is disposable.”
A review record should explicitly say:
May replace: the new bl02 system disk recorded in this plan.
Must preserve: bl01, baseline/recovery copies, host disks and shared data.
Unexpected disk or size: stop and reconcile the VM definition.
Recovery if this install fails: recreate only bl02's disposable target;
                                keep verification records and notes.
This is not a request to make every administrative action bureaucratic. It is a way to catch an expensive class of mistake before the irreversible write begins.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Completed plan for the guided lab
text:
Completed plan for the guided lab
Fill in the measured fields rather than leaving them as assumptions:







Decision
Planned value or required record




Purpose
Inspect a second installation and its guided LVM layout


VM/guest name
bl02 / bl02


Artifact
Verified 26.04 LTS amd64 server ISO; exact filename and digest


Firmware
UEFI; actual Secure Boot setting recorded


Resources
2 vCPUs, 4096 MiB, new 32-GiB disk


Storage
Guided whole-disk LVM; encryption off for this lab


Disk target
Actual host image path and guest-visible identifiers


Access
Graphical console; local learner account


Setup network
Actual inspected NAT network name


Practice network
blpractice, one NIC, no external forwarding


Software choices
Standard server selection; no optional bundles


Expected changes
Installer refresh decision and package retrieval recorded


Acceptance
Installed boot, login, storage map, privilege check, network-phase check


Recovery
Preserve bl01; recreate only the disposable bl02 target if necessary

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
section: Practice: explain a change before approving it
text:
Practice: explain a change before approving it
Review three hypothetical changes to the plan:

The guest needs to restart unattended while its owner is away, and encrypted root storage is required. What unlock and recovery decisions are missing?
The VM manager shows a 32-GiB disk, but the installer lists two writable disks of that size. What must be reconciled before continuing?
The installation must be repeatable in six months without Internet access. Which artifact and repository assumptions need to change?

A good answer names the dependency rather than simply selecting another checkbox. The first needs an approved unattended-unlock design and recovery route. The second needs exact attachment/target identification. The third needs retained media, required packages and initialization inputs, plus a way to validate their provenance and applicability later.

title: Planning Firmware, Storage, Identity and Networking
text:
Recall card

Define the machine’s role and acceptance checks before selecting defaults.
Keep host, VM and guest identities separate.
Firmware mode, partition layout, Secure Boot and encryption solve different problems.
Plan capacity at host, virtual-disk, volume and filesystem layers.
Record access and recovery requirements before committing storage changes.
The exact destructive target must be identifiable, not merely familiar-looking.
Repeating a policy and reproducing exact artifacts are different goals.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Create the target and reconcile its identity
text:
Create the target and reconcile its identity
In Virtual Machine Manager’s system QEMU/KVM connection, create a new VM from the verified local ISO. Set the planned resources, a new qcow2 disk, the name bl02 and the inspected setup network. Choose to review hardware before beginning installation.
Confirm UEFI, the selected Secure Boot setting, one writable disk and one NIC. Check that no original lab disk, host filesystem share or spare experiment disk was accidentally attached. Record the new disk’s actual host path and the ISO path. A VM name alone is not proof that the storage is new.
On the host, you can inspect the definition through libvirt:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02 --details
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domiflist bl02
An optical device is separate from the writable system disk. If the VM manager is still at a pre-creation wizard stage, complete creation first and inspect before accepting destructive storage changes in the installer. The important boundary is the disk-write confirmation, not whether the GUI has already opened a display.
Open the graphical console and boot the installer. If the console displays an existing login prompt before you have installed anything, investigate the selected VM and disk instead of assuming the image completed an unattended installation.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Turn installer screens into recorded decisions
text:
Turn installer screens into recorded decisions
The Subiquity installer walkthrough describes the supported screen sequence. Labels and optional screens can vary with the image and installer refresh. Follow the intended decisions below and record the actual result rather than relying on an exact screenshot.
Select the appropriate language and keyboard layout. If an installer refresh is offered, make the decision recorded in your plan and note whether it occurred. Select the standard server installation for this pass. Verify DHCP on the one setup NIC, enter a proxy only if required, and let the installer test the chosen mirror.
Do not treat a failed mirror test as permission to make unrelated storage changes first. Resolve required source access or explicitly choose a supported offline path with its limitations recorded. A progress indicator does not replace the final operation result.

Review the proposed storage map
Choose guided use of the entire new 32-GiB disk, select LVM if offered, and leave encryption off for this introductory comparison. Before accepting the storage summary, identify:

The exact disk whose partitions will be replaced.
The ESP and its intended mount point.
Any separate /boot filesystem.
The partition or device that will become an LVM physical volume.
The volume group and root logical volume.
The filesystem mounted at / and any capacity left unallocated.

The terms were introduced in the planning chapter; the table below connects them to review questions.







Proposed object
Review question




Disk/partition table
Is this the disposable disk recorded for bl02?


ESP
Is there a firmware-readable boot partition for the selected UEFI path?


/boot
Is this separate from root, and what size is proposed?


LVM physical volume
Which partition supplies the pool?


Volume group
How much capacity will it contain?


Root logical volume
How much of the pool is allocated to root?


Root filesystem
What type and mount point will be created?



Save a transcription or screenshot of the summary outside the guest. This becomes evidence to compare with the installed state. Do not publish an installer screen containing passwords or other secrets.
Only accept the destructive confirmation when the map matches the plan. Once confirmed, installation can begin writing in the background while later questions are answered. Closing the console is not an undo operation. The detailed storage guide explains guided disk selection and supported storage objects.


Finish identity and software selection
Set hostname bl02 and create the planned learner account with its unique password. Keep the graphical console as the access method for this pass. Skip optional SSH installation and optional software bundles so the initial comparison has a small, deliberate scope.
Read the installation result and any failed steps. If installation completes, reboot when offered and detach the ISO when requested. Keep the virtual system disk attached. The intended next boot is from installed storage, not another run through the installer.
If a later screen fails after storage was committed, assume the disk may be partially installed. Preserve the relevant error and plan before deciding whether to recreate this disposable target. Do not describe a partially completed installer as though no change occurred.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Prove that the installed guest booted
text:
Prove that the installed guest booted
Log in through the bl02 graphical console. Record identity and the root mount:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
The observed hostname should match the plan. The root mount should be the installed filesystem rather than the installer’s temporary live environment. A hostname alone is insufficient because it can be duplicated; combine it with the manager’s selected VM and the storage evidence.
Check the firmware context:
if test -d /sys/firmware/efi; then
  printf 'This guest boot used UEFI\n'
else
  printf 'No EFI firmware interface found; reconcile the boot mode\n'
fi
If available, inspect the guest firmware boot entries without changing them:
sudo efibootmgr -v
efibootmgr reports UEFI boot-manager information when the required firmware-variable interface is available. Its manual also documents mutation options; none are needed here. Record BootCurrent, the boot order and relevant entry paths if reported. An entry in the list is evidence of configuration, not a guarantee that every fallback path has been tested.
If the utility is absent, record that fact and continue with the available firmware and filesystem observations. Do not modify boot order or delete entries just to make output resemble an example.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Draw the storage stack from observations
text:
Draw the storage stack from observations



A guided UEFI installation can place root on LVM while keeping boot files on separate partitions.


Start with the guest block-device tree:
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
The lsblk manual explains these columns. A deliberately simplified, illustrative result is:
NAME                      SIZE TYPE FSTYPE      MOUNTPOINTS
vda                        32G disk
├─vda1                      1G part vfat        /boot/efi
├─vda2                      2G part ext4        /boot
└─vda3                     29G part LVM2_member
  └─ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv 14.5G lvm  ext4        /
This is a teaching example, not a promise of the installer’s exact defaults. Names, sizes, partition numbers and filesystem choices can differ. Rounded sizes also hide partition alignment and metadata overhead. Use your own output in the installation record.
Read the tree from the outside inward:

vda is the disk presented to the guest.
vda1, vda2 and vda3 are partitions on that disk.
vda1 contains the FAT-family ESP filesystem mounted at /boot/efi.
vda2 contains a separate filesystem mounted at /boot.
vda3 is used by LVM rather than directly mounted as a filesystem.
The LVM logical volume provides the block device on which the root filesystem lives.

The doubled hyphens in a device-mapper name can be an escaping representation of hyphens in LVM names. Do not decode a complex name by guesswork when the LVM tools can report the volume-group and logical-volume names explicitly.
If your output shows root directly on a partition rather than on an LVM logical volume, compare it with the storage summary you accepted. That may be a different valid layout, but it does not match this chapter’s intended LVM experiment. Record the deviation; do not run LVM creation commands over a mounted root in an attempt to retrofit the example.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Distinguish three kinds of free space
text:
Distinguish three kinds of free space
Inside this one VM, “free space” can mean at least three different things:








Location
Meaning
Typical observer




Outside partitions
Disk sectors not assigned to a partition
Partition-layout inspection


Inside a volume group, outside logical volumes
LVM extents available for allocation
vgs, pvs


Inside a filesystem
Filesystem capacity available for file data/metadata
df



There is also free space on the host filesystem containing the qcow2 image. It belongs to a different administrative layer.
An extent is an allocation unit used by LVM. The volume group can have free extents even while the root filesystem has no free blocks left. The Subiquity storage-layout reference explains that its LVM layout can reserve capacity for later use rather than allocating all of it to root immediately.
Inspect the three LVM views:
sudo pvs -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_size,pv_free
sudo vgs -o vg_name,vg_size,vg_free
sudo lvs -o lv_name,vg_name,lv_size,lv_path
pvs reports physical volumes, vgs volume groups, and lvs logical volumes. The respective pvs, vgs and lvs manuals define their report fields. These are inventory commands; they do not ask LVM to resize anything.
Suppose your measured volume group is roughly 29 GiB and its root logical volume is roughly 14.5 GiB. A report of roughly 14.5 GiB unallocated in the group would account for the difference. Those extents are not automatically usable as files under /; allocation and filesystem growth would be separate changes.
Now inspect the mounted filesystem:
df -h /
df -i /
The filesystem’s displayed capacity can be smaller than the logical volume because the filesystem uses some space for its own structures and may reserve capacity. Unit conventions and rounding also affect displayed values. Do not add figures from different layers as if they were independent disks.

Worked diagnosis: “the installer lost half my disk”
The report is that a 32-GiB VM has a root filesystem around half that size. Competing explanations include a deliberately smaller root logical volume, another partition consuming capacity, an unexpectedly smaller virtual disk, or an inspection of the wrong mount.
A discriminating sequence is:

Confirm the VM manager’s selected guest and virtual capacity.
Check lsblk for the guest disk and partition tree.
Use findmnt --target / to identify the actual root source.
Use vgs and lvs to compare group capacity with logical-volume allocations.
Use df / only after identifying the filesystem being measured.

If the difference is free volume-group capacity, the explanation is reserved allocation, not lost storage. Whether to extend root depends on workload requirements and the intended use of that reserve. This chapter stops at a supported explanation; later storage work performs growth with prerequisites and verification.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Connect persistent mount intent to current mounts
text:
Connect persistent mount intent to current mounts
A filesystem has an on-disk identity as well as a current device pathname. A UUID is an identifier commonly used to refer to a filesystem independently of a changing enumeration name. A partition can have its own PARTUUID, which is a different identifier.
Inspect both types and the installed mount configuration:
lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE,UUID,PARTUUID,MOUNTPOINTS
cat /etc/fstab
findmnt --target /boot --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
findmnt --target /boot/efi --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
/etc/fstab describes persistent mount and swap configuration. A typical filesystem entry includes a source, mount point, type and options, followed by fields used by maintenance tools. The fstab manual defines those fields. Do not paste UUIDs from an example into your installed configuration: they belong to specific objects.
Compare intent with observation. An fstab entry shows a requested persistent configuration; findmnt shows the current mount view. The findmnt manual distinguishes finding the filesystem containing a target path from querying an exact mount point.
This distinction matters for /boot. If it is not a separate mount, findmnt --target /boot can report the root filesystem that contains that directory. That is not an error by itself. It is evidence about the chosen layout. For our illustrative guided layout, expect separate mount results and reconcile any difference with the installer summary.
Do not edit fstab during this inspection. A wrong persistent mount reference can become a boot problem after the next restart, even while the current mount still works. The boot and storage parts provide deliberate exercises for those changes.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Observe swap without assuming its form
text:
Observe swap without assuming its form
Swap supplies a location where selected memory pages can be stored outside ordinary RAM management. It may be backed by a partition, a file or another supported arrangement. An installed swap file is not necessarily visible as a separate block-device row in lsblk.
Inspect active swap:
swapon --show
free -h
The reporting form of swapon lists active areas; it does not activate a new one. Its manual distinguishes reporting from configuration operations. Record what is actually active, including an empty result if no swap is enabled.
An fstab entry and an active swap report answer different questions, just as they do for mounts. Also separate swap capacity from application memory requirements: swap does not make a small VM equivalent to one with enough RAM for its working set. Later memory and storage chapters examine reclaim behavior, encryption and performance implications.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Verify access and compare the two installations
text:
Verify access and compare the two installations
Before calling the installation complete, confirm that the planned account can log in after a reboot and that administrative authorization is as intended:
id
sudo -l
sudo -l reports allowed commands according to the account’s policy and may request authentication. Do not publish its output if it exposes sensitive local policy. An unexpected restriction or broad grant belongs in the acceptance record, not in a silent workaround using another account.
Make a comparison table using observations from each guest:









Property
bl01
bl02
Explanation of difference




Exact installer/build record
Your value
Your value
Media or installer refresh


Running kernel
Your value
Your value
Installed/activated updates


Firmware mode
Your value
Your value
Selected virtual firmware


Root source and filesystem
Your value
Your value
Storage choice


Volume-group free capacity
Your value or not applicable
Your value
Allocation policy


/boot and ESP
Your values
Your values
Boot layout


Active swap
Your value
Your value
Installer/configuration choice


Console login and privilege check
Observed result
Observed result
Account policy


Current NIC source
Host observation
Host observation
Lab phase



Do not fill the table from memory of the settings you clicked. Use the installed evidence. Intended configuration and resulting configuration are separate columns in a good installation record.
After completing any required setup-network maintenance, shut down bl02, move its one NIC to blpractice, and restart it through the console. Verify its address, route and host-side NIC source as in Part 01. The loss of external repository access is expected in the isolated phase.
If bl01 and bl02 run together, they are separate installations with distinct guest identities. This differs from starting two unprepared copies of the same disk image. Keep the old baseline and recovery clones shut off.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
section: Diagnose installation failures at the correct stage
text:
Diagnose installation failures at the correct stage







Symptom
Evidence to collect before retrying




Installer never starts
Verified attached media, guest architecture, firmware selection and console message


Storage target differs from the plan
Host disk attachments, guest disk sizes and installer summary


Mirror or package step fails
Exact source, network phase, address/route and installer error


Installation completes but no bootable disk is found
Firmware mode, optical-media state, boot entries and installed disk attachment


Login succeeds but root layout differs
Accepted storage summary, block tree, LVM reports and current mounts


Root seems smaller than the virtual disk
Partition, volume-group, logical-volume and filesystem capacities



Keep a failure record before recreating the target. For this disposable VM, reinstalling may be reasonable, but it should test a changed hypothesis rather than repeat the same unknown failure. A failed install on a real machine with existing data would require a different recovery plan; do not transfer the lab’s permission to recreate a disk into another environment.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
text:
Practice and completion criteria
Draw your own storage map from the host image path to the guest root mount. Label the ESP, any separate /boot, physical volume, volume group, root logical volume, filesystem and free allocation at the relevant layers. Explain any difference from the illustration.
Then answer:

Why can whole-disk guided installation leave free volume-group capacity?
Why does a root-filesystem free-space report not establish free space on the host?
What does an fstab entry establish that a current mount report does not, and vice versa?
What evidence proves you booted the installed guest rather than the live installer?

Completion means a successful installed boot and login, a storage map derived from commands, a reconciled comparison with the installer summary, and a documented final network phase. Keep the resulting record outside the guest before creating a new baseline.

title: Guided Installation and the Resulting Storage Layout
text:
Recall card

The storage confirmation is a destructive boundary; review the exact target first.
Trace capacity through disk, partition, volume and filesystem layers.
Whole-disk selection does not imply whole-disk allocation to root.
UUIDs, device names and mount paths describe different identities and relationships.
Persistent configuration and current activation require separate observations.
A successful installation is a verified result against a plan, not only a completed progress bar.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
text:
Start with mount responsibilities
A partition describes a region of a disk. A filesystem gives that region a structure for files. A mount attaches a filesystem to a path in the running system. These three decisions are related but different: naming a directory /srv does not create a partition, reserve capacity, or encrypt its contents.
For this exercise, /srv will hold a small demonstration file representing future service data. No real service is installed yet. Use this teaching layout:








Object
Allocation
Purpose




EFI System Partition
Installer-created; record actual size
UEFI boot files; mounted at /boot/efi


Root partition
24 GiB, ext4, mounted at /
Operating system, home directory and logs


Service-data partition
8 GiB, ext4, mounted at /srv
A separately measurable data filesystem


Swap partition
2 GiB, swap use
A small disk-backed swap area for this lab


Unallocated space
Remainder
Visible reserve for a future storage exercise



The sizes are a lab budget, not a production sizing formula. Account for the ESP, partition-table metadata and alignment before expecting the remainder to equal a particular number. Check how the installer interprets its size units and record the displayed result.
This unencrypted design keeps /boot as a directory on the root filesystem. The ESP is still a separate filesystem. A separate /boot is useful or necessary for some other boot/storage arrangements; it is not synonymous with the ESP.

Why separate service data?
A separate filesystem makes its capacity boundary easy to see. If /srv fills, it does not consume the free blocks in the root filesystem. However, application logs or temporary files elsewhere can still fill root. Separation also introduces another mount that must succeed and another allocation that can be badly sized.
Consider two imagined workloads:

A small learning VM with little persistent data benefits from a simple layout and few failure points.
A server storing growing application data benefits from an explicit data budget, but needs monitoring and a growth/restore plan for that budget.

Neither layout creates redundancy. Both partitions in this lab depend on the same virtual disk and host storage. Deleting that image loses both filesystems.



Storage boundaries have different jobs.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
text:
Build the custom layout
In Virtual Machine Manager, create bl02-manual with the specified resources and fresh disk. Before accepting any installer storage changes, inspect the guest definition on the host:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02-manual --details
Confirm that its writable image is different from both existing guests. Keep only the new disk and installation ISO attached. Record the image path outside the guest, together with the intended layout.
Boot the installer in UEFI mode. At storage selection choose Custom storage layout. On the new disk select the boot-device action, inspect the ESP the installer creates, then add the root and /srv GPT partitions with the sizes, filesystems and mounts above. Add a 2-GiB partition with swap use. Leave the remainder unallocated. Canonical documents these controls and the automatic ESP creation in its Subiquity storage guide.
Screen wording can vary with the installer build or refresh. If an action differs, inspect its summary before proceeding. Do not substitute shell formatting commands against a guessed /dev/vda to force agreement with the lesson.
Before the final disk-write confirmation, reconcile all four intended objects. There must be exactly one root mount, the intended ESP mount, one /srv filesystem, and the selected swap area. Check that the remaining capacity is genuinely unallocated rather than silently absorbed into the last partition. Save the summary outside the guest.
Complete installation with hostname bl02-manual, the planned learner account and no optional SSH server or software bundles. Detach the ISO at the requested stage and boot from the new disk.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
section: Verify boundaries rather than partition numbers
text:
Verify boundaries rather than partition numbers
In the installed guest:
hostnamectl
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,UUID,MOUNTPOINTS
findmnt --mountpoint / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
findmnt --mountpoint /srv --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
findmnt --mountpoint /boot/efi --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
findmnt --target /boot --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
swapon --show
cat /etc/fstab
--mountpoint asks for an exact mount. --target asks which mounted filesystem contains a path. Thus this design should return a distinct /srv mount, while /boot should resolve to the root mount. The findmnt manual explains the distinction. A missing /srv result needs investigation even if the directory exists.
Use your observed device names and UUIDs; partition numbering is not an acceptance criterion. Record the actual swap arrangement too. If the installer also configured a swap file, explain that deviation and its capacity rather than silently claiming the partition is the only active swap.
Compare capacity at the filesystem layer:
df -h / /srv
df -i / /srv
Expect two different filesystem sources. The formatted capacity will differ from the requested partition size. df -i counts inodes, the filesystem records needed to represent files; running out of these can prevent creation even with free data blocks.
Create a small acceptance marker only after confirming the exact /srv mount:
printf 'bl02-manual storage acceptance\n' | sudo tee /srv/installation-check.txt
sudo cat /srv/installation-check.txt
The shell pipe sends the text to tee, which writes it using administrative privilege. There is no need to make all of /srv writable by every user.
Reboot through the console, log in again, repeat the exact mount check and read the marker. Persistence of the text proves little by itself: a file accidentally written beneath an absent mount can also survive a reboot. The file and its filesystem source together are the evidence.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
section: Choose encryption by the recovery requirement
text:
Choose encryption by the recovery requirement
Block-device encryption transforms stored blocks so that unlocking material is required to interpret their contents. Linux installations commonly use LUKS, a format that manages encrypted-volume metadata and key slots, together with the kernel’s device-mapper encryption facility. An unlocked mapping presents a usable block device to the layers above it.
For an installation using encrypted LVM, a possible data path is:
partition → LUKS container → unlocked mapping → LVM → filesystem → mount
Observe the actual order rather than assuming every encrypted system uses this one. Encryption and volume management answer different questions: access to stored blocks versus allocation of capacity.
A passphrase prompt creates an operational dependency. Who can supply it after a power failure? Can that person reach the virtual console? Where is the recovery material stored if the VM or its host is unavailable? Record the answers before installing an encrypted root.
Encryption protects covered data while locked. It does not prevent an authorized process on the running, unlocked system from reading that data. Boot partitions may remain outside that coverage. A host administrator who controls the running VM also occupies a different trust position from someone holding only a powered-off disk image.

Optional encrypted installation comparison
Use another disposable guest, bl02-crypt, with a fresh 40-GiB disk and the same remaining hardware budget. Shut down the other guests if host RAM is limited. In guided storage select LVM and its passphrase encryption option. This is a separate comparison, not a requirement to reproduce the manual partition scheme inside encryption. The installer storage documentation describes this guided choice.
Store the unique unlock passphrase in a trusted password manager outside the guest. Do not put it in screenshots, command history or the installation record. Record only where authorized operators retrieve it.
After installation, perform a full shutdown and start through the VM manager. A saved-memory resume does not test an unlock from cold boot. Observe the unlock prompt, supply the passphrase and verify console login. Then inspect:
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
sudo cat /etc/crypttab
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
swapon --show
/etc/crypttab describes encrypted devices to establish at boot; its fields include the mapping name, source device, key specification and options. It is not a listing of mounted filesystems. See the crypttab manual. Treat the configuration as sensitive inventory and do not publish any referenced key material.
Draw the root device’s ancestry from the observed tree. Identify the unencrypted boot objects separately. This exercise proves the tested passphrase and boot path work; it does not prove recovery from damaged encryption metadata. Keep this guest disposable until a separate backup and recovery design exists.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
section: Swap is part of the data-protection decision
text:
Swap is part of the data-protection decision
Swap can contain information from process memory. An encrypted root does not establish that every swap location is encrypted. Trace each active area: a swap file inside a covered filesystem has a different storage path from an independent unencrypted swap partition.
For the main manual lab, the swap partition is deliberately unencrypted and the guest holds no sensitive workload. For the optional encrypted guest, record whether swap is present and where its backing storage sits relative to the encryption layer. Do not assume a swapfile will appear as its own block-device row.
The 2-GiB allocation is simply a bounded lab choice. Production swap sizing depends on workload, memory pressure, storage latency and recovery policy. Hibernation adds requirements for saving and resuming memory state; it is not part of this server VM exercise. No universal multiplier of RAM substitutes for those decisions.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
text:
Diagnose a layout mismatch








Symptom
Distinguishing evidence
Appropriate next action




/srv exists but exact mount lookup is empty
Compare fstab, UUIDs and current mounts
Preserve evidence; do not start writing service data there


/srv and / show the same source
Exact mount query versus containing-filesystem query
Reconcile the installed layout with the recorded summary


Swap report is empty
Compare active state with installer summary and fstab
Record missing activation; avoid inventing a device path


Encrypted guest never reaches login unattended
Console shows an unlock prompt
Supply the planned credential; evaluate unattended-boot needs separately


Unlock fails after restart
Keyboard layout, selected guest and stored credential
Check identity and input; formatting is not a password-recovery action


Partition budget differs
Installer units, ESP allocation, rounding and remaining space
Explain the arithmetic before resizing anything



An accidentally omitted /srv mount can hide a further trap. Files written into the underlying root directory become hidden when another filesystem is later mounted there. They are not automatically transferred into the mounted filesystem. Capture the current state and plan recovery before adding or removing a mount over existing data.
For an installation mistake on this empty teaching guest, recreating its verified disposable disk and reinstalling is a valid reset. First preserve the evidence explaining the mistake. On a populated server, preserving and restoring data comes before repartitioning.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
text:
Practice and acceptance record

Install the manual guest and record the accepted storage summary.
Explain which objects share the same failure domain despite having separate mounts.
Prove /srv is a distinct filesystem before and after reboot, and confirm the marker’s contents.
Record active swap, root free space and the unallocated reserve at their respective layers.
If you completed the encryption extension, demonstrate a cold-boot unlock and identify what remains outside encryption.

Keep the manual guest powered off as comparison evidence, or retire it using the VM manager after saving the record. Before deleting any image, verify its path is the one assigned to this guest. Continue the next chapter on the guided bl02 installation.

title: Manual Storage Choices, Encryption and Swap
text:
Recall card

A path, a mount, a filesystem and a partition are different objects.
Separate capacity is useful only when its size and mount lifecycle fit the workload.
Encryption adds an unlock and recovery dependency; it does not create a backup.
Swap protection follows its backing storage, not the hostname’s security label.
Accept the installed layout using observed sources and a reboot, not installer intent alone.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
text:
Prove access before changing software
Open the VM console and log in as learner. Confirm identity:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
id
sudo -l
sudo id -u
The hostname should be bl02. id describes the current account and groups; sudo -l reports its permitted administrative commands. The final command should print 0 if policy allows it, demonstrating that this invocation ran with root’s numeric user ID. Group membership by itself is not a complete policy test.
If authentication or authorization fails, stop the update workflow. Check the selected guest, username and keyboard layout first. Preserve the exact error. Use a separately established administrator or the documented lab recovery route if available. Do not weaken policy globally to obtain a successful-looking test. On this fresh disposable guest, a documented reinstall is preferable to improvising an untracked privilege bypass.
Create a private notes directory in the guest:
umask 077
mkdir -p "$HOME/first-boot-record"
date -Is > "$HOME/first-boot-record/started.txt"
uname -r > "$HOME/first-boot-record/kernel-before.txt"
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id > "$HOME/first-boot-record/boot-id-before.txt"
umask 077 restricts permissions on newly created files and directories in this shell. It does not repair permissions on pre-existing files. The boot ID identifies this boot instance; it is different from the installed machine’s persistent identity. Copy the final notes outside the guest using the lab’s established evidence procedure. A record only on the failed disk is a poor recovery aid.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
text:
Establish an update preflight
Check the resources and dependencies the package transaction needs:
df -h / /boot /boot/efi
df -i /
ip -brief address
ip route
timedatectl status
The filesystem checks identify available capacity and inode pressure. The network commands show interface addresses and routes, not proof that a repository is reachable. timedatectl reports the clock and available synchronization status. An obviously wrong clock can affect validation and confuse the evidence timeline; establish correct time before interpreting expiry errors.
Inspect configured APT sources without changing them:
ls -l /etc/apt/sources.list.d
sudo cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources
If this file is absent, inspect the actual source files listed in that directory and /etc/apt/sources.list if present. Newer installations commonly use deb822 .sources files; imported configurations can use .list entries. Record the configured release suites and repository locations. A suite is a named collection of packages, such as a release’s main or update collection. Do not paste an example from another Ubuntu release into this guest.
The Ubuntu package-management guide describes source configuration and package administration. Review local source content before sharing it: private mirror URLs or proxy configuration may disclose internal information.



A first-boot acceptance pass includes verification after restart.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
section: Refresh metadata and review the transaction
text:
Refresh metadata and review the transaction
Run these commands one at a time and read each result:
sudo apt update
apt list --upgradable
sudo apt --simulate upgrade
apt update refreshes repository metadata; it does not install upgrades. If it reports failed downloads or validation errors, do not treat a partial refresh as a clean result. Keep the error and investigate before proceeding.
The simulation previews proposed package changes without applying them. Review package names, download size, disk-space impact and any packages left unchanged. A simulation is a plan against the current state, not a reservation: another package job can change that state before the real transaction.
When the plan is understood, run:
sudo apt upgrade
Read the actual confirmation before accepting. This command can install new dependencies but does not remove installed packages to satisfy an upgrade. full-upgrade has different removal behavior; do not switch to it simply to make a pending count disappear. These distinctions are documented in Ubuntu’s apt manual.
Allow the command to complete. Package hooks can update boot artifacts or restart services. If a configuration-file question appears, inspect the proposed difference and record your decision; there is no universal answer that fits both a fresh file and a deliberately customized one.
Review the final result and package history:
sudo tail -n 80 /var/log/apt/history.log
sudo tail -n 80 /var/log/apt/term.log
sudo dpkg --audit
History records package operations; the terminal log supplies transaction detail. The dpkg manual defines the audit of package-database consistency and partial installation state. A clean audit normally produces no output, but that alone does not prove every application works. Keep both the transaction result and the post-reboot checks.

An automatic update may already be running
A fresh host can have background package activity. Inspect it before assuming a lock is stale:
systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager
systemctl status apt-daily.service apt-daily-upgrade.service --no-pager
sudo journalctl -b -u apt-daily.service -u apt-daily-upgrade.service --no-pager
A scheduled timer, an active job and a completed update are different observations. A lock error should lead to identifying the current package process and waiting for legitimate work to complete. Deleting a lock file or killing an updater can turn harmless serialization into damaged state. If work appears stuck, preserve its status and logs before choosing recovery.
Inspect the installed automatic-update configuration separately:
apt-config dump | grep -E 'APT::Periodic|Unattended-Upgrade'
No matching lines is an observation, not a reason to invent defaults. Canonical’s automatic-updates guide describes the settings and logging. Record whether unattended installation and automatic reboot are configured; an enabled update timer does not alone establish either policy. This first-boot pass leaves policy changes for the dedicated package chapter.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
section: Inventory what the machine is running
text:
Inventory what the machine is running
Collect four views before reboot:
systemctl --failed --no-pager
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --no-pager
sudo ss -lntup
These views answer different questions:







View
Question




Failed units
What has entered a failed state?


Running services
Which service units are currently running?


Service unit files
What service definitions and enablement states exist?


Listening sockets
Which TCP listeners and UDP endpoints are bound?



Enabled does not mean running. An inactive service may be started on demand; a successful one-shot job can finish without remaining running. The systemctl manual defines these states and listings. Do not enable every inactive unit or clear failure records merely to make the inventory look healthy.
In ss, -l selects listening sockets, -n keeps numeric addresses and ports, -t and -u select TCP and UDP, and -p requests process details. Root privilege helps reveal ownership. A loopback address such as 127.0.0.1 limits that binding to local access; a wildcard address can accept traffic on more interfaces, subject to routing and policy. A socket listing is not a remote reachability test. The ss manual documents the filters and process reporting.
For this console-only installation, an SSH listener is an unexpected finding to explain. Check package/service choices and any socket activation rather than assuming a port number alone identifies the application. NAT does not make every guest listener irrelevant to other guests or the host.
For each unexpected item, record its name, purpose, owner and evidence before deciding whether to change it. This avoids disabling a service that provides the network or other dependency used by the current investigation.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
section: Reboot and repeat the acceptance checks
text:
Reboot and repeat the acceptance checks
Inspect Ubuntu’s reboot-request marker if present:
if test -f /run/reboot-required; then
  cat /run/reboot-required
  if test -f /run/reboot-required.pkgs; then
    cat /run/reboot-required.pkgs
  fi
fi
uname -r
An installed kernel package and the running kernel are different states. The marker is a useful package-maintenance signal, not a complete certification that no restart is needed when absent. For this lab, perform one planned reboot after the successful update transaction regardless, with the console open:
sudo systemctl reboot
Wait for normal startup and log in again. Then inspect:
hostnamectl
sudo id -u
uname -r
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
systemctl --failed --no-pager
sudo ss -lntup
Compare the boot ID with the saved value: it should have changed. Compare the kernel with kernel-before.txt: it may remain the same if this transaction installed no different kernel. Do not invent an expected version number. Root must still resolve to the intended installed storage, administrative access must work, and any new failures or listeners need explanation.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
text:
Worked diagnosis: repository refresh fails
Suppose the console works but apt update reports a name-resolution failure. The evidence points to an update dependency before any package upgrade has started.

Preserve the exact repository hostname and error from the output.
Inspect the guest NIC and default route using the preflight commands.
Run getent hosts followed by that actual hostname, without the URL scheme or path. This asks the configured host-lookup system for its addresses.
Check the VM manager’s network attachment against the recorded setup NAT network.
If the guest was deliberately moved to the isolated network, restore the planned setup attachment and repeat the checks.

A successful lookup only narrows the problem: proxies, transport access, repository availability and signature validation can still fail. A signature error with successful network access calls for checking time, source identity and trust configuration, not disabling authentication. After correcting the identified cause, repeat apt update and require a clean result before reviewing an upgrade.
For a failed reboot, keep the console message and identify whether firmware, the bootloader, early startup or the normal service manager is visible. Avoid repeated forced resets. Use the known baseline to restore this disposable lab if necessary, recording that updates applied after that baseline will need to be repeated. A checkpoint restores captured state; it is not equivalent to a package-by-package downgrade.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
text:
Practice and acceptance record
Complete a table with observed results:







Acceptance item
Evidence to retain




Correct guest and administrator
Hostname, selected VM, successful policy test


Update prerequisites
Capacity, time, network attachment and sources


Package change
Reviewed proposal, completion result and history


Normal restart
New boot ID and observed console login


Intended root
Mounted source and filesystem


Services and endpoints
Explained failed units and listeners


Recovery
Location of baseline and notes outside the guest



An unresolved failure belongs in an open-issues entry, not in an accepted baseline. Once checks pass, shut down normally and use the checkpoint method established in the lab chapter to label this state bl02-first-boot-accepted. Retain the earlier baseline until the new one has been verified. Keep credentials out of the label and notes.
As a bounded exercise, disconnect the setup NIC in the VM manager while retaining console access. Observe the changed address/route state and failed repository access, then restore the same attachment and verify a clean metadata refresh. Do not start an upgrade while connectivity is intentionally broken. The success criterion is a documented fault, its discriminating evidence and demonstrated restoration.

title: First Boot: Administrative Access, Updates and Service Inventory
text:
Recall card

Test administrative access before making changes that depend on it.
Metadata refresh, package installation and activation after reboot are separate steps.
Review update errors and lock ownership before attempting repair.
Running, enabled, listening and remotely reachable are different claims.
Accept the baseline only after a normal reboot and repeated checks.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
text:
From presentation to usable interface
A physical bus exposes devices and identifying information to the kernel. In a VM, the hypervisor presents virtual hardware according to the guest definition. A virtual NIC may be backed by a host network, but the guest sees the virtual device model, not necessarily the physical NIC in the host. A driver is kernel code that knows how to operate a device. Driver binding associates a discovered device with a suitable driver; the driver probes and initializes it. The kernel driver-model documentation explains matching and binding.
After successful initialization, the kernel can expose an interface such as a network device or a block device. /sys gives a view of kernel objects and their relationships. Device events can reach systemd-udevd, which applies userspace rules and stores properties. Some devices also have nodes under /dev; network interfaces normally do not need a /dev node. The udevadm manual describes querying the udev database.



Device discovery produces several complementary views.


There is no guarantee that each step succeeds. A device can appear on a bus with no bound driver, bind while failing a later function, or provide a working interface whose network configuration is wrong. A readable device node does not prove its application-level use is correct.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
text:
Establish what the guest sees
Start bl02 with its original setup NIC and open its console. Confirm the guest and running kernel:
hostnamectl
uname -r
ip -brief link
ip -brief address
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
Record the original interface name and hardware address from ip -brief link. The address here is the link-layer MAC address, not the IP address. Record the root disk and current mounts from lsblk, but do not assume a particular /dev/vdX name or change any disk.
For PCI devices, use these commands if lspci is installed:
lspci -nn
lspci -nnk
-nn shows numeric vendor and device identifiers as well as names where available; -k adds driver information. The Ubuntu lspci manual defines the options. A missing utility means this view is unavailable, not that no PCI devices exist. If the lab has a working setup network, you can inspect the package proposal with apt show pciutils and sudo apt --simulate install pciutils, then install pciutils with sudo apt install pciutils after reviewing it. If the network is unavailable, continue with the views already present and record that limitation.
In lspci -nnk, Kernel driver in use is evidence of a bound driver for the listed PCI function. Kernel modules lists candidates, not a promise that each candidate is active. A built-in driver may be in use without appearing in lsmod; lsmod lists loaded modules, not all code built into the running kernel.
For USB devices, lsusb, when available, supplies another bus view. A USB device will not necessarily appear in the PCI listing. Conversely, a virtual NIC can appear behind a virtual transport and have additional objects in the kernel hierarchy. Select the bus relevant to the actual device instead of treating one command as an inventory of everything.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
section: Connect an interface to its kernel and udev records
text:
Connect an interface to its kernel and udev records
Substitute the actual original interface name for INTERFACE below. lo is the local loopback interface and is not the virtual NIC in this exercise. Use the selected name as one shell variable so the commands inspect the same object:
IFACE=INTERFACE
ip -details link show dev "$IFACE"
readlink -f "/sys/class/net/$IFACE/device"
udevadm info --query=property --path="/sys/class/net/$IFACE"
For example, replace IFACE=INTERFACE with IFACE=enp1s0 only if that is the name actually observed. The link details show the interface’s current state and MAC address. The sysfs link points towards its underlying device hierarchy; the resulting path depends on the driver and transport. udevadm info reports properties known to udev. An absent property or path is evidence to investigate, not proof that every device on the bus is missing.
If available, inspect the driver associated with the network interface:
ethtool -i "$IFACE"
ethtool may not be installed; record that and use the sysfs and PCI views. On a layered virtual device, the network interface’s driver can differ from the driver shown for its parent PCI function. Follow the sysfs path instead of declaring a contradiction from two different layers. The reported driver version or firmware version can be empty or uninformative on virtual devices.
Check the kernel messages for the current boot:
sudo journalctl -k -b --no-pager | grep -Ei 'firmware|virtio|network|error|fail'
This filtered view is a starting point, not a complete diagnostic. It can return no lines or unrelated warnings. The pipeline’s exit status can be nonzero when grep finds no matches. Look at the surrounding unfiltered journal for the actual device and time before attributing a line to your interface. Keep the complete relevant messages, including device identifiers, when saving evidence.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
section: Distinguish driver code from device firmware
text:
Distinguish driver code from device firmware
System firmware, such as UEFI, starts the machine and participates in boot. Device firmware can be code or data that a driver requests for a device after the kernel starts. The kernel firmware documentation describes these requests, which can include optional data as well as required firmware.
A missing-firmware message does not automatically mean that the missing file caused the symptom. Establish the exact filename, device, driver and whether the subsequent initialization failed. Some drivers request alternatives or optional files. Conversely, no matching log line does not prove that all firmware dependencies are satisfied.
On Ubuntu, investigate the installed files and package ownership before changing anything:
dpkg-query -W linux-firmware
apt-cache policy linux-firmware
If the package query reports that the package is absent, record that rather than assuming all devices need it. Package availability and versions depend on enabled sources and updates. For a filename actually reported in the log, inspect the path and ownership after identifying the file on the host. For example, with the observed absolute path substituted for /actual/path/to/file:
ls -l /actual/path/to/file
dpkg-query -S /actual/path/to/file
The owner query can identify an installed package providing an existing path; a missing path has no installed owner to report. Do not copy an arbitrary binary from a forum or change module policy just to suppress a message. Check the distribution’s package, the hardware/vendor documentation and the running kernel’s support for that exact device. Package installation is a change: review its source and proposed transaction, retain console access and plan the required restart if the documented remedy calls for one.
For a boot-critical storage device, missing support can prevent reaching the installed root at all. That is a different recovery context from a missing secondary network interface: preserve the boot console message, use known-good recovery media and avoid changing the only working boot path during this lab.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
section: Lab: add a second virtual NIC and observe its lifecycle
text:
Lab: add a second virtual NIC and observe its lifecycle
The experiment tests presentation and enumeration, not Internet connectivity. It needs no packet exchange and does not require configuring the new interface. The original NIC remains attached as recorded; the second NIC connects only to blpractice, the host-local practice network. That network includes the host and any attached guests; it is not an Internet connection and does not protect against a compromised host.

Save the initial ip -brief link output. On the host run sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domiflist bl02 and save its output. Ensure the accepted bl02 baseline is available and the console works.
Shut bl02 down cleanly. In Virtual Machine Manager, add a second network interface using the blpractice virtual network. Select a model supported by your installation, such as virtio, if the manager offers it. Do not edit the original NIC, system disk, firmware or boot order. Apply the change while the guest is off.
On the host inspect the persistent guest definition and record both MAC addresses, models and network sources:

sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system dumpxml --inactive bl02
Find the two <interface> elements; identify the added one by its blpractice source and MAC address. Domain XML can contain host paths and other local details, so redact before sharing. Do not run both cloned guests at once merely to compare them: their guest identities were copied.

Start bl02, log in through the graphical console and inspect:

ip -brief link
ip -brief address
lspci -nnk
sudo journalctl -k -b --no-pager | grep -Ei 'virtio|network|firmware|fail'
Omit lspci if the utility is unavailable and note the missing view. Match the new guest interface to the recorded MAC address. Names and PCI addresses can vary. The interface can be administratively down and have no IP address; either is compatible with successful enumeration. If it has an address, record it, but do not infer that it has an Internet route.

Substitute the new interface name in the IFACE commands from the earlier section. Record its sysfs path, udev properties and, if available, ethtool -i driver. Compare the two interfaces by MAC address rather than by guessed names. If the new MAC is not visible, use the diagnosis table before making changes.
Shut down the guest, remove only the added NIC in Virtual Machine Manager, and apply the change. Inspect the inactive XML again to verify the original NIC and its original network source remain. Restart and confirm the original console login and NIC, and that the added MAC no longer appears in ip -brief link. Do not remove a disk or delete a network definition during cleanup.

The success record has a before/after MAC list, the second interface’s observed driver or a stated observation limit, and a cleanup check. Rebooting after removal tests the persistent guest definition. If the original guest configuration has been altered unexpectedly, stop and reconcile it with the accepted baseline before proceeding.

A worked diagnosis: the new NIC is not in ip link
Suppose the manager shows an added NIC, but the guest lists only the original one and loopback. First compare the host’s inactive definition with the configuration you intended and check that the VM was restarted after applying the change. A pending persistent change is not evidence that the currently running guest has received it; the live definition can be inspected with sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system dumpxml bl02 while running.
If the NIC is present in the running definition, inspect lspci -nnk, the kernel journal and sysfs. A new PCI function without a driver suggests a different next investigation from no new bus object at all. If there is a bus object and a driver but no expected interface, inspect probe messages and the actual device hierarchy. If the interface appears with a different name, the recorded MAC resolves the identity without changing network settings.
A driver binding is still not an end-to-end network test. A bound NIC with no IP address may simply lack configuration or a reachable address server. Configuration, routing and network services have their own evidence and are developed later.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
text:
Common observations and next questions








Observation
What it supports
Next question




Device absent from guest bus inventory
No matching object in that particular view
Is it present in the running VM definition, and is this the correct bus?


PCI device listed without driver in use
Enumeration occurred; binding is not shown
Does the running kernel support the numeric ID, and what does the journal report?


Firmware request failed
A driver requested a file
Was the file required, and did initialization of this device fail?


Interface exists but no IP address
The network interface was registered
Is it up and configured, and is the intended network available?


Device appears only after restart
Persistent configuration differed from running state
Was the intended hardware change applied to the live guest?


Device works but a user cannot open it
Kernel registration alone is insufficient
Which node, permissions and process identity apply to this device?



Avoid testing by unbinding a root-disk driver, removing a production NIC, or repeatedly loading random modules. Record the observed boundary, form a specific hypothesis and choose a reversible test that does not cut off the recovery path.

title: Hardware and Virtual-Device Discovery
text:
Acceptance and recall
Save the host definition evidence and guest observations outside the VM, redacting MAC addresses, serial numbers or host paths before sharing as appropriate. The original NIC should be restored and usable, the added NIC removed, and the original root disk still mounted. Note any unresolved driver or firmware question rather than marking it fixed from a package name alone.

A VM exposes its configured virtual hardware; host hardware inventory is a different view.
Enumeration, driver binding, device initialization and working configuration are separate claims.
/sys, udev, bus listings and the journal show different evidence about the same device.
A firmware request must be tied to an actual device and failure before choosing a remedy.
Use a MAC address and before/after observations to identify the experimental NIC and verify cleanup.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
section: Two ways to produce a machine
text:
Two ways to produce a machine
An installation image contains an installer and a source from which an operating system can be assembled onto a target. An autoinstall configuration answers installer questions about that target. The installer still creates partitions, installs files and configures the system. The input file is not itself an installed disk.
A prebuilt machine image, in contrast, already contains an operating-system filesystem and boot configuration in a disk image. A provisioning system creates an instance from that image and applies instance-specific information such as hostname, credentials and network settings on first boot. The image must match the platform, architecture and boot method; merely copying the installer ISO does not make it a bootable installed disk.








Decision
Installer with configuration
Prebuilt machine image




Base
Installer media and package sources
Prepared filesystem and bootable disk


Target storage
Created during installation
A new disk or copy derived from the image


Host-specific inputs
Installer configuration and, optionally, later first boot
Instance metadata and first-boot configuration


Evidence
Installer result, logs and installed state
Image provenance, initialization result and instance state


Recovery concern
Reproduce inputs and preserve data before reinstalling
Keep a trusted base and separate persistent data/identity



An image can speed up deployment, but image age matters: an old image still requires a patch and acceptance process. An installation that uses a live repository may resolve different package versions on different dates even when its configuration is unchanged. Reproducibility requires recording media, configuration, sources and results, not just retaining one YAML file.



Provisioning starts with a common input and ends with an individually verified host.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
section: Identity is not the same as a disk copy
text:
Identity is not the same as a disk copy
The recovery clone in the first lab deliberately copied an existing machine, including its guest identity and credentials. It was kept powered off and used one copy at a time. A machine intended to run as an independent instance needs its own hostname, machine identity, credentials, network attachment and, when used, SSH host keys. A distinct VM name or MAC address does not by itself replace everything stored inside the guest disk.
Cloud images commonly use cloud-init, which reads an instance’s configuration from a datasource and runs initialization stages. Its first-boot explanation describes how cached state and instance IDs influence whether per-instance configuration runs. Copying an initialized disk and simply changing a name is not a complete image-preparation procedure. Do not run cloud-init clean on the existing lab hosts as a shortcut; it changes state and must be part of a deliberate image lifecycle.
An installer has its own context. Cloud-init can deliver data to the live installer, while Subiquity interprets the nested autoinstall configuration; cloud-init on the eventual installed system has its own first-boot role. Canonical’s interaction guide explains the distinction. A successful installer-data read alone is not proof that every target-side initialization step succeeded.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
text:
Prepare a local installer seed
A seed is a small source of provisioning data. This lab uses a local NoCloud seed ISO, attached separately from the verified server installer ISO. It avoids depending on a configuration web server. The seed contains a password hash, so keep its files and disk image private; a hash is still sensitive because an attacker can attempt offline guesses.
On the host, in a private shell session, create a working directory and check for the required utilities:
umask 077
mkdir -p "$HOME/bl02-auto-seed"
cd "$HOME/bl02-auto-seed"
command -v cloud-localds
command -v openssl
If cloud-localds is unavailable on an Ubuntu host, inspect apt show cloud-image-utils and sudo apt --simulate install cloud-image-utils, then install it with sudo apt install cloud-image-utils after reviewing the proposal. On another host distribution use its package documentation or prepare the seed on a trusted Linux machine. openssl must also be available. Do not put the seed on a shared web server.
Create a unique lab password and keep it in your password manager. In the terminal run:
openssl passwd -6
Enter the password at the prompts; this generates a salted SHA-512 password hash without placing the plaintext on the command line. The terminal will display the hash. Do not use a production password, paste the hash into a public issue, or record it in shell history. Keep console scrollback private as well.
Create user-data in your editor with the following content. Replace the entire REPLACE_WITH_HASH string with the generated hash, keeping the single quotes around it. Do not include the plaintext password.
#cloud-config
autoinstall:
  version: 1
  identity:
    hostname: bl02-auto
    username: learner
    password: 'REPLACE_WITH_HASH'
  storage:
    layout:
      name: direct
  ssh:
    install-server: false
  shutdown: poweroff
The first line marks cloud-config data. autoinstall contains the installer’s instructions; indentation is significant. The identity section establishes the initial account. The direct storage layout installs to the selected disk without the guided LVM layer used on bl02. It replaces data on that disk. The SSH server is not requested by this configuration; verify actual listeners later. The completion action asks the installer to power off so the media can be detached before the next boot. These settings are described in the autoinstall reference.
Create the required metadata file and the seed image:
printf 'instance-id: bl02-auto-installer-01\n' > meta-data
cloud-localds seed.iso user-data meta-data
ls -l user-data meta-data seed.iso
The instance-id labels this installer instance’s seed. It is not a substitute for the installed system’s machine ID or a universal identity-reset mechanism. If repeating the exercise on a new target, use a distinct seed instance ID and hostname. The NoCloud datasource reference describes the local data source, and the installer quick start demonstrates cloud-localds for installer data.
Run these commands in the private directory. umask affects files created in the current shell; if the directory or files existed already, inspect their permissions explicitly. Any user who can read seed.iso can extract its configuration. Restrict directory traversal and grant the libvirt/QEMU process only the access needed for this lab; the exact file permissions and access-control rules depend on the host. If the VM manager cannot open the file, use a suitable private libvirt storage location or its documented access controls rather than making the directory world-readable. Record the seed path, but not its contents or hash in shared notes.

Review before allowing writes
Check the exact user-data file in your editor for the header, indentation, hostname, username, quoted hash, direct layout and poweroff. Check there is no remaining placeholder. If you have a matching Subiquity source checkout and its validator dependencies, Canonical provides pre-validation instructions. A schema check cannot prove that the intended disk is attached or that runtime installation will succeed. Never execute an unfamiliar installer configuration or its commands without reviewing them.
This minimal configuration omits explicit network, mirror, locale and keyboard settings. Installer defaults and network access can affect the result. Record the installer image/build, network and source observations; do not claim byte-identical reproduction across different runs. The chapter’s scope is an introductory seed, not a fleet policy.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
section: Install on a new, single-disk guest
text:
Install on a new, single-disk guest
In Virtual Machine Manager create bl02-auto with UEFI, the resource budget above, one new 32-GiB writable system disk, the verified server installer ISO and the setup NAT network. Choose to review hardware before installation. Add seed.iso as a second read-only CD-ROM. Both optical images are sources; neither is the writable target disk. If your manager cannot add a second optical device, follow Canonical’s local-seed workflow using a supported virtual-machine interface and keep the same disk isolation conditions.
Before booting, inspect the selected VM on the host:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02-auto --details
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domiflist bl02-auto
