Confirm exactly one writable guest system disk, its new host path, both intended optical sources and the expected NIC source. Verify that no disk from bl01, bl02, a baseline or your host filesystem is attached. A new VM name is not evidence of a new disk. If the seed cannot be read because of host permissions, fix access to the intended file and recheck the definition; do not select a different disk as a workaround.
Boot the server installer ISO through the graphical console, leaving the seed attached. Do not add the autoinstall kernel parameter in this exercise. With the local configuration detected, the installer should ask for confirmation before modifying a disk; this behavior is described in the local-volume quick start. The parameter suppresses that confirmation, so it is deliberately omitted.
At the confirmation, stop and reconcile the actual target with the host-side single-disk record. The direct layout’s default selects the largest eligible disk. With only one writable system disk this is bounded, but “largest” is unsafe as a general selection rule on a multi-disk machine. If the target is ambiguous, cancel and investigate; validation of the YAML does not validate the target. After confirming the disposable target, allow installation to continue and observe its outcome.
If the usual full interactive installation screens appear instead of an autoinstall confirmation, the installer may not have received the seed. Stop and investigate the seed attachment and format before making storage changes. If installation fails after confirmation, the disk may already be partially written. Preserve the relevant error and treat the target as changed.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
section: Detach sources and verify the result
text:
Detach sources and verify the result
After the installer reports completion and powers off, remove both the installer ISO and seed ISO from this guest’s virtual optical devices, leaving its system disk and NIC in place. Inspect domblklist again, then boot the installed disk. Log in at the console as learner with the lab password.
Collect the following evidence inside bl02-auto:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
id
sudo -l
sudo id -u
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
systemctl --failed --no-pager
sudo ss -lntup
The hostname should be bl02-auto; administrative access should work according to the intended policy; root should be on the newly installed disk. Compare the actual partition and filesystem layout with the direct-layout intent and with bl02’s recorded LVM layout. Names and sizes are observations, not fixed strings to copy from this book. Investigate unexpected failures or listeners before accepting the host.
If cloud-init is installed on the target, inspect its own status and logs without assuming that they are the installer’s logs:
cloud-init status --long
sudo journalctl -b -u cloud-init-local.service -u cloud-init.service -u cloud-config.service -u cloud-final.service --no-pager
Service names or available output can differ; record unavailable views. A status indicating completion does not prove all application requirements. The installer’s own records are typically under /var/log/installer/ on an installed Ubuntu system. Inspect filenames before reading them; generated installation records can contain credential hashes, network details or other sensitive inputs. Restrict access and redact before sharing.
Perform the first-boot update and reboot checks established earlier when this guest is going to be kept. Keep the acceptance record outside the VM. Detaching the seed prevents accidental reuse at the next boot; it does not securely erase the seed or any installer logs copied into the guest.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
text:
Diagnose by stage








Observation
Check
Recovery direction




Installer starts interactively
Both optical sources, seed contents, #cloud-config header and autoinstall indentation
Correct the seed, rebuild it and boot the disposable target again


Cannot attach seed
Host file path and QEMU access permissions
Grant appropriate access to the intended seed; do not expose it publicly


Configuration rejected
Installer error and schema validation
Fix the reported field; validate again and retain the failure record


No safe target is evident
Host disk list and installer’s selected disk
Stop before confirmation; detach unrelated writable disks


Installer fails after disk confirmation
Installer console and logs
Treat target as partially modified; recreate only the verified disposable target


Login fails on installed guest
Selected guest, username, keyboard and password-hash substitution
Preserve evidence; use the lab recovery/reinstall plan rather than copying a shared password


Guest re-enters installer
Optical attachments and boot source
Shut down, detach installation media and boot the installed disk



When a seed was modified after cloud-localds ran, the already-created ISO still contains the earlier data. Rebuild it from the corrected files before booting again. If access to installer logs is needed during a failed run, use the installer console’s reported log location and capture only the relevant, redacted evidence.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
text:
Practice and cleanup
Create an acceptance record containing the installer ISO identification, VM/disk and seed paths, seed instance ID, selected storage intent, observed root source, console login and sudo result, failed-unit/listener review, and media-detachment check. Keep the password and hash out of the record.
As a thought experiment, plan a second instance: list which values must differ and which can remain shared. A real second run needs a new disk, hostname, instance ID and unique credentials; it must also have separate guest identity and an explicit network role. Compare installed results as observations rather than assuming a matching input implies an identical system.
To finish, power off the guest if it will not be used. Retain or retire its dedicated disk only after checking the exact VM and host path. Delete the private seed files and ISO when they are no longer needed, according to your host’s data-handling practice; ordinary deletion is not a guarantee of secure erasure. Do not remove the verified installer ISO or any other guest’s disk. If preserving the guest, keep its account recovery method and separately protected record.

title: Image-Based and Unattended Installation
text:
Recall card

An installer plus configuration creates a target; a prebuilt machine image already contains a system.
A provisioning seed is both a configuration input and a potential secret-bearing artifact.
Installer data and installed-system first-boot data operate in different contexts.
Review the target disk at the write boundary; a schema-valid file can still select the wrong device.
Accept a host only after confirming its identity, access, storage and operating state.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
text:
Decide what recovery means
A repair attempts to return the existing installation to working order. A reinstallation creates an operating system again on a target disk. Reprovisioning builds a replacement from specified inputs and configuration. A restore brings selected prior state back from a saved copy. An incident can require more than one of these actions.
Before changing a failed machine, ask what must survive and what should be regenerated. A replacement guest used alongside the original has a distinct identity; a replacement that takes over the original’s role needs an explicit cutover that prevents duplicate identities and conflicting access. This exercise stops before cutover and uses a new hostname.








Category
Example
Decision in this exercise




Reproducible base
Installer, packages and updates
Install a fresh base and verify it


Host-specific configuration
An explicitly chosen demonstration config
Copy, review and restore this one file


Workload data
A small demonstration data file
Restore and compare its content


Machine identity
Hostname and /etc/machine-id
Keep the replacement’s newly created identity


Secrets and trust
Passwords, SSH host keys, service certificates
Do not include them in this lab bundle


Hardware-dependent state
Filesystem UUIDs, network interface names, firmware variables
Observe the replacement and configure against its own values


External dependencies
DNS, upstream services, data stores
Record dependencies; this demonstration has none



A machine ID is confidential, should normally be unique, and is not a file to copy casually from one running host to another. The Ubuntu machine-id manual explains its role. SSH host keys and certificates also have lifecycles of their own: preserving an identity may be required for some migrations, while unplanned duplication or replacement can break trust. Treat that as a deliberate service-specific decision.



A replacement is accepted after selected state is restored and verified.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
text:
Define a small recovery contract
For this lab, success means:

The original bl02 remains intact and shut down during offline export.
A fresh guest called bl02-recovery boots from its own disk and has working console and administrator access.
The selected configuration and data files are restored from the host-side bundle.
Both restored files match their source copies byte for byte and remain present after reboot.
The replacement retains its own hostname and disk identities; no automatic network cutover occurs.

The two demonstration files are not a real application’s configuration format. They represent an operator-controlled setting and a small persistent data record. Their values contain no passwords or personal data.

Identify what would be needed for a real host
Before reinstalling a real service, inventory its packages and versions, configuration ownership, service units, data locations, mount sources, users and numeric ownership, certificates, keys, network addresses, external dependencies and restore order. Also record which software or configuration is generated and which authoritative system owns it.
A blanket copy of /etc can overwrite fresh network settings, account databases, filesystem references or machine identity with values from different hardware. Old /etc/fstab UUIDs can point nowhere or to the wrong device; old interface names can refer to a different adapter. A package list does not include application data, and a data directory copied while a database is writing may not be a consistent backup. Select and validate each component for its owner and recovery method.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
text:
Prepare the demonstration on bl02
Start the original guest and log in through its console. Confirm that this is the intended system:
hostnamectl
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
sudo id -u
The hostname should be bl02, root should match its recorded installation, and the administrative check should return 0. If any value is unexpected, stop and reconcile the selected VM and disk with your lab record.
Create the two lab-only files. Stop if either directory already exists: it may contain a previous experiment that you should preserve rather than overwrite.
sudo test ! -e /etc/bl-recovery-demo
sudo test ! -e /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo
Both commands must finish successfully with no output. If either fails, do not run the following creation commands; inspect and choose a fresh lab name instead. Otherwise:
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/bl-recovery-demo /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo
printf 'mode=observe\n' | sudo tee /etc/bl-recovery-demo/settings.conf
printf 'inventory-record=alpha\n' | sudo tee /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo/record.txt
Record the paths and their purpose in your change notes. In this demonstration both files are nonsecret and readable by the local learner. Real configuration and workload data can have stricter permissions and may require application-specific backup tools.

Assemble and inspect a selected bundle
As learner inside bl02, create a new private staging directory. This command fails if the directory already exists; choose a new name rather than mixing old and new contents.
umask 077
mkdir "$HOME/bl-recovery-export"
mkdir "$HOME/bl-recovery-export/config" "$HOME/bl-recovery-export/data"
cp /etc/bl-recovery-demo/settings.conf "$HOME/bl-recovery-export/config/"
cp /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo/record.txt "$HOME/bl-recovery-export/data/"
cd "$HOME/bl-recovery-export"
sha256sum config/settings.conf data/record.txt > SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
Both lines should report OK. The checksum records the bytes selected at export; it does not establish provenance or prove that a running application was consistent. This tiny demonstration has no writer and no application transaction. For a real workload, use the application’s quiescing or backup method and test its restore.
Create an archive in the home directory, then inspect its members and hash:
cd "$HOME"
tar -cf bl-recovery-demo.tar bl-recovery-export
tar -tf bl-recovery-demo.tar
sha256sum bl-recovery-demo.tar
The archive should contain only the staging directory, its two subdirectories, the two files and SHA256SUMS. Record the archive hash in your private lab notes outside the VM. A checksum comparison detects unintended changes when the expected hash is protected separately; it is not a signature or a substitute for trusted handling.
Shut the guest down cleanly:
sudo poweroff
On the host, confirm that the system libvirt domain is actually shut off:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl02
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02 --details
Proceed only when it reports shut off and the disk matches your record. Paused or saved-memory state is not a clean shutdown. Leave it off until the offline read is complete.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
section: Export the bundle to the host
text:
Export the bundle to the host
The following workflow uses guestfish, a libguestfs tool that can inspect a shut-down guest filesystem. On an Ubuntu host, its package is guestfish; inspect the proposed installation with apt show guestfish and sudo apt --simulate install guestfish before using sudo apt install guestfish if needed. Other distributions package the tooling differently. The guestfish manual documents --ro, automatic inspection (-i) and the libvirt connection option. If automatic inspection cannot open the installation, stop and use a separately documented export method; do not guess block-device paths or write to the original disk.
On the host, create a new private handoff directory. This intentionally fails if the name already exists, so old recovery material is not silently replaced:
sudo mkdir -m 0700 /var/tmp/bl02-recovery-handoff
sudo guestfish --ro -i -c qemu:///system -d bl02 \
  download /home/learner/bl-recovery-demo.tar \
  /var/tmp/bl02-recovery-handoff/bl-recovery-demo.tar
sudo sha256sum /var/tmp/bl02-recovery-handoff/bl-recovery-demo.tar
Compare the host hash with the separately recorded guest hash. Both must match before proceeding. The absolute source path assumes the learner home created in the installation lab; if your actual home differs, use the observed path. The host directory belongs to root and is a staging location, not encrypted storage. Real archives may contain sensitive data and need protected access, encrypted storage and a separate failure domain.
The host copy and the original guest disk are distinct files but reside on the same host in this lab. Loss of the host or its storage can destroy both. If a truly independent backup is required, transfer the verified artifact to separately managed storage and demonstrate retrieval; this exercise does not claim to have done so.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
section: Install a replacement without touching the original
text:
Install a replacement without touching the original
Create a new VM named bl02-recovery with a new 32-GiB disk, UEFI, two vCPUs, 4096 MiB RAM and the setup NAT network. Attach the verified Ubuntu Server installer ISO. Use the guided-install workflow from earlier, with hostname bl02-recovery and a new unique learner password. It is acceptable for this fresh installation to have a different storage layout from bl02 because the two demonstration files will be restored by path, not by copying a filesystem image.
Before accepting disk writes in the installer, inspect the host definition:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02-recovery --details
Confirm the system disk path differs from bl02 and all baseline disks, and that no old writable disk is attached. After installation, detach the ISO and boot from the new disk. Verify hostname, root mount, console login and sudo id -u. Update the new system using the first-boot procedure as appropriate; record its installed and running versions. Shut it down cleanly before the host writes the handoff file into it.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
section: Deliver and inspect the bundle on the replacement
text:
Deliver and inspect the bundle on the replacement
On the host confirm both guests are off and identify the replacement disk:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl02
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl02-recovery
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02-recovery --details
Both states should be shut off, and the destination disk should be the new replacement disk. Do not proceed if a domain is running or if another tool is editing either disk. The virt-copy-in manual warns that writing into a live guest disk can corrupt it.
Copy the archive into the replacement’s existing /var/tmp directory:
sudo virt-copy-in -c qemu:///system -d bl02-recovery \
  /var/tmp/bl02-recovery-handoff/bl-recovery-demo.tar /var/tmp
virt-copy-in is also supplied by the Ubuntu guestfish package. This is a write to the replacement disk; -d bl02-recovery is the destination identity, not the source. If the tool cannot inspect the target, stop rather than trying other domains. Leave bl02 shut down, start bl02-recovery, and log in through its console.
Compare the replacement copy against the recorded archive hash:
sudo sha256sum /var/tmp/bl-recovery-demo.tar
sudo tar -tf /var/tmp/bl-recovery-demo.tar
Require the expected hash and the exact member list from the source before extracting. Only extract the archive you created and controlled in this lab. Archive extraction from untrusted sources requires additional path, link and provenance checks; do not apply an unfamiliar archive to system directories.
Create a fresh private restore workspace, extract there, then verify the contents:
umask 077
mkdir "$HOME/bl-recovery-restore"
sudo install -m 0600 -o "$(id -u)" -g "$(id -g)" \
  /var/tmp/bl-recovery-demo.tar "$HOME/bl-recovery-restore/bundle.tar"
tar -xf "$HOME/bl-recovery-restore/bundle.tar" -C "$HOME/bl-recovery-restore"
cd "$HOME/bl-recovery-restore/bl-recovery-export"
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
Both checks must say OK. A failure is a stop condition: preserve the failing copy and compare the source and host hashes before retrying. The archive and checksums can be changed together by an attacker, so the independently recorded archive hash and trusted transfer still matter. The install step makes a private working copy owned by the logged-in user, so extraction does not require root. Ownership and access controls must be explicitly checked for real data.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
section: Apply selected files, then prove the result
text:
Apply selected files, then prove the result
First ensure the destination paths do not already exist:
sudo test ! -e /etc/bl-recovery-demo
sudo test ! -e /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo
Only if both checks succeed, create the directories and install the reviewed files from the restore workspace:
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/bl-recovery-demo /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo
sudo install -m 0644 config/settings.conf /etc/bl-recovery-demo/settings.conf
sudo install -m 0644 data/record.txt /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo/record.txt
cmp config/settings.conf /etc/bl-recovery-demo/settings.conf
cmp data/record.txt /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo/record.txt
cmp prints nothing and exits successfully when each pair of files matches. The explicit install commands establish the destination mode; they do not recreate arbitrary ownership, ACLs, extended attributes or application state. Those are deliberate limitations of this demonstration, not a complete backup method.
Reboot bl02-recovery, log in again, and repeat the comparison from the restore workspace:
cd "$HOME/bl-recovery-restore/bl-recovery-export"
cmp config/settings.conf /etc/bl-recovery-demo/settings.conf
cmp data/record.txt /var/lib/bl-recovery-demo/record.txt
hostnamectl
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
sudo id -u
Success is two silent, successful comparisons, the replacement hostname, the expected root filesystem and working administrative access. Check exit status for each cmp before running the next command if it is unclear; a later successful command does not erase an earlier failure. The payload’s presence alone does not prove a real service consumes it. For an actual workload, add the service’s own configuration validation, startup, client request, data integrity and access-control tests.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
section: Worked diagnosis: restored configuration points to an old device
text:
Worked diagnosis: restored configuration points to an old device
Suppose a recovered config refers to the old guest’s filesystem UUID, but the replacement has a freshly created filesystem. The file can match the saved copy perfectly and still be wrong for the new machine.

Keep the old file in the restore workspace as evidence; do not apply it blindly to /etc/fstab.
Identify the intended role of the mount and use lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE,UUID,MOUNTPOINTS and findmnt to observe the replacement’s actual storage.
Determine whether the required data filesystem was restored or needs to be attached separately. A new root UUID alone is not proof that the old data exists.
Plan a configuration change using the replacement’s verified object and a recovery route. Test it with the appropriate mount and service checks before accepting the change.

This separates faithful file recovery from correct behavior on new hardware. A copied UUID, interface name, IP address or certificate may need adaptation, reissuance or an explicit cutover depending on the service.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
text:
Record, reset and retain
Save an acceptance record outside the guests: original and replacement VM/disk identities, the selected file paths, the archive hash, extraction and cmp results, reboot check, and any unresolved differences. Keep machine IDs, passwords, host keys and sensitive configuration out of shared notes.
Leave bl02 powered off until the offline-copy operations have finished. It can then be started for later work. The replacement is a separate teaching guest; shut it down when finished. Retain the host bundle only as long as needed and remove the temporary guest archive and workspaces using the exact recorded paths when they are no longer needed. Ordinary file deletion is not assured secure erasure. Do not delete either VM disk or any baseline as part of this cleanup.
The original’s two demonstration files can remain as documented lab state, or be removed later after verifying their exact paths and that no later experiment depends on them. A real host retirement additionally needs service cutover, data retention, credential revocation and an independently verified recovery plan.

title: Reinstallation and Host Configuration Recovery
text:
Recall card

Reinstallation creates a base; restoring selected configuration and data completes only part of a service recovery.
Preserve identity, regenerate it or migrate it only by an explicit service-specific plan.
Work on shut-down guest disks for offline writes and verify the selected source and destination.
Checksums compare bytes; they do not establish trusted provenance or application consistency.
Prove recovery after reboot and test the behavior a user or dependent service actually needs.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
The first handoff
When a machine starts, firmware initializes enough of the platform to select something to execute. In a VM, the hypervisor supplies virtual firmware, virtual devices and persistent firmware-variable storage. The UEFI boot manager can use configured boot options to locate an EFI application on a device. On this lab guest, an installed Ubuntu boot path normally starts from an EFI executable on disk, then continues through a bootloader and Linux startup.
A simplified sequence is:
power on → UEFI boot manager → EFI executable → bootloader → kernel
This is a map, not proof that every machine uses exactly the same executables. Booting from a network or removable medium introduces other paths. Linux also supports other firmware and boot arrangements; GPT alone does not prove the current boot used UEFI, and a UEFI interface does not prove that a particular disk uses GPT.
The UEFI boot-manager specification describes firmware boot options and their ordering. The later chapters follow the bootloader, kernel and early userspace; here the boundary ends at identifying the EFI application selected by firmware.



UEFI selects an EFI file through a boot option and a partition.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
Establish firmware and guest identity
Open the bl02 graphical console and log in. Check the selected VM in the manager as well as the guest hostname:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
if test -d /sys/firmware/efi; then
  printf 'This running system exposes the EFI firmware interface\n'
else
  printf 'EFI firmware interface is not available in this boot\n'
fi
On this UEFI lab guest, expect the interface to be present. If it is absent, check that you are in the intended installed guest rather than a different VM or a live installer, then inspect the guest’s firmware settings on the host. Do not switch firmware modes on the existing VM simply to force a match; the installed boot path and stored firmware variables depend on that choice.
The directory is evidence about the current boot environment. It does not by itself identify the exact firmware entry or prove that the next boot will use the same path.
On the host, inspect the configured virtual machine and its disks:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02 --details
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system dumpxml bl02
Find the system disk and the firmware loader and NVRAM-related settings in the XML, if present. The domain definition describes the configured virtual hardware; it is not a transcript of the firmware’s last decision. A live and persistent definition can differ after hardware changes. If necessary, sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system dumpxml --inactive bl02 shows the persistent definition. Protect the XML before sharing: it can contain host paths, MAC addresses and other local details.
UEFI variables for a guest may live in a separate virtual NVRAM file, while its ESP is inside the virtual disk. A VM disk copy and a firmware-variable copy therefore need to be considered separately in a recovery plan. Verify the actual XML and storage for your VM; do not assume two clones have the same or different NVRAM files from their names alone.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
Read the firmware’s boot options
If efibootmgr is available in the guest, request a verbose listing:
sudo efibootmgr -v
This form reads the boot variables; it does not alter boot order. If the tool is absent, record that and continue with disk inspection. On the setup network you may review apt show efibootmgr and sudo apt --simulate install efibootmgr, then install it with sudo apt install efibootmgr after reviewing the transaction. If access to EFI variables is unavailable, preserve the error and check the current firmware mode and permissions. An installed tool cannot manufacture firmware services for a non-UEFI boot.
A deliberately shortened, illustrative result might look like:
BootCurrent: 0003
BootOrder: 0003,0001
Boot0001* UEFI Virtual DVD ...
Boot0003* ubuntu HD(1,GPT,11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555,...)/File(\EFI\ubuntu\shimx64.efi)
Read this as follows:







Field
Meaning and limit




Boot0003
One firmware boot option numbered 0003; its label is ubuntu


*
The option is marked active in this display


BootOrder
The ordered list of options normally considered by firmware


BootCurrent
The option reported for the current boot, when firmware provides it


HD(...,GPT,...)
A device-path component referring to a GPT partition; the GUID identifies that partition


File(...)
An EFI file path on the selected filesystem, using firmware-style backslashes



BootNext, when present, requests an option for the next boot once; it is not the same as the persistent BootOrder. The UEFI boot manager can also offer a boot menu or follow platform-specific recovery behavior. A listed option is configuration evidence, not proof that its device and file are currently usable. BootCurrent is stronger evidence about the selected entry for this boot, but does not prove what the bootloader did afterwards or guarantee the next attempt.
Labels and numbers are not portable identities. Another VM can have a Boot0003 named ubuntu that points to a different disk. The sample GUID and path above are invented; never copy them into a repair command.
If the current option refers to removable media, network boot or an unexpected entry, reconcile it with the VM manager and console history before assuming the installed disk was selected. Do not use efibootmgr mutation options in this chapter. Changing or deleting firmware variables can affect future boots and belongs in a planned recovery exercise.

Where variables are exposed
Linux can expose UEFI variables through efivarfs. Inspect whether that filesystem is mounted:
findmnt --mountpoint /sys/firmware/efi/efivars \
  --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
An empty result means that exact mount was not found in the current mount namespace; it does not by itself explain why. The kernel efivarfs documentation explains that variables can be modified through this interface. Treat it as live firmware state. Do not delete, edit or clear files there to make a diagnostic command work.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
Identify the partition map
In the guest, inspect the disk and its partitions:
lsblk -o NAME,PATH,TYPE,SIZE,PTTYPE,PARTTYPE,PARTUUID,FSTYPE,UUID,MOUNTPOINTS
If the output wraps on a narrow console, widen the display or run separate commands with fewer columns. The lsblk manual explains that this is a view assembled from system information and that relationships can be more complex than a single tree.
Read the columns at their own layers:

PTTYPE identifies the partition-table type on a disk, such as gpt.
PARTTYPE describes a GPT partition’s type: a category, not the identity of this particular partition.
PARTUUID identifies the individual partition in the partition table.
FSTYPE and UUID identify a filesystem and its filesystem identifier, when present.
MOUNTPOINTS reports current mount locations; it is not a firmware boot option.

The GPT type GUID for an EFI System Partition is c12a7328-f81f-11d2-ba4b-00a0c93ec93b. Several ESPs can share that type; their partition UUIDs should distinguish the individual partitions. Compare identifiers case-insensitively where tools display a different letter case. The GPT specification describes partition types, unique GUIDs and the primary and backup tables. A backup partition table helps detect or recover certain metadata problems; it is not a backup of the files inside the partitions.
A filesystem UUID and a partition UUID can both be called “UUID” in conversation. They are not interchangeable. For the GPT hard-drive device path shown in the example above, compare its partition GUID with PARTUUID, not with the FAT filesystem’s UUID. lsblk may show additional layers such as LVM below another partition; do not expect the root filesystem to be a direct partition on every host.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
Inspect the EFI System Partition
An EFI System Partition (ESP) is a partition intended to hold EFI boot-related files in a firmware-readable filesystem. The guided Ubuntu UEFI installation normally mounts one ESP at /boot/efi. That path is Linux’s mount location after boot; firmware uses its device path and EFI file path independently of that Linux mountpoint. Canonical’s storage guide describes the installer’s UEFI boot-device setup.
First ask for an exact mount at the expected lab location:
findmnt --mountpoint /boot/efi --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
If the command produces a row, compare its source with the partition’s PARTUUID, filesystem type and disk in the lsblk output. Do not assume the ESP is mounted just because the /boot/efi directory exists. If there is no exact mount, stop before listing files at that path: a directory on root can otherwise look like an empty ESP. Investigate the installed layout and persistent mount intent first:
cat /etc/fstab
findmnt --target /boot/efi --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
The --target query identifies the filesystem containing a path and may therefore report / when /boot/efi is not mounted. An fstab entry represents mount intent, while findmnt reports current mounts. An ESP can also be mounted elsewhere on another system. Do not add a guessed fstab entry or format a partition to reproduce the example.
After confirming the exact ESP mount on the intended guest, list its EFI directory:
sudo ls -la /boot/efi/EFI
If the firmware entry refers to \EFI\ubuntu\shimx64.efi, and the matched ESP is the one mounted at /boot/efi, the corresponding Linux path in this example is /boot/efi/EFI/ubuntu/shimx64.efi. Inspect the actual directory and file named by your entry; filenames, capitalization and paths vary. A file with a plausible name is evidence of presence, not proof of signature validity or that it can boot the current system.
Some systems also place a removable-media fallback executable at an architecture-specific path such as EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI for x86-64. Its presence does not prove that the firmware will use it for a particular failure. Secure Boot and signed components are examined later; do not remove or replace EFI files during this inspection.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
section: Lab: build a boot-path evidence table
text:
Lab: build a boot-path evidence table
Collect observations in a private record and reconcile them in this order:








Question
Evidence
Your observation




Which guest and disk?
VM manager, domain disk list and hostnamectl
Record name and host disk path


Which firmware context?
VM definition and /sys/firmware/efi
UEFI for this running boot, or an explained difference


Which boot option?
efibootmgr -v, if available
BootCurrent, relevant option and path


Which partition?
GPT device path and lsblk PARTUUID
Matching partition on the intended disk


Which mounted filesystem?
Exact findmnt result and lsblk
ESP source, filesystem type and mountpoint


Which file?
Listed path on the matched ESP
Actual EFI file, or an explained mismatch


What is the recovery route?
Existing baseline, console and installer record
Location and limitations of those resources



For a simple local-disk GPT entry, the device-path partition GUID should match the observed ESP’s PARTUUID. If it does not, do not declare the boot broken immediately: the boot option may point to another ESP, or you may be examining a different boot entry or mount. Identify the actual objects first. A network or removable-media boot may not offer the same GPT comparison at all.
When a link is unavailable, mark the record unresolved. For example, the guest can run with an inaccessible variable interface; record the disk and mount evidence and the missing efibootmgr result separately. Do not invent a BootCurrent value.
Save the record outside the guest using the established lab evidence procedure. Redact device identifiers, host paths and firmware details before sharing outside your trusted environment. There is no need to publish a complete variable dump.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
Worked diagnosis: “the ESP is empty”
Suppose ls /boot/efi appears empty even though the system booted successfully. Candidate explanations include an ESP that was not mounted after boot, an ESP mounted at another location, a different boot disk, or genuinely missing files.

Confirm the selected guest and current boot context.
Run the exact mount query. If it is absent, inspect the containing filesystem and /etc/fstab rather than assuming the directory is the ESP.
Inspect lsblk for candidate ESP partition types and their individual identifiers.
If firmware variables are available, compare the actual selected boot option’s device path with the candidate partition UUIDs.
Once the correct ESP is mounted through a documented recovery procedure, inspect its actual EFI path and record the result.

This is an evidence sequence, not an instruction to mount or repair the ESP now. Do not mount or format a guessed device while the identity is unresolved. A successful past boot does not prove the relevant file still exists; the disk could have changed after firmware loaded it.
For a guest that cannot boot at all, preserve the console message, its VM definition and storage identity. Keep the existing disks untouched, use the verified recovery media and known baseline as the starting point, and determine whether the failure is firmware selection, loader, kernel, early root or later startup. Later chapters develop offline inspection and repair. A powered-off clone is a recovery aid with its own disk and NVRAM assumptions, not an independent backup against host loss.

title: Firmware, UEFI Variables, GPT and the EFI System Partition
text:
Practice and recall
On bl02, complete the evidence table and explain how the partition GUID in an observed GPT boot path relates to PARTUUID, while the filesystem UUID describes a different object. Identify one conclusion that would remain unproven if efibootmgr were unavailable. Compare your record with the installation chapter’s stored layout; explain any change before accepting the baseline.

Firmware chooses an EFI boot option before the Linux root filesystem is mounted.
Boot option number, partition type, partition UUID, filesystem UUID and mountpoint are different identifiers.
BootCurrent describes a reported current-boot selection; BootOrder describes configured priority.
A directory at /boot/efi is not evidence that an ESP is mounted there.
Preserve boot evidence and a recovery route before changing firmware variables or disk metadata.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
text:
Two decisions before Linux runs
UEFI selects an EFI executable through a firmware boot option or another firmware boot path. That executable can be a bootloader, an intermediary such as shim, or another EFI application. A bootloader can then present its own menu and choose a kernel, initial RAM filesystem and command line. The first decision is made by firmware; the second is made by the selected boot software.



GRUB and systemd-boot obtain menu entries differently.


On a typical Ubuntu UEFI installation, firmware may load shimx64.efi, which participates in loading GRUB. The actual path depends on installation, architecture and security configuration. On other systems firmware may load systemd-boot directly. The presence of files for both loaders is not enough to establish which one was selected.
Inspect the previously recorded BootCurrent and its path with sudo efibootmgr -v if the tool and EFI variable interface are available. On systems supporting the relevant interface, bootctl status can report additional loader information:
sudo efibootmgr -v
bootctl status
A missing command, unavailable variable or incomplete bootctl report is an observation limit. In particular, bootctl provides more detailed selected-loader information when the loader implements its interface; a GRUB system need not report everything a systemd-boot system would. See the bootctl documentation. Compare the firmware entry, mounted ESP and actual console boot behavior; do not install a different loader to make the report match an example.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
section: How an Ubuntu GRUB menu is produced
text:
How an Ubuntu GRUB menu is produced
GRUB is a bootloader with its own configuration language and menu. On the Ubuntu installation used here, commonly inspected inputs include /etc/default/grub, optional local defaults under /etc/default/grub.d/, scripts under /etc/grub.d/, and the installed kernel artifacts they discover. The generated menu is usually /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
Inspect the actual host before assuming those paths or a particular value:
sudo cat /etc/default/grub
sudo ls -la /etc/default/grub.d /etc/grub.d
sudo ls -l /boot/grub/grub.cfg
sudo grep -E '^[[:space:]]*(menuentry|submenu) ' /boot/grub/grub.cfg
A missing optional directory can produce an error; inspect the paths that actually exist. The final command is a quick view, not a parser for all GRUB syntax or conditional behavior. Menu titles and submenus can change when installed kernels change. A displayed menu entry or generated configuration does not prove that its referenced files are readable at boot.
Ubuntu’s update-grub manual identifies it as the wrapper that generates /boot/grub/grub.cfg using grub-mkconfig. Treat that file as generated output: a hand edit can be overwritten by the next generation. Inspect configuration inputs and package-owned scripts before modifying them. Files in /etc/default/grub.d/ can override assignments from the main file, so reconcile their order and actual contents on your installation instead of assuming a single line controls the outcome.
In the GNU GRUB configuration reference, GRUB_TIMEOUT_STYLE=menu requests a visible menu, while GRUB_TIMEOUT controls the wait in seconds under normal menu behavior. Generated code can include conditional paths, for example after a recorded boot failure. A value in the source file is intent; generated output and the next boot provide additional evidence.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
section: Prepare a disposable GRUB test guest
text:
Prepare a disposable GRUB test guest
The exercise changes local configuration and reboots. Use a full powered-off clone, not the original. In bl02, shut down cleanly. On the host:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl02
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02 --details
Require shut off and reconcile the single system disk with the earlier record. Ensure there is enough host space for a full copy. The destination VM name and disk path in the following command must not already exist:
sudo virt-clone --connect qemu:///system \
  --original bl02 --name bl03-loader-lab \
  --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/bl03-loader-lab.qcow2
This follows the powered-off clone method established in Part 01. Inspect the original and clone with domblklist --details and dumpxml, using the same qemu:///system connection. Confirm distinct disk paths and distinct UEFI NVRAM files. If the definition has extra disks, shared state, a backing chain or TPM state, stop; those require a different copy and recovery plan. Keep bl02 shut off throughout the test because the clone also contains the original guest’s hostname, machine ID and credentials. In the manager, attach the clone’s NIC to the isolated blpractice network while it is shut down. The graphical console supplies access and no package download is needed.
Start only bl03-loader-lab. The login hostname can still say bl02; use the console window’s VM identity and the host-side disk record to distinguish the clone. Verify administrative access, root mount and the GRUB paths. If this is not a GRUB installation with /etc/default/grub and /boot/grub/grub.cfg, stop this GRUB-specific exercise. Do not install GRUB over the existing boot path merely to continue.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
section: Change a menu timeout and roll it back
text:
Change a menu timeout and roll it back
In the clone, first record the original configuration and inspect any local overrides:
sudo cat /etc/default/grub
sudo ls -la /etc/default/grub.d
sudo grep -nE '^[[:space:]]*GRUB_(TIMEOUT|TIMEOUT_STYLE)=' \
  /etc/default/grub /etc/default/grub.d/*.cfg
If the optional directory or matching files do not exist, the glob can produce an error. Record that and inspect any files that do exist. If local overrides or a management system own these settings, stop and plan with those inputs instead of relying on the simple edit below.
Create a private backup of the source file under a new name:
sudo test ! -e /etc/default/grub.bl03-original
sudo cp -a /etc/default/grub /etc/default/grub.bl03-original
Proceed with the copy only if the first command succeeds. Record that backup’s path. Using your editor as administrator, edit /etc/default/grub so its effective assignments for these two variables are:
GRUB_TIMEOUT_STYLE=menu
GRUB_TIMEOUT=5
Change existing assignments rather than leaving conflicting duplicates. Do not change the default boot entry, kernel arguments, firmware variables or other settings. Review the diff and regenerate:
sudo diff -u /etc/default/grub.bl03-original /etc/default/grub
sudo update-grub
sudo grub-script-check /boot/grub/grub.cfg
diff normally exits with status 1 when it finds differences; here that is expected if only the intended lines changed. Stop if the diff shows unintended edits. Run the generation and syntax check only after reviewing it. Record the output and exit status of each; a syntax check does not prove that a boot entry points to working files.
If generation or validation fails, do not reboot. Preserve the error and restore the original source, then regenerate and check again:
sudo cp -a /etc/default/grub.bl03-original /etc/default/grub
sudo update-grub
sudo grub-script-check /boot/grub/grub.cfg
If rollback generation or validation also fails, leave the clone running, keep the console and evidence, and use the separate baseline/recovery route. Do not keep editing generated configuration at random.
After successful generation and validation, reboot the clone with the console open. Observe whether the menu is visible and approximately how long the countdown waits without a keypress. Boot the default entry and verify login and uname -r. A console or firmware timing difference can hide a menu; if the expected behavior is absent, compare the actual generated configuration, overrides and selected loader before concluding the edit failed.
Restore the source file using the rollback commands above. Confirm the source matches the backup with sudo cmp /etc/default/grub.bl03-original /etc/default/grub, then reboot and observe the restored behavior. A pre-existing hidden or zero-timeout menu may not be visible; a successful login and the restored source plus successful generation are distinct pieces of evidence. Shut down the clone. Leave its disk available for inspection or retire it only after verifying its unique path. The untouched original can then be started for later chapters.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
text:
What changes for systemd-boot?
systemd-boot is a UEFI boot manager that discovers entries from the ESP and, where configured, the Extended Boot Loader partition (XBOOTLDR). It can read Boot Loader Specification Type #1 entry files and discover Type #2 unified kernel images. Its documentation describes the locations and features. This is a comparison, not a recommendation to replace Ubuntu’s existing loader.
On a system already using systemd-boot, first identify the actual ESP and optional XBOOTLDR mount. Then inspect, where present, loader/loader.conf, loader/entries/ and EFI/Linux/ on those filesystems. bootctl status reports available status; bootctl list lists entries it knows how to discover. A list can include discoverable entries even when another loader was used to boot. Absence of a particular directory is not proof of failure if another supported entry mechanism is in use.
Unlike the Ubuntu GRUB workflow, update-grub does not generate systemd-boot entries. Configuration and entry ownership may belong to a distribution package, kernel-install, an image builder or an administrator. Find that owner before editing. Runtime EFI variables can affect selection too; a file alone may not describe the effective next boot. Use the installed version’s manual and distribution procedure for any change and provide a console and rollback before applying it.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
text:
Diagnose the correct selection layer








Symptom
First distinction
Evidence




Firmware reports no boot option
Firmware selection versus loader menu
BootOrder, selected device and ESP path from the prior chapter


GRUB appears but expected kernel is absent
Loader configuration versus installed artifacts
Generated menu, inputs and /boot inventory


GRUB source changed but behavior did not
Input versus generated output versus selected loader
Overrides, generation result, console and active boot path


systemd-boot list differs from current boot
Discoverable entries versus selected loader
bootctl status, firmware selection and relevant mounts


A menu entry appears but fails after selection
Menu existence versus working kernel/root
Preserve console error and identify the next failed stage



For the original host, preserve a known working boot choice and console access before any persistent change. Do not use a one-time firmware choice, a loader’s one-time selection and a permanent default as interchangeable operations. Recovery of a deliberately broken boot entry is developed after the remaining boot stages are understood.

title: Bootloader Selection: GRUB and systemd-boot
text:
Practice and recall
Record the selected firmware path, loader evidence, configuration owner, generated or discovered entries, and the clone’s before/change/rollback observations. Explain which settings can persist after reboot and which observation applies only to the current boot.

Firmware selects an EFI application; a loader selects its own boot entry.
GRUB’s source configuration and generated menu have different owners and lifecycles.
systemd-boot discovers entries from its supported boot partitions and formats.
A valid menu file and an existing menu entry do not prove a successful boot.
Test persistent configuration changes on a recoverable clone and verify rollback.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
text:
A versioned boot set
A kernel image is the executable kernel selected for boot. An initramfs is an initial filesystem image supplied to the kernel for early userspace; it can contain tools, configuration and modules needed before the real root filesystem is available. A kernel module is code that can be loaded into a running kernel when needed. Some functionality is built into the kernel instead and is not a separately loaded module.
For a common Ubuntu installation, versioned artifacts have names resembling:
/boot/vmlinuz-<release>
/boot/initrd.img-<release>
/lib/modules/<release>/
Here <release> stands for the complete kernel release string, including distribution and flavor suffixes. Do not type the angle-bracket placeholders as paths. Other distributions, boot mechanisms, architectures and unified kernel images may arrange artifacts differently. The following inspection is specific to the current Ubuntu lab layout.



A boot entry selects inputs that must be interpreted as a set.


A loader can pass a command line alongside the selected image. Early userspace and the kernel use some of its arguments at different stages. For example, a root= value may help identify the intended root device, but it is not by itself proof of the filesystem ultimately mounted there.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
section: Identify the running kernel and root
text:
Identify the running kernel and root
Log in to the original bl02 console and confirm the host and root:
hostnamectl
uname -r
cat /proc/cmdline
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
uname -r reports the release of the running kernel. /proc/cmdline reports the command line exposed by this boot; it is stronger evidence of effective input than a default value in an ungenerated configuration file. findmnt shows the current mounted root source and filesystem.
An illustrative output might include:
6.x.y-example-generic
BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinuz-6.x.y-example-generic root=/dev/mapper/example--vg-root ro
These are fictional values. Actual releases, paths and arguments will differ. BOOT_IMAGE can be supplied by the bootloader as a hint, and its pathname is interpreted in the bootloader’s context; it is not guaranteed to be a directly usable Linux path. Compare it with the loader’s configuration and mounted /boot rather than mechanically prepending a directory.
ro on the initial command line can request an initially read-only root. A later mount operation can make the live root read-write, so inspect current mount options rather than concluding that the current root is read-only from the command line alone. Avoid placing passwords or other secrets on a kernel command line: it is visible to processes through /proc/cmdline on typical systems and may be retained in logs.
The kernel parameter documentation describes many kernel-recognized arguments and notes that other arguments can be passed to init. An argument’s presence is not proof that a particular component recognized or applied it. Confirm the relevant component’s documentation and observed behavior.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
section: Inventory files for the running release
text:
Inventory files for the running release
Set a shell variable from the actual running kernel and inspect the matching conventional paths:
KREL=$(uname -r)
printf 'Running release: %s\n' "$KREL"
ls -l "/boot/vmlinuz-$KREL" "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL"
ls -ld "/lib/modules/$KREL"
findmnt --target /boot --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
For the reference installation, the image, initramfs and module directory should normally exist for the running release. If a path is missing, preserve the error and investigate how this particular kernel was booted and packaged. A missing conventional on-disk initramfs does not prove the system never booted: the booted image may have been supplied from another location or the file could have changed after startup.
The /boot query reports the filesystem containing /boot. It may be root or a separate mount. If the prior installation record expects a separate /boot, check it with findmnt --mountpoint /boot as well. Looking at an unmounted directory on root can make a healthy separate boot filesystem appear empty.
List candidates without assuming that the highest-looking filename is the current one:
ls -lh /boot/vmlinuz-* /boot/initrd.img-*
ls -1 /lib/modules
A shell glob with no matches can produce an error; record it instead of treating the literal pattern as a file. Names usually associate a kernel image and initramfs by their full release string. Multiple releases can coexist. A newer installed release is an available candidate only if its files, loader entry and boot dependencies are correct; installation does not itself switch the already running kernel.
Package metadata supplies another view:
dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${binary:Package} ${Version}\n' \
  'linux-image-*' 'linux-modules-*'
Rows can include package states other than installed. Read the status abbreviations and actual versions rather than counting every row as an active kernel. If no packages match one pattern, dpkg-query may report that fact. Package inventory, files on disk and the running release answer related but different questions.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
section: Follow a module without loading it
text:
Follow a module without loading it
The running kernel’s module directory contains modules and metadata associated with its release. lsmod shows modules currently loaded into the kernel:
lsmod | head -20
This is a snapshot of loaded modules, not a complete inventory of built-in drivers, available modules or working devices. Earlier device discovery showed how to relate a network interface to its actual driver. If that driver is named virtio_net and modinfo is available, inspect it without loading or unloading anything:
modinfo -k "$(uname -r)" virtio_net
Use your observed driver name if different. modinfo can report a module’s filename, aliases, dependencies, supported parameters and other metadata; fields vary. A built-in driver may be represented as built-in or may lack a separate module file. A module file’s existence does not prove that it is loaded, bound to the intended device, compatible with the running kernel or permitted by the host’s module-signing policy. The modinfo manual describes lookup by kernel release.
The exact version string matters. Copying an arbitrary .ko file into a different release directory does not establish compatibility. An out-of-tree driver may need a build for each kernel and may also need to satisfy signing policy. Diagnose its package, build and signing evidence before changing anything; do not disable security checks or unload a working disk or network driver during this lab.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
section: Distinguish planned arguments from this boot
text:
Distinguish planned arguments from this boot
For the GRUB installation, compare current observations with the configuration sources and generated output:
cat /proc/cmdline
sudo grep -nE '^GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX(_DEFAULT)?=' /etc/default/grub
sudo grep -nE '^[[:space:]]*(linux|initrd)[[:space:]]' /boot/grub/grub.cfg
The source assignments express defaults used when configuration is generated. Drop-ins, scripts, menu selection, one-time edits and conditional logic can alter the resulting choice. The generated linux and initrd lines are candidates; several entries can be present. Do not assume the first line printed is the one that booted. Reconcile the selected menu entry with the console record and /proc/cmdline; if the exact selection was not captured, mark it uncertain.
GRUB can use paths relative to a filesystem it selects, while Linux presents mounted paths after boot. A line mentioning /vmlinuz-... can refer to a file on a separately mounted /boot filesystem. Determine the preceding GRUB search/root commands and the partition map before comparing paths. The command-line arguments are not a safe place to improvise boot fixes on the original host.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
section: Worked diagnosis: new kernel installed, old one running
text:
Worked diagnosis: new kernel installed, old one running
Suppose package inventory shows releases A and B, but uname -r shows A after an update. Ask whether a reboot was expected and whether B was actually selected:

Compare the update record and current boot time; do not infer a reboot from package installation.
Verify the B image, initramfs and module directory using the observed complete B release string, without removing A.
Inspect the loader’s available entries and console selection. A generated entry does not prove it was successfully booted.
Check the current /proc/cmdline, uname -r and root mount after any planned reboot.
If B fails while A works, retain the failure message and the working entry. Investigate the failing stage and matching artifacts before attempting repair.

If an update left no B initramfs or module tree, that is an inconsistency to investigate with package and installation logs. Rebuilding initramfs or repairing a package is a change with prerequisites; the next chapter explains early userspace and its construction. Do not delete a working older kernel merely because the newer one is installed.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
text:
Practice and acceptance
Create a table with the current release, current command line, root mount, filesystem containing /boot, matching image/initramfs/module paths, and any other installed candidate. Record whether each observation is runtime evidence, an on-disk artifact or configuration intent. Explain one reason these views could differ without implying corruption.
If you have no second installed kernel, use the fictional A/B scenario above as a reasoning exercise. Do not install or remove kernels just to manufacture one. Keep the record outside the guest and redact sensitive path or identity details before sharing.

title: Kernel Images, Command Lines and Matching Modules
text:
Recall card

Installing a kernel and running it are different events.
Compare the full release across image, initramfs and module tree; layouts can vary.
/proc/cmdline is current-boot input, while loader configuration describes choices.
A module on disk, a loaded module and a driver bound to a device are different states.
Preserve a known working boot path while investigating a failed update.

title: Initramfs and Reaching the Real Root
section: From boot image to installed root
text:
From boot image to installed root
The loader supplies a kernel, command line and, in this installation, an initramfs image. The kernel unpacks the initial filesystem into memory and runs its initial program. That early program and its tools discover the devices needed for root, possibly unlock encryption or activate LVM, mount the real root, and hand control to the installed system’s init program.



Early userspace prepares the installed root.


An initramfs is an archive used to populate an in-memory filesystem. The familiar Ubuntu filename initrd.img-<release> is historical terminology; it does not imply that every machine uses the older block-device initrd mechanism. Systems can use different early-userspace implementations, or boot without a separate initramfs where their design permits it. The systemd boot overview describes the general stages.
For our guided LVM guest, the dependency chain is approximately virtual disk → partition → physical volume → volume group → root logical volume → root filesystem. An encrypted installation can add an unlock dependency before the volume group. This is a dependency map, not a claim about the exact order of every script on every image.

title: Initramfs and Reaching the Real Root
section: Inspect the installed image and its inputs
text:
Inspect the installed image and its inputs
On bl02, confirm the current release, root and boot filesystem:
hostnamectl
uname -r
cat /proc/cmdline
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
findmnt --target /boot --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,UUID,MOUNTPOINTS
Match the root source with the observed storage tree. A root= argument is an input to early boot, while findmnt describes the current mount. It is possible for a command line and a mounted source to use different names for the same object. Resolve identifiers before declaring them inconsistent.
On Ubuntu systems using initramfs-tools, inspect the configuration and the image associated with the running release:
KREL=$(uname -r)
ls -l "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL"
ls -la /etc/initramfs-tools
cat /etc/initramfs-tools/initramfs.conf
sudo lsinitramfs "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL" > "$HOME/bl-initramfs-list.txt"
head -40 "$HOME/bl-initramfs-list.txt"
lsinitramfs lists archive members; it does not execute them. Check that the listing command succeeded before interpreting the file. If the image or utility is missing, determine the host’s actual boot method and packaging rather than creating an empty image. The lsinitramfs manual describes supported image listing and its limitations with multi-segment images.
Look for evidence related to the actual storage stack, for example:
grep -Ei '(^|/)(init|lvm|cryptsetup)(/|$|\.)' "$HOME/bl-initramfs-list.txt"
No match is not a complete diagnosis: names, packaging, compressed module filenames, built-in drivers and implementations differ. A matching filename establishes presence, not that a script ran successfully or that a device was unlocked. The initramfs-tools documentation separates image-building hooks from boot-time scripts.

title: Initramfs and Reaching the Real Root
text:
Construction and dependencies
A generated initramfs is a snapshot of selected files, scripts and configuration. Changes to early-boot inputs may require regeneration; editing the live root’s configuration does not retroactively edit an existing image. Package installation can also trigger generation. The output is tied to a particular kernel release and may contain selected modules for that release.
Keep four questions distinct:







Question
Evidence




What input is configured?
/etc/initramfs-tools and the installed package’s hooks


What is in the generated image?
lsinitramfs for the identified image


Which image did the loader select?
Bootloader entry and console/boot record


Did early userspace reach root?
Successful current root mount and boot evidence



A successful normal boot does not prove that every installed fallback image works. Nor does it prove the image currently on disk is byte-for-byte the one loaded earlier if it was replaced after boot.

title: Initramfs and Reaching the Real Root
section: Optional lab: rebuild one image on a clone
text:
Optional lab: rebuild one image on a clone
This exercise writes a boot artifact and reboots. First shut down bl02, confirm it is shut off and inspect its system disk using the host-side virsh procedure from the loader chapter. This clone method applies only to the documented single writable disk, no backing chain, no shared writable disk and no TPM state. Confirm sufficient host space and that the destination name and disk path are new. On the host:
sudo virt-clone --connect qemu:///system \
  --original bl02 --name bl03-initramfs-lab \
  --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/bl03-initramfs-lab.qcow2
Inspect original and clone disk paths and distinct UEFI NVRAM files in their domain definitions as in the loader chapter. Keep the original off, attach the clone to blpractice, and use the graphical console. The clone still reports hostname bl02; identify it by the manager’s VM name and unique disk.
On the clone, confirm the running release and existing image, and inspect free space:
KREL=$(uname -r)
ls -l "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL"
findmnt --target /boot --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
df -h /boot /
Stop if /boot is not the expected filesystem, the image is absent, capacity is insufficient, the root stack differs from the record, or the clone’s recovery path is uncertain. Do not remove old kernels to make room. Save the image’s pre-change hash and a list of its contents outside the guest using the established evidence procedure:
sudo sha256sum "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL"
sudo lsinitramfs "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL" > "$HOME/bl-initramfs-before.txt"
With the clone’s console and original baseline available, update the existing image for the currently running release:
sudo update-initramfs -u -k "$KREL"
sudo lsinitramfs "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL" > "$HOME/bl-initramfs-after.txt"
sudo sha256sum "/boot/initrd.img-$KREL"
Run each command only after the previous one succeeds. -u updates an existing image; -k selects the release. Consult the locally installed man update-initramfs for the version in use. Hashes and member ordering may change even without an intentional configuration change, so equality is not the success criterion. Compare relevant members, retain the command result, and verify that the bootloader still refers to the intended image.
If generation or inspection fails, do not reboot. Preserve the error and keep the original guest and baseline intact; investigate the clone or discard and recreate it after verifying its unique disk path. After a successful rebuild, reboot the clone through its console and verify login, uname -r, the expected root source and systemctl --failed. This demonstrates the tested boot path, not every fallback path. Shut down the clone before restarting the original.

title: Initramfs and Reaching the Real Root
text:
Diagnose an early-root failure
Suppose the console reports that the root device cannot be found and offers an early shell. Candidate causes include a wrong root identifier, missing storage driver, incomplete LVM activation, a failed encryption unlock, missing device, or an initramfs that lacks required components.

Preserve the exact console error, boot entry, kernel release and time.
Identify the expected storage chain from the installation record and compare it with the VM’s attached disk.
Determine whether the failure is before the real root mount; ordinary service logs may not yet exist on that root.
Use a known-good entry or verified recovery media according to the established recovery plan. Inspect the relevant image and configuration offline before changing them.
After a justified repair, perform a normal boot and check the root source and dependent services.

An early shell may have different tools and device names from the installed system. Do not format, recreate a volume group, or paste another machine’s UUID just to leave the shell. Detailed external-media and offline repair procedures follow later in this part.

title: Initramfs and Reaching the Real Root
text:
Practice and recall
Record the running release, selected image evidence, root storage chain and at least one limitation of the archive listing. If you used the clone, retain the rebuild result and post-reboot root check.

Early userspace prepares the real root before the installed manager can run.
Build inputs, archive contents, selected image and successful execution are different observations.
An image must fit the kernel release and the actual storage dependencies.
Test rebuilds and recovery on a disposable copy before changing a working boot path.

title: Root Handoff, PID 1 and the Boot Transaction
section: From temporary root to installed manager
text:
From temporary root to installed manager
Early userspace prepares the real root and hands over execution to an init program on it. On the reference Ubuntu installation, that installed system manager is systemd. PID 1 is the first userspace process and has special responsibilities, including adopting orphaned processes and coordinating the system’s lifecycle. The handoff mechanism and whether systemd also runs in the initramfs depend on the early-userspace implementation; do not assume every initramfs is a systemd initrd.



The installed manager coordinates boot toward a selected target.


A unit is an object managed by systemd: service, mount, socket, device, target and other types. A job is an operation such as starting or stopping a unit. Starting a target can pull other units into a transaction, and systemd orders applicable jobs according to dependency rules. Many jobs can proceed concurrently. The bootup overview describes the major targets and the parallel nature of startup.

title: Root Handoff, PID 1 and the Boot Transaction
text:
Observe PID 1 and this boot
In the guest console:
ps -p 1 -o pid,comm,args
readlink -f /proc/1/exe
systemctl is-system-running
systemctl --failed --no-pager
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
On the reference host, PID 1 should identify systemd. is-system-running may report running, degraded, starting or another state; a nonzero exit status for a state such as degraded is diagnostic information, not a command to reset failures. A degraded system can be usable while one unit has failed. The root mount is runtime evidence, not a complete history of how it was found.
Inspect boot messages:
journalctl --list-boots --no-pager
sudo journalctl -b -p warning --no-pager
sudo journalctl -b -u systemd-remount-fs.service --no-pager
-b selects the current boot and -p warning selects warning priority and more severe messages. A unit may not exist, may have completed successfully without much output, or may not be responsible for the symptom. An empty query is an observation. Journal persistence and access depend on configuration; the previous boot may not be retained after a reboot. Do not assume the system journal captures all firmware or early-initramfs messages.

title: Root Handoff, PID 1 and the Boot Transaction
text:
Requirement and ordering are different
A dependency can express that one unit wants or requires another. Ordering expresses which job should precede another when both jobs are present. After= alone does not pull a unit into the transaction. Wants= or Requires= alone does not by itself specify a start order. Requires= has stronger failure relationships than Wants=, but it is not a general substitute for an application-level health check.
For an imaginary service report.service using data.mount:







Relationship
Effect to reason about




Wants=data.mount
Attempt to include the mount without the same failure coupling as a requirement


Requires=data.mount
Express a stronger requirement, with documented failure and stop behavior


After=data.mount
If both start jobs are present, order the service after the mount job



A real filesystem dependency can be expressed through appropriate mount-related mechanisms; the example isolates the concepts rather than prescribing a unit. The systemd unit reference defines the detailed semantics.
Inspect relationships of a unit present on your host:
systemctl list-dependencies --all multi-user.target
systemctl show multi-user.target -p Wants -p Requires -p After -p Before
systemctl list-jobs
The dependency tree is not a timeline, and list-jobs is only a snapshot of jobs currently queued. Empty output after boot is normal. Properties include implicit as well as explicit relationships; use systemctl cat UNIT with an actual unit name to inspect its definitions and drop-ins. A static list cannot prove the service’s client-facing behavior.

title: Root Handoff, PID 1 and the Boot Transaction
text:
A transaction can succeed partially
Suppose multi-user.target is active while a nonessential service failed. The target’s state, the failed unit and the service’s client test answer different questions. Find the failed unit with systemctl --failed, inspect systemctl status UNIT and journalctl -b -u UNIT using its actual name, then determine its role and dependencies. Do not clear the failed state as the first step; doing so removes a useful signal without repairing the cause.
An error involving the root filesystem before the installed manager starts belongs to the earlier boot boundary. A failed service after login belongs to the installed manager or application boundary. If uncertain, use the console’s last visible message and timestamps to establish the boundary before changing configuration.

title: Root Handoff, PID 1 and the Boot Transaction
text:
Practice and recall
Record PID 1, current root, system state, failed units and one target’s Wants, Requires and After properties. Choose one observed relationship and explain why it does or does not establish ordering. Compare that static relationship with current job state and the journal.

Root handoff starts the installed system’s work; it does not establish workload readiness.
Units represent managed objects; jobs are operations on them.
Requirement and ordering answer different questions.
A reached target and an empty job queue are not complete health checks.

title: Targets, Activation, Readiness and Boot Timing
text:
What a target tells you
A target is a systemd unit that groups or orders other units. On a conventional system, default.target commonly resolves to multi-user.target for a non-graphical host or graphical.target for a graphical one. The actual alias and dependencies are configuration, not a universal promise. The systemd special-unit reference documents common targets.
Inspect the default and current target state:
systemctl get-default
systemctl list-units --type=target --all --no-pager
systemctl status multi-user.target --no-pager
systemctl --failed --no-pager
get-default reports the configured default for normal boot. Active targets describe current manager state. A target can be active while a wanted service has failed, while an application is still warming up, or while a service that will be started on demand has not yet been invoked. A graphical target can also include the multi-user target; the two labels do not represent mutually exclusive running modes.
network.target and network-online.target are especially easy to overread. A reached target is not a guarantee that DNS, a particular remote endpoint or the Internet is reachable. Whether a wait service is configured and what it considers online depend on the network manager and local configuration. Inspect the actual units, then test the dependency your application needs.

title: Targets, Activation, Readiness and Boot Timing
text:
Activation and readiness are separate
Some services start during boot. Others are activated by a socket, path, timer, device or an explicit request. A listening socket can exist before the service process, and a service can remain inactive until its first request. The system manager may consider a service started at different points according to its Type= and implementation.
For Type=simple, manager activation does not wait for a service-specific ready notification. A Type=notify service can send a readiness notification, but that signal’s usefulness depends on what the service actually checks. A Type=oneshot service may complete successfully and exit. The systemd service reference defines the service types and their lifecycle semantics.








Observation
What it supports
What remains to test




Unit is active
Manager considers the unit active
The actual application operation


Socket is listening
A local socket is bound
Whether a request is served correctly


Target is reached
Its activation transaction reached that milestone
Independent or later work and external dependencies


Client check succeeds
The tested operation worked at that time
Other operations, clients and failure modes



Design a readiness check around an expected operation: for example, a query returning a known record, or an HTTP response containing an expected value. Name the client location, credentials, timeout and success condition. A process existing is weaker evidence than the operation it is meant to provide.



Startup timing and client readiness measure different events.

title: Targets, Activation, Readiness and Boot Timing
section: Read timing without assigning blame too quickly
text:
Read timing without assigning blame too quickly
Run:
systemd-analyze time
systemd-analyze blame
systemd-analyze critical-chain
The reported phases and available timestamps depend on the firmware, loader and initramfs. blame reports unit activation durations, not the complete reason the machine was slow. A long duration can include waiting for a dependency; some unit types do not provide a meaningful activation duration. critical-chain is a view of a time-critical ordering chain, not a complete trace of all concurrent work or timed-out jobs. The Ubuntu systemd-analyze manual documents these limits.
