If a unit appears slow, inspect its actual status and current-boot log, substituting its observed name:
systemctl status UNIT --no-pager
sudo journalctl -b -u UNIT --no-pager
systemctl show UNIT -p Type -p After -p Wants -p Requires
Replace UNIT with the full unit name; it is a placeholder, not a unit to create. Compare timestamps and ask what the unit was waiting for. A network wait service taking time can reflect a missing link or an intentional network policy. Disabling it may shorten a graph while breaking a service that relies on it.

Worked example
A synthetic timeline shows multi-user.target at six seconds and an optional activation finishing at nine. A client request at seven seconds succeeds. It would be wrong to add all unit durations together to claim a fifteen-second boot, or to say that the nine-second unit blocked that client without a dependency and request trace. The target time, optional activation and client test are separate evidence.
For a real incident, define a user-visible start and finish, collect several comparable boots, and control for cache, updates, workload and network conditions. Use a client probe that checks the actual expected response; record failures as well as the first success. More detailed performance methods come later.

title: Targets, Activation, Readiness and Boot Timing
text:
Practice and recall
Record the default target, current active targets, system state, time, and one entry from critical-chain. For that unit, identify one plausible dependency and inspect its log. Explain which observation would prove a particular client operation works and why it is not supplied by the target name alone. Do not change a target or service as part of this inspection.

A target is a manager milestone, not a complete application health test.
Activation can be boot-driven or triggered later by another event.
Service type affects when the manager considers startup complete.
Timing output is evidence for a question, not a list of services to disable.

title: Shutdown, Reboot and Services That Delay Shutdown
text:
What a clean transition attempts
A normal shutdown asks the system manager to stop services and sessions, terminate remaining processes, unmount filesystems where possible and complete the requested transition. Dependencies and ordering affect stop jobs too; stop ordering is generally the reverse of start ordering when both jobs are ordered. Some final work happens after ordinary userspace services have stopped. The systemd boot and shutdown overview describes this lifecycle.







Request
Intended outcome




Reboot
Shut down the running system and start it again


Poweroff
Shut down and request power removal


Halt
Stop the system; whether power is removed depends on platform and command behavior


Suspend
Preserve a running session for later resume; not a shutdown


Forced VM power cut
Remove virtual power without waiting for guest cooperation



The VM manager’s shut off state and a blank console are not identical observations. A guest may have powered off while the console window remains open. Conversely, a blank display does not establish that the guest has stopped writing.

title: Shutdown, Reboot and Services That Delay Shutdown
text:
Preflight the transition
On the clone’s console:
hostnamectl
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
systemctl is-system-running
systemctl --failed --no-pager
systemctl list-jobs
systemd-inhibit --list --no-pager
Record the VM identity from the manager and the boot ID from the guest. Inhibitors can request a block or delay for operations such as shutdown; they are distinct from a service’s stop job. The systemd-inhibit manual describes their modes. An empty list does not guarantee that every service will stop quickly.
A privileged shutdown request can behave differently from an unprivileged desktop request and may override certain inhibitors. Do not bypass an inhibitor to make this lab faster. Identify its owner and reason; wait for the legitimate operation or coordinate with its owner before a real shutdown.

title: Shutdown, Reboot and Services That Delay Shutdown
text:
Reboot and compare boot instances
With the console open, request a normal reboot:
sudo systemctl reboot
Wait for the guest to return and log in. Check:
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
systemctl is-system-running
systemctl --failed --no-pager
journalctl --list-boots --no-pager
The boot ID should differ from the pre-reboot value. If the journal retained the previous boot, inspect its final messages:
sudo journalctl -b -1 -e --no-pager
-b -1 means the previous boot in the available journal, not an absolute guarantee of the immediately preceding physical boot. If the journal was volatile, there may be no previous boot to inspect. Record the unavailable evidence instead of assuming a clean shutdown. Journal timestamps and final messages can show progress, but missing final messages do not alone prove an abrupt power loss.
Now request a normal poweroff:
sudo systemctl poweroff
In the host’s VM manager, wait for the clone to show shut off. If needed, check from the host:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl03-loader-lab
Use the actual clone name if you created a fresh equivalent. A normal shutdown followed by an observed shut-off domain is the acceptance result. Do not select a forced power action merely because the console has stopped updating for a few seconds.

title: Shutdown, Reboot and Services That Delay Shutdown
section: Diagnose a slow or blocked shutdown
text:
Diagnose a slow or blocked shutdown
Before starting a shutdown on an accessible system, systemd-inhibit --list, systemctl list-jobs, service status and logs show different classes of evidence. During a slow transition, the console may show a stopping job and elapsed time. Preserve the unit name and message. If another console session remains usable, inspect jobs and the affected service without restarting it; access may disappear as shutdown progresses.







Observation
Next question




A shutdown inhibitor is listed
Who holds it, what operation is underway, and is it block or delay?


A stop job waits for a service
Is the service finishing work, blocked on a dependency, or failing to exit?


A mount cannot unmount
Which process or nested mount is keeping it busy, and what data is at risk?


Domain is already shut off
Is the manager window simply still open?


A guest stops responding entirely
What was the last console evidence, and what recovery point exists?



A service stop timeout is not automatically proof that its process is safe to kill. An uninterruptible task can be waiting for I/O; storage and remote dependencies require their own investigation. Do not set all timeouts to zero, issue repeated forced resets, or kill random processes. In a real incident, weigh data consistency and availability, record the decision and use the service’s recovery procedure. In this disposable clone, the established baseline supplies a bounded reset if a controlled experiment cannot complete.

title: Shutdown, Reboot and Services That Delay Shutdown
text:
Practice and recall
Record the clone name, boot IDs before and after reboot, any inhibitors, failed units, prior-boot journal availability and final host-side domain state. Explain why a missing prior journal and an empty inhibitor list cannot each prove a clean shutdown.

Reboot, poweroff, halt, suspend and forced power removal are different transitions.
Inhibitors and stopping jobs are different sources of delay.
Preserve the console message and service evidence before interrupting a stuck transition.
Verify the guest’s actual state from the host after poweroff.

title: Secure Boot, Unified Images and Measured Boot
text:
Four related mechanisms








Mechanism
Operational question
What it does not establish by itself




A unified kernel image (UKI)
Which boot resources are packaged in one EFI executable?
That it is signed, trusted or selected


Secure Boot verification
Will a verifier accept the next executable under its configured trust policy?
That every later file and runtime action is protected


Measured boot
What measurements were recorded or extended during boot?
That the measured state was automatically judged trustworthy


TPM-bound unlock policy
Under what conditions can a protected secret be released?
That a recovery credential exists or that all boots will satisfy the policy






Packaging, verification, measurement and unlock are separate decisions.


These mechanisms can be combined, but none implies all the others. Secure Boot without encrypted storage does not make an offline disk confidential. Encryption does not prove that the booted software was authorized. A measurement is evidence of a state, not an access decision unless another component evaluates it.

title: Secure Boot, Unified Images and Measured Boot
section: Secure Boot and a chain of trust
text:
Secure Boot and a chain of trust
UEFI Secure Boot applies firmware trust policy to EFI executables. In the Ubuntu UEFI path, firmware can load a signed shim, which participates in the verification chain for subsequent boot components; the actual chain depends on installed software and configuration. Canonical’s Secure Boot documentation describes Ubuntu’s implementation and key handling.
A signature is useful only with a verifier, trusted key or certificate, and policy. Trust databases and revocation state matter as well as the file’s signature. A file’s presence on the ESP does not establish that it is signed, accepted by current firmware, selected on the next boot, or the same file that ran earlier.
Secure Boot is not a general guarantee that every byte read after boot is authenticated. Coverage depends on the boot chain, configuration and mechanisms in use. Module-signing enforcement is a related but distinct kernel policy; an out-of-tree module can fail to load even when the kernel booted successfully. Diagnose the exact rejected component and policy rather than disabling verification as a generic repair.

Inspect without changing trust
In the guest:
hostnamectl
if test -d /sys/firmware/efi; then
  printf 'EFI firmware interface is present\n'
else
  printf 'EFI firmware interface is unavailable in this boot\n'
fi
if command -v mokutil >/dev/null; then
  mokutil --sb-state
else
  printf 'mokutil is not installed; Secure Boot state was not checked\n'
fi
mokutil --sb-state reports the state available through the tool on a supported EFI system; record its output or error. An absent tool is not evidence that Secure Boot is disabled. If the guest firmware was created without Secure Boot support, or the relevant variable interface is unavailable, investigate the actual VM firmware configuration. Do not change the firmware mode or key database to obtain a particular answer.
Record the previously observed BootCurrent and EFI path if available. That is the firmware’s reported selection for this boot, not a complete proof of every verification step. If a verification failure prevents boot, the firmware or loader console is often more useful than a journal on an inaccessible root.

title: Secure Boot, Unified Images and Measured Boot
text:
What a UKI packages
A unified kernel image is a UEFI executable containing a boot stub and Linux kernel, optionally an initrd and additional resources such as command-line data. The UKI specification defines its structure. An actual UKI can be started by firmware directly or through a suitable bootloader.
Packaging can simplify distributing and signing a coherent set of boot inputs. It does not mean that every command-line source or external resource is covered by the same signature: that depends on the stub, loader, platform security state and policy. It also does not imply that every initramfs file on an Ubuntu host is inside a UKI. The separate /boot/vmlinuz-* and /boot/initrd.img-* files inspected earlier are one valid layout.
On a host already using systemd-boot, bootctl status and bootctl list may help identify its ESP and discoverable entries. Those commands do not prove that a discoverable UKI was the image selected for this boot. Compare firmware selection, loader evidence and the actual boot record. Do not install systemd-boot or create a UKI merely to complete this inspection.

title: Secure Boot, Unified Images and Measured Boot
text:
Measurements and policy
A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) can maintain platform configuration registers, or PCRs. Measurements are extended into PCRs in sequence: the resulting value depends on both earlier state and the new measurement. A verifier can compare measurements or evaluate a signed policy, and a local unlock mechanism can require an approved state before releasing a secret.
The chosen PCRs, event log, banks, firmware and policy determine what a measurement means. A PCR value without its measurement context is not a complete explanation of what booted. A legitimate firmware, bootloader, configuration or kernel update can change a policy-relevant measurement. A failed automatic unlock therefore calls for investigating the selected policy and update history; it does not automatically establish compromise.
For LUKS2, a TPM-backed enrollment can be one of several unlock methods. The systemd-cryptenroll reference describes both TPM policy options and recovery keys. Such an enrollment is a change to a real encrypted volume and is not part of this lab. A separately protected, tested recovery credential and documented recovery procedure are essential before an operator depends on automated unlock.

Read-only availability check
If the guest has a TPM device exposed, Linux commonly shows an entry under /sys/class/tpm:
if test -d /sys/class/tpm; then
  ls -la /sys/class/tpm
else
  printf 'No TPM class directory is exposed\n'
fi
An empty or missing directory is an observation about this environment, not proof about the physical host’s hardware. A virtual TPM, if configured, is a separate virtual device with its own persistent state and recovery implications. Do not attach a new TPM to the existing lab or assume the ordinary VM disk clone includes its state.
On a system whose installed systemd-analyze supports it, the following can provide additional TPM availability information:
systemd-analyze has-tpm2
Record the output and exit status; the command can report limited support or return nonzero. If the subcommand is unavailable, use the installed manual and record the limitation. TPM availability does not prove that Secure Boot is enabled, that a PCR policy exists or that disk unlock uses it.

title: Secure Boot, Unified Images and Measured Boot
section: Worked diagnosis: update followed by an unlock prompt
text:
Worked diagnosis: update followed by an unlock prompt
A host normally unlocks automatically; after an update it requests a recovery credential. The administrator should:

Preserve the console message and identify the host and encrypted volume without exposing the credential.
Use the established recovery credential through the trusted console, if the recovery plan authorizes it. A prompt is not a reason to reformat the disk.
Record what changed: firmware, trust databases, loader, kernel, initramfs, UKI or unlock policy. Confirm which components actually booted.
Inspect the existing enrollment and policy using the platform’s documented tools and authorized procedure. Compare relevant measurement evidence with the expected policy; do not assume a universal PCR set.
Plan and test a policy update with a retained recovery path and an explicitly verified subsequent boot.

A valid recovery unlock demonstrates access through that credential; it does not by itself prove why the automatic policy failed. Policy changes, key rotation and signed artifacts require the actual platform’s procedures and are developed with storage and security operations later.

title: Secure Boot, Unified Images and Measured Boot
text:
Practice and recall
Record the guest’s EFI interface, mokutil result or observation limit, boot path evidence, TPM availability result and whether this lab actually uses encrypted root. For each item state what it proves and one thing it does not. Keep firmware-variable dumps, device identifiers and recovery material out of shared notes.

A UKI packages resources; trust depends on the verifier and policy.
Secure Boot verifies selected executables, while measured boot records state for later evaluation.
TPM availability does not establish an unlock policy.
A legitimate update can change measurements; keep a tested recovery path before relying on automatic unlock.
Inspect the rejected stage and preserve evidence before changing trust or encryption settings.

title: Rescue, Emergency and External-Media Recovery
text:
Identify the failed boundary



Recover at the boundary where startup stopped.










Last reliable observation
Likely boundary to investigate
Useful evidence




Firmware cannot find a boot option
Firmware, device or EFI path
VM disk attachment, boot entry, ESP identity


Bootloader appears but cannot load an image
Loader configuration or boot filesystem
Selected menu entry and exact error


Kernel starts but root cannot be found
initramfs, device discovery or storage stack
Console message, root argument, storage record


Installed manager reports a failed required mount
Installed root, mount intent or device
Console, fstab and actual filesystem identity


Login works but a service fails
Service or later dependency
Unit status, logs and client test



This table narrows an investigation; a single message does not prove a root cause. Preserve the exact wording, selected VM, timestamp, recent changes and boot entry. A retry or forced reset can hide the first failure. Never format a disk, reset encryption, rewrite all boot variables or disable verification to silence a symptom.

title: Rescue, Emergency and External-Media Recovery
section: Know which root and manager you are using
text:
Know which root and manager you are using
Rescue mode is a reduced installed-system environment intended for maintenance; emergency mode is more minimal and can be reached when essential startup work fails. Their exact mounts and available authentication depend on the failure and distribution. The systemd special-unit reference describes the targets. An Ubuntu installation may have a locked root password, so an emergency login prompt is not necessarily usable with the ordinary learner password. Plan an external route rather than assuming a shell will be granted.
An initramfs shell appears earlier, before the installed root has necessarily been mounted. It uses the early environment’s tools and device view. An external live environment boots its own kernel and root from trusted media; the installed system is a separate disk to identify and mount. uname -r in that environment describes the live kernel, not the installed kernel.
A shell prompt does not prove that / is the installed root, that it is writable, or that its separate /boot and ESP are mounted. Establish that explicitly with findmnt, lsblk, the VM definition and the installation record. A chroot changes the root path used by a process; it does not boot the installed kernel or give it an independent service manager.

title: Rescue, Emergency and External-Media Recovery
text:
Prepare the controlled fault
On the host, shut down bl02 cleanly and verify its disk and state using virsh as in the prior clone exercises. The following assumes one writable system disk, no backing chain, shared writable storage or TPM state. Verify adequate host space and that both destination names are unused:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl02
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02 --details
sudo virt-clone --connect qemu:///system \
  --original bl02 --name bl03-rescue-lab \
  --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/bl03-rescue-lab.qcow2
Only clone after the state reports shut off. Compare the original and clone domain XML and disk paths, including distinct UEFI NVRAM files. Attach the clone’s NIC to blpractice while it is off; no network access is required for the fault. Keep the original off because the cloned guest retains its internal hostname, machine ID and credentials. Use the manager’s bl03-rescue-lab console and confirm its disk path before proceeding.
Inside the clone, ensure the reserved lab directory and backup file do not exist:
sudo test ! -e /mnt/bl-fault && sudo test ! -e /etc/fstab.bl03-before
The combined check must succeed. If either fails, stop and inspect rather than overwriting prior work. Choose a deliberately nonexistent filesystem UUID and verify no matching filesystem is reported:
sudo blkid -t UUID=11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555
No output with exit status 2 means blkid found no matching device in this view. Any matching output or another error means stop and choose a new unused UUID after checking it. This check does not make the string a general-purpose identifier; it merely bounds this one guest’s exercise.
Create the empty mountpoint and a preserved copy of the current configuration:
sudo mkdir /mnt/bl-fault
sudo cp -a /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bl03-before
sudo cmp /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bl03-before
Proceed only after the comparison succeeds. Append exactly one required mount entry with a short device wait:
printf '%s\n' 'UUID=11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555 /mnt/bl-fault ext4 defaults,x-systemd.device-timeout=15s 0 2' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
Review sudo tail -n 3 /etc/fstab and compare it with the backup. The intended difference is one new line; the system’s existing root and boot entries must remain unchanged. The line requests a filesystem that does not exist, and deliberately omits nofail. The x-systemd.device-timeout= option controls the device wait when interpreted by systemd’s fstab generator; see the systemd mount documentation. The directory contains no useful data and is not a root or boot filesystem.
If the file differs in any other way, restore the backup while the clone is still running, verify it and stop. Do not run mount -a: the intended experiment is the next boot, and mounting all configured filesystems is broader than necessary.

title: Rescue, Emergency and External-Media Recovery
section: Observe the fault and choose recovery
text:
Observe the fault and choose recovery
With the clone console open, reboot normally. Allow time for the device timeout and observe the exact message and resulting mode. A typical systemd installation enters emergency handling for the missing required mount, but distribution policy and boot configuration can differ. Record the result instead of assuming the prompt is usable. Do not enter credentials into an unidentified environment.
If the host reaches an ordinary login instead, inspect systemctl --failed, findmnt --mountpoint /mnt/bl-fault, and the current-boot journal from the clone. Reconcile the actual behavior with the appended line. In either case, the next chapter repairs the clone using verified external media, so a locked root account is not a blocker.
After recording the failure, shut down the clone through its available normal controls if possible. If it cannot respond to a normal shutdown, the disposable clone’s manager power-off may be used as a last resort after recording that fact; never apply that step to another guest. Wait for shut off. Leave its disk attached and keep bl02 off. The next chapter continues from this stopped, deliberately faulty guest.

title: Rescue, Emergency and External-Media Recovery
text:
Practice and recall
Record the selected clone and disk, the saved fstab path, the fault line, the observed console boundary and whether a normal shutdown succeeded. Explain why the installed root password might not open an emergency shell and why external media can still offer a separate recovery environment.

Identify firmware, loader, early root, installed mounts and service failures separately.
A rescue shell’s root and kernel depend on where it came from.
Preserve the fault and recovery evidence before making further changes.
Keep a known-good original and a verified external route when testing boot failures.

title: Offline Inspection, Chroot Repair and the Next Normal Boot
text:
Boot a separate environment
Confirm on the host that the clone is off and that its writable disk is the recorded clone disk:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl03-rescue-lab
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl03-rescue-lab --details
Attach the verified installer ISO as a read-only optical device to this clone. Keep the single system disk attached. Boot the ISO using the VM manager’s one-time boot selection and open the console. Do not begin a new installation or accept storage formatting. On Ubuntu Server’s live installer, switch to an available installer shell according to its console instructions. The shell runs the live system, not the installed guest. If the ISO or console is not the verified one, stop.
In the live shell inspect:
cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
lsblk -o NAME,PATH,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,UUID,MOUNTPOINTS
sudo pvs
sudo vgs
sudo lvs -o lv_name,vg_name,lv_path,lv_size
The live kernel release and live / do not describe the installed guest’s running kernel or root. Match the disk size, volume-group and logical-volume names to the recorded clone. If the expected LVM tools or logical volume are unavailable, or multiple volumes make the target ambiguous, stop. Activation of a volume group is a separate operation. If the recorded root LV is present but inactive, and only the verified clone disk is attached, identify its exact volume-group name in vgs. Set VG_NAME to that observed name in the live shell and activate only that group:
printf '%s\n' "$VG_NAME"
test -n "$VG_NAME" && sudo vgchange -ay "$VG_NAME" &&
  sudo lvs -o lv_name,vg_name,lv_path,lv_attr
Stop if the name is empty or ambiguous, duplicate volume groups are present, or the activation fails. Do not activate every volume group indiscriminately.

title: Offline Inspection, Chroot Repair and the Next Normal Boot
text:
Mount the verified installed root
The goal is to restore one known fstab backup on the root filesystem. No separate /boot, ESP or pseudo-filesystem mount is needed for this specific repair.
First ensure /mnt/bl-target does not already exist in the live environment:
sudo test ! -e /mnt/bl-target
sudo mkdir /mnt/bl-target
Run mkdir only if the test succeeds. From lvs, select the actual root LV path that matches the lab record. Assign that observed absolute path to ROOT_DEVICE in the live shell; for example, ROOT_DEVICE=/dev/mapper/observed-name is only a shape, not a value to copy. Check it before mounting:
printf '%s\n' "$ROOT_DEVICE"
test -b "$ROOT_DEVICE"
sudo lsblk -f "$ROOT_DEVICE"
Stop if the variable is empty, the device check fails or its identity is not the recorded clone’s root. The mount below is intentionally writable because the next step repairs the clone:
sudo mount "$ROOT_DEVICE" /mnt/bl-target
findmnt --mountpoint /mnt/bl-target --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
sudo cat /mnt/bl-target/etc/os-release
sudo tail -n 4 /mnt/bl-target/etc/fstab
sudo ls -l /mnt/bl-target/etc/fstab.bl03-before
Require an exact mount of the intended device, the expected Ubuntu installation and the deliberate fault line plus backup file. If the evidence differs, unmount and investigate; do not restore a file into a directory on the live root by mistake. If inspection alone is needed in a real incident, use an appropriate read-only procedure first and account for filesystem-specific recovery behavior. This planned lab write is not a general instruction to mount damaged production filesystems read-write.



External media and a chroot have different roles.

title: Offline Inspection, Chroot Repair and the Next Normal Boot
text:
Repair the specific file
Review the saved backup and fault:
sudo diff -u /mnt/bl-target/etc/fstab.bl03-before /mnt/bl-target/etc/fstab
The expected difference is the one deliberately appended mount line. diff exits with status 1 for differences. If unrelated changes appear, stop and understand them; restoring an old copy could discard legitimate configuration.
Enter a chroot rooted at the mounted clone:
sudo chroot /mnt/bl-target /bin/bash
The shell now resolves /etc/fstab within the installed filesystem, but uses the live kernel. It has not booted the installed system, and normal systemd service operations are not available merely because paths changed. The chroot manual describes this changed root directory.
Inside the chroot, verify the fault and backup once more, then restore the lab’s saved file:
hostname
cat /etc/fstab
ls -l /etc/fstab.bl03-before
cp -a /etc/fstab.bl03-before /etc/fstab
cmp /etc/fstab.bl03-before /etc/fstab
exit
The hostname command reports the live kernel’s hostname, not authoritative proof of the installed guest’s hostname. The exact mounted source and inspected files were the target checks. cp -a restores the saved file and its attributes; cmp should be silent and successful. exit returns to the live shell. Do not continue into package, GRUB or initramfs repair: those require additional correctly mounted filesystems and a different plan.
Outside the chroot, verify the target mount and repaired file again:
findmnt --mountpoint /mnt/bl-target --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
sudo cmp /mnt/bl-target/etc/fstab.bl03-before /mnt/bl-target/etc/fstab &&
  sudo umount /mnt/bl-target
Unmount only after leaving the chroot and ensuring no process is using that tree. If unmount fails, inspect the busy mount and processes; do not detach the disk or force a shutdown while writes may still be in progress. The findmnt manual distinguishes an exact mountpoint from the filesystem containing a path.

title: Offline Inspection, Chroot Repair and the Next Normal Boot
section: What a broader chroot repair would require
text:
What a broader chroot repair would require
A bootloader or initramfs repair may need the installed /boot, ESP and kernel interfaces such as /dev, /proc and /sys mounted in the right places. Each must be identified and mounted deliberately; bind-mount propagation, cleanup order, architecture, installed kernel version, package ownership and EFI variables all matter. Do not use the live kernel’s uname -r as the installed release. Do not share the live /run blindly. Firmware variables exposed to the live environment are those of this VM and can be changed by repair tools.
The diagram shows those possible relationships, not an instruction to mount all of them for the fstab exercise. Chroot is not a security boundary or an independently running VM. Restore from a known-good copy when that is the selected plan; use a separate verified backup if the original storage may be damaged. Recovery media and VM clones on the same host do not constitute an independent backup.

title: Offline Inspection, Chroot Repair and the Next Normal Boot
text:
Boot normally and verify
Shut down the live environment cleanly. In the VM manager detach the installer ISO, retain the clone disk and restore its normal disk boot selection. Confirm the original bl02 remains off. Start bl03-rescue-lab, log in through its console and inspect:
hostnamectl
findmnt --target / --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
systemctl --failed --no-pager
sudo cmp /etc/fstab.bl03-before /etc/fstab
findmnt --mountpoint /mnt/bl-fault
The hostname may still say bl02 because this is a clone. The manager’s name and disk path distinguish it. Success requires normal login, the recorded root source, a successful cmp, no unexplained failed units, and no exact mount at /mnt/bl-fault. The last command normally returns no output and a nonzero status when no such mount exists; that is expected here. Also inspect the current-boot journal if a failure remains. A repaired file alone is not proof that the normal boot path works.
Remove the now-unused empty /mnt/bl-fault directory from the clone with sudo rmdir /mnt/bl-fault only after confirming it is not a mount and contains no files. Retain the backup and notes until the exercise is reviewed. Shut down the clone before starting the original. Do not delete or reformat a disk as part of cleanup.

title: Offline Inspection, Chroot Repair and the Next Normal Boot
text:
Recall card

External media runs its own kernel and root; identify the installed disk separately.
A writable mount is a deliberate repair action, not proof that a filesystem is healthy.
Chroot changes path resolution; it does not boot the target system.
Mount only the components needed for the planned repair and unmount them cleanly.
The acceptance test is the next normal boot plus the expected root and service state.

title: UIDs, GIDs, Groups and Ownership
text:
Names describe numeric identities
A user ID (UID) identifies a user to the kernel. A group ID (GID) identifies a group. Files record an owner UID and group GID; processes have user and group credentials used in access checks. Tools commonly translate the numbers into names for display. If a name lookup is unavailable, the number can still exist on the file.
The special UID 0 has extensive administrative privilege, but a process’s actual authority also depends on capabilities, namespaces and other restrictions. Do not assume that a username containing admin, or membership in a group with a familiar name, automatically grants every operation.
id
id -u
id -g
id -G
id shows the current process’s identity and group list. -u gives the effective UID, -g the effective primary GID, and -G the group IDs. A process can also have supplementary groups. The account database’s current membership and the credentials already held by a running process can differ after an administrative change: start a new session and inspect its actual credentials.



Process credentials and file ownership meet at an access check.

title: UIDs, GIDs, Groups and Ownership
text:
Read ownership and permissions
Create a private lab directory and file:
umask 077
mkdir "$HOME/bl-identity-lab"
If the directory already exists, stop and inspect it instead of overwriting its contents. Only after mkdir succeeds, create and inspect the file:
printf 'identity lab\n' > "$HOME/bl-identity-lab/note.txt"
ls -l "$HOME/bl-identity-lab/note.txt"
ls -ln "$HOME/bl-identity-lab/note.txt"
stat -c 'uid=%u gid=%g mode=%a name=%n' "$HOME/bl-identity-lab/note.txt"
umask affects newly created objects in this shell; it does not change existing permissions. The named and numeric ls views describe the same file. stat prints the stored numeric owner and group, plus the permission mode in octal.
For a simple regular file with mode 0640, the owner has read and write, the group has read, and others have no permission. For directories, the same letters have different operational meanings: read permits listing names, write permits changes to entries subject to other rules, and execute permits traversal. Access to a file also requires traversal through each parent directory. A readable file behind an inaccessible home directory is not necessarily readable by another user.
A normal mode-bit check considers the applicable owner, group or other class; access control lists and other policies can add rules. Privileged processes and capabilities can alter outcomes. Deeper permissions and policy are covered later; this first model is enough to avoid assuming that a displayed username is the entire authorization rule.

title: UIDs, GIDs, Groups and Ownership
text:
Primary and supplementary groups
The primary group is part of a process’s credentials and normally influences the group of newly created files. A parent directory with the set-group-ID bit or filesystem policy can change the resulting group. Supplementary groups provide additional group memberships for access checks.
Inspect both a process and an account lookup:
id
id learner
getent passwd learner
The first command reports this process’s credentials; id learner asks for the named account’s identity and group information, which may differ from an already running session. getent queries the configured name-service database. These reports do not themselves grant or revoke access.
A file’s stored owner is a number. If an account is deleted and that UID later assigned to another account, old files can appear owned by the new account. This is why account retirement must include an inventory and ownership decision; deleting a username does not erase every file created by that user.

title: UIDs, GIDs, Groups and Ownership
section: Worked diagnosis: group was added but access still fails
text:
Worked diagnosis: group was added but access still fails
An administrator adds a user to a group. The user keeps an old terminal open and still gets permission denied. Possible causes include stale process credentials, missing directory traversal permission, a different group owning the file, an ACL or another policy.

In the failing session run id; record its effective IDs and supplementary groups.
Inspect the intended file and every relevant parent directory with ls -ld and ls -ln.
Start a new authorized login session and run id again; a database change does not rewrite the credentials of existing processes.
Repeat the specific operation and record the result. If it still fails, inspect the applicable ACL and security policy rather than making the whole tree world-writable.

Do not use sudo as the test of ordinary-user access: it tests a different process identity. Likewise, changing a group record does not automatically terminate existing processes or sessions.

title: UIDs, GIDs, Groups and Ownership
text:
Practice and recall
Compare the named and numeric owner/group of note.txt with id. Explain why changing a displayed username would not itself change the file’s stored UID. Verify the directory and file modes, then remove only the lab file and empty directory when done:
rm "$HOME/bl-identity-lab/note.txt"
rmdir "$HOME/bl-identity-lab"
rmdir refuses a nonempty directory. If it fails, inspect the contents instead of deleting unrelated files.

Processes use numeric credentials; names are lookup results.
Files store numeric owner and group identities.
Existing sessions retain their own group credentials until replaced or otherwise changed.
File access also depends on directory traversal and other policy.

title: Account Databases, NSS and Identity Lookup
text:
Local records have different purposes
/etc/passwd contains local account information such as login name, numeric UID, primary GID, home directory and login shell. It is commonly readable by local users because programs need identity metadata. The password field commonly contains a placeholder indicating that password data is stored separately; do not infer that an account has a usable password merely from that placeholder.
/etc/group records local groups and may list supplementary members. A user’s primary group is specified in the account record and may not appear in the group’s member list. Protected /etc/shadow holds local password-related data and aging fields. It is sensitive: do not print, copy or publish its hashes for this exercise. Additional mechanisms may provide identity or authentication without a local shadow entry.
Inspect your own local records and the system’s configuration:
getent passwd "$(id -un)"
getent group "$(id -g)"
rg '^passwd:|^group:|^shadow:' /etc/nsswitch.conf
If rg is unavailable inside the guest, use:
grep -E '^(passwd|group|shadow):' /etc/nsswitch.conf
getent uses the Name Service Switch (NSS), the library mechanism that consults configured sources. The getent manual describes the supported databases. /etc/nsswitch.conf controls source order and can include action clauses; its manual defines those rules. Do not change NSS configuration in this chapter.
A passwd-style result has colon-separated fields:
name:password-field:UID:GID:comment:home:shell
Names and values are examples of field roles, not values to paste into account files. The database reports identity metadata; an actual login also involves authentication, account policy, session setup and the availability of the home directory and shell. Those mechanisms are developed later.

title: Account Databases, NSS and Identity Lookup
section: A lookup is not the whole login
text:
A lookup is not the whole login



Name lookup and authentication answer different questions.


A successful getent passwd learner establishes that this lookup returned a record. It does not establish which credentials are accepted, whether the account is expired, whether the shell can run, or whether a particular service permits login. Conversely, an authentication failure does not automatically mean that identity lookup failed.
Compare the local source with the effective lookup:
grep '^learner:' /etc/passwd
getent passwd learner
id learner
On this lab’s local account, expect a local record and a successful effective lookup. If either is absent, check the selected guest and actual account name before changing anything. A local line and getent may be textually equal without proving that no other source contains a duplicate name. Source ordering and status actions matter.
For groups, compare:
grep '^learner:' /etc/group
getent group "$(id -g)"
id learner
The private primary group may have the same name as the user, but that convention is not guaranteed. A group membership list in getent group is not a complete substitute for id learner, because the latter also accounts for the primary group and lookup behavior.

title: Account Databases, NSS and Identity Lookup
text:
Worked diagnosis: a lookup fails
Suppose getent passwd example returns no entry. First verify the spelling and guest identity. Then inspect the passwd: source order, query the known local file, and record the command’s exit status. A remote source, if configured, introduces service and network dependencies; enumeration may be unavailable even when a lookup by key works.
Do not add a duplicate local account or change NSS source order to hide the failure. A reused name or UID can attach existing files to the wrong identity. Determine the authoritative identity source and its health before making a change. Later identity and networking chapters cover directory integration once those dependencies have been introduced.

title: Account Databases, NSS and Identity Lookup
text:
Practice and recall
Record the source order for passwd and group, your own effective lookup and the numeric IDs from id. Explain why the primary group need not list the username as a supplementary member and why successful lookup does not prove successful login. Redact account details before sharing the record.

Local account files hold different kinds of data; shadow hashes are sensitive.
NSS chooses identity sources; getent tests an effective lookup.
Identity lookup, authentication, account policy and authorization are separate steps.
A database change does not automatically replace credentials in existing sessions.

title: Account Creation, Locking, Expiration and Removal
section: Plan the identity and its scope
text:
Plan the identity and its scope
The exercise creates one local user blstudent and one supplementary group blreviewers. This is a human-style test identity, not an administrative or service account. It has no deliberate sudo grant and no real data. Before creation, ensure both names are unused:
getent passwd blstudent
getent group blstudent
getent group blreviewers
test ! -e /home/blstudent
Each getent query should return no record and exit with status 2 for a missing key; the home-path test must succeed. Check each result separately. An error other than a missing key, an existing name, or a remote identity source you do not understand is a stop condition. Inspect /etc/nsswitch.conf as in the previous chapter; a local tool may not know every remote identity that could later appear. Choose a different lab name rather than reusing an existing identity.
Record the available console and baseline. Before real provisioning, also specify a unique numeric UID/GID policy, identity authority, ownership scope, expiration, credentials, approval and recovery owner. Default automatic UID allocation in this disposable lab is not a fleet-wide identity plan.

title: Account Creation, Locking, Expiration and Removal
text:
Create and verify
Ubuntu provides the interactive adduser tool; this lab uses explicit lower-level useradd options so the intended home and shell are visible. The useradd manual describes the options and notes Debian-family preferences.
sudo useradd -m -U -s /bin/bash blstudent &&
  sudo passwd blstudent &&
  sudo groupadd blreviewers &&
  sudo usermod -aG blreviewers blstudent
The && operators stop the sequence if a command fails. If it stops, inspect the partial state before retrying. -m requests a home, -U a same-named private group, and -s the login shell. Enter a unique disposable password at the interactive prompts; do not place it in the command line or record it in notes. -aG appends a supplementary group. Using -G without -a can replace the supplementary group list; the usermod manual documents that distinction.
Inspect the result:
getent passwd blstudent
getent group blreviewers
id blstudent
sudo passwd -S blstudent
ls -ldn /home/blstudent
Record the observed UID, primary GID, supplementary group and home ownership. Verify a new session from the learner console:
su - blstudent
Authenticate with the lab user’s password. In the new shell run id, pwd and exit. The group should appear in the new process credentials and the home should be usable. If su fails, retain the error and inspect the account, password state, shell and local authentication policy; do not grant sudo or edit protected databases by hand. A new group entry is not proof that an existing session received the group.

title: Account Creation, Locking, Expiration and Removal
text:
Lock, expire and recover deliberately
A password lock disables that local password as an authentication method. It is not a universal account disable: an existing session or a different authentication method may still work. Account expiration is a separate account-policy input, and services can interpret policy differently. The passwd manual describes password lock and status.
With the blstudent session exited and the learner administrator session retained:
sudo passwd -l blstudent
sudo passwd -S blstudent
The status should indicate a locked password. From the ordinary learner shell, an attempted su - blstudent using the previously working password should fail under the lab’s local policy. Do not run this test through sudo, which uses a different authorization path. If the test behaves differently, preserve the evidence and stop rather than assuming the account has no access. Restore the prior usable password state for this known lab account:
sudo passwd -u blstudent
sudo passwd -S blstudent
Unlocking is appropriate here because the account had a working password before the lock. It is not a general instruction to unlock unknown accounts or create passwordless access.
Demonstrate an expired account with an explicit past date, then remove that expiration:
sudo usermod --expiredate 1970-01-02 blstudent
sudo chage -l blstudent
sudo usermod --expiredate '' blstudent
sudo chage -l blstudent
Read the displayed account-expiration field after each step. Expiration and password locking are distinct controls; neither command proves existing sessions have ended. These changes affect only the test user, never learner.

title: Account Creation, Locking, Expiration and Removal
section: Revoke membership and retire the test user
text:
Revoke membership and retire the test user
Remove the test user’s supplementary membership and check the database view:
sudo gpasswd -d blstudent blreviewers
id blstudent
getent group blreviewers
Previously running processes may retain old credentials. For a real departure, coordinate session termination, remote keys, tokens, scheduled jobs, application accounts and service ownership as applicable. Changing a local group list alone is not complete revocation.
Before deleting the lab account, make sure no blstudent session remains and record its UID and home path. Remove only the account record, leaving its home as evidence:
sudo userdel blstudent
getent passwd blstudent
ls -ldn /home/blstudent
The lookup should no longer return the local account; check its exit status. The numeric owner on the retained home illustrates that deleting a name does not remove every file. A different NSS source with the same name would complicate this result; stop if one appears. userdel may also remove the user’s private group according to local policy. It does not establish that files outside the home, jobs or credentials elsewhere have been handled. The userdel manual describes its scope.
After confirming blreviewers has no other intended members or use, remove this lab-only group:
getent group blreviewers
sudo groupdel blreviewers
getent group blreviewers
Do not use forced deletion or reuse the old UID while retained files remain. Keep the home and its ownership record on this disposable clone until a deliberate cleanup or retirement. Shut the clone down before returning to the original guest. A real account removal requires an explicit data retention, ownership transfer and credential-revocation plan.

title: Account Creation, Locking, Expiration and Removal
text:
Diagnose and recall
If creation fails, distinguish an existing name, unavailable identity source, occupied home path and insufficient privilege. If a login fails, distinguish lookup, password state, expiration, shell and session policy. If access persists after revocation, inspect the running process credentials and other authentication paths. Preserve a separate administrator and console recovery path throughout.

Create identities only after checking name, numeric ownership and source authority.
Append supplementary groups intentionally; verify a new session’s credentials.
Password lock, account expiration and session termination are different controls.
Deleting an account does not decide what happens to its files or external credentials.

title: Home Directories, Skeletons and Session Environments
section: A record, a directory and an environment
text:
A record, a directory and an environment
The account record contains a home path and login shell. On a conventional system, the home holds a user’s persistent files and personal configuration. Its location is not necessarily /home/NAME: it may be on another local filesystem or a network mount. $HOME is an environment variable inherited or set by session-starting software. It is not itself proof of the account record, a mounted filesystem or correct ownership.
Inspect the current session:
id
getent passwd "$(id -un)"
printf 'HOME=%s\nSHELL=%s\n' "$HOME" "$SHELL"
pwd
ls -ldn "$HOME"
findmnt --target "$HOME" --output TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
umask
pwd is the current working directory, which can differ from $HOME. $SHELL commonly identifies a configured or inherited shell, but does not prove which executable is running. A containing-filesystem query does not prove home is its own mount. Compare the numeric owner with id -u and consider parent directory traversal. The getent manual describes the effective identity lookup.
Avoid dumping the entire environment into shared notes: it may contain credentials, tokens, private paths or other sensitive values. A user’s shell startup files can also change variables after login; a non-login command or service can receive a different environment. This chapter inspects values rather than teaching a separate shell course.



A home path and session are distinct observations.

title: Home Directories, Skeletons and Session Environments
text:
Skeletons are initial copies
On Ubuntu, account-creation tools can populate a new home from a skeleton directory, commonly /etc/skel. These are initial copies, not a synchronization service: later changes to the skeleton do not automatically update existing users’ homes. Tool options, pre-existing destination paths and distribution configuration affect the result. The Ubuntu adduser manual describes its account-creation behavior; useradd has its own options and defaults.
Inspect the skeleton without changing it:
ls -la /etc/skel
getent passwd learner
A dot-prefixed name is ordinarily hidden by a plain ls. Do not copy private credentials into a shared skeleton, and do not assume a skeleton file has the right settings for every user. Existing home contents may have been customized since account creation.

title: Home Directories, Skeletons and Session Environments
section: Lab: create and inspect a fresh home
text:
Lab: create and inspect a fresh home
Use a new lab name blhome. Check each condition before creating anything:
getent passwd blhome
getent group blhome
test ! -e /home/blhome
Both lookups should return no record with status 2, and the home-path test must succeed. An existing name, path or lookup error means stop. Consider configured NSS sources too, as in the account-lifecycle chapter.
Create the local user and set a unique disposable password:
sudo useradd -m -U -s /bin/bash blhome && sudo passwd blhome
If either step fails, inspect the partial state before retrying. Do not record the password in notes. Inspect the resulting account and directory:
getent passwd blhome
id blhome
sudo ls -ldn /home/blhome
sudo ls -la /home/blhome
sudo ls -la /etc/skel
Compare filenames and ownership; if a skeleton file is present in both places, compare a specific nonsecret file with sudo cmp /etc/skel/FILE /home/blhome/FILE after replacing FILE with the actual name. A comparison proves byte equality at that moment, not that the files remain synchronized.
Start a new session from the ordinary learner shell:
su - blhome
After authenticating, run id, pwd, printf '%s\n' "$HOME", and findmnt --target "$HOME". Confirm the account’s observed home and process credentials, then exit. The login shell may source startup files; output and exact environment vary with configuration.

title: Home Directories, Skeletons and Session Environments
section: Diagnose a missing or inaccessible home
text:
Diagnose a missing or inaccessible home
Suppose authentication succeeds but the home is unavailable. Check the account’s actual home field with getent passwd, the mount containing that path with findmnt, and the directory plus parents with ls -ldn. Compare its numeric owner with the account’s UID. A missing network mount, a stale UID, denied traversal and a nonexistent directory require different remedies. Do not recursively chown a guessed path, recreate a mountpoint over hidden data, or broaden permissions for all users.
For a real migration, plan the copy method, numeric identities, ACLs, extended attributes, capacity, consistency and the old and new home paths. Verify a fresh login and data access before retirement of the original. Changing the account record alone does not copy files.
For lab cleanup, exit every blhome session, record the UID and home, and remove only the account record with sudo userdel blhome. The home remains for inspection; it may display a numeric owner. Retain it on this disposable clone until a deliberate cleanup. Do not reuse the UID while its files remain. The original learner account must continue to work.

title: Home Directories, Skeletons and Session Environments
text:
Recall card

Account home, mounted filesystem, $HOME and current working directory are distinct.
A skeleton supplies initial files; it does not update existing homes.
Inspect numeric ownership and parent traversal before changing permissions.
Test a new login session and preserve existing administrative access.

title: Passwords, Credential Storage and Policy
section: Passwords are not stored as login text
text:
Passwords are not stored as login text
A local system normally stores a password verifier, not the plaintext password. A verifier includes parameters and a salt that allow a candidate password to be checked. Salting makes identical passwords produce different verifier values; a stolen verifier can still be attacked offline. A password hash is therefore sensitive even though it is not the plaintext.
On this Ubuntu-style local-account setup, /etc/shadow contains protected password and aging fields. The shadow manual documents their semantics. Do not print or copy its contents into a ticket, book notes or a shared terminal recording. A locked password field prevents use of that UNIX password but does not automatically disable SSH keys, other credentials or already running sessions.
Use status tools to inspect a known local account instead:
sudo passwd -S learner
sudo chage -l learner
These report status and aging information; do not change learner’s password or aging for the exercise. chage reports local shadow information and may not describe policy applied by an external identity provider. The chage manual explains password and account expiration fields.

title: Passwords, Credential Storage and Policy
text:
Separate the controls








Control
What it addresses
What it does not automatically do




Password change
Replaces a local password verifier
Revoke every other credential or active session


Password lock
Prevents use of that password verifier
Disable keys, tokens or every service


Password aging
Determines when a password must be changed
Define the account’s full lifetime


Account expiration
Restricts account use according to the enforcing service
Terminate all running processes or revoke external identities


Authentication policy
Defines how a service checks a credential
Prove the user is authorized for every requested operation



Strong unique passwords, controlled enrollment, secure storage and recovery procedures all matter. Password policy applies to a specific identity source and login flow: local shadow settings do not define a remote directory’s rules. Do not assume a particular hashing algorithm, cost or automatic-update policy from a distribution name; inspect the installed configuration and relevant package documentation when making a change.

title: Passwords, Credential Storage and Policy
section: Lab: create an account and observe its policy
text:
Lab: create an account and observe its policy
First verify the new account and private-group names and home path are unused:
getent passwd blpass
getent group blpass
test ! -e /home/blpass
Check each result. Both lookups should return no record with status 2, and the path test must succeed. An existing identity, path or lookup error is a stop condition. Create the account and set a unique lab password interactively:
sudo useradd -m -U -s /bin/bash blpass && sudo passwd blpass
If either command fails, inspect partial state before retrying. Never pass the plaintext as an argument or store it in shell history. Confirm status without displaying the verifier:
getent passwd blpass
sudo passwd -S blpass
sudo chage -l blpass
From the ordinary learner shell, run su - blpass, authenticate using the new password, run id, and exit. This confirms the particular local su flow and session at that time, not every login service.
Set a bounded maximum password age for this disposable user:
sudo chage -M 30 blpass
sudo chage -l blpass
Record the displayed maximum and resulting dates. A policy change in /etc/login.defs can affect defaults for account creation, but is not evidence that existing records were updated; the login.defs manual documents the shadow suite’s settings. PAM and a remote identity provider can apply additional policy. Do not edit global policy to perform this lab.
Keep blpass for the next chapter’s controlled authentication failure. Its 30-day value is a teaching example, not a recommended universal rotation period. For real users, choose policy based on the environment, current guidance, credential type and incident recovery requirements.

title: Passwords, Credential Storage and Policy
section: Diagnose and recover a failed password login
text:
Diagnose and recover a failed password login

Identify the service, exact user, time and observed message without recording the password.
Verify the account resolves through getent and determine whether it is local or externally managed.
For the local test account, inspect passwd -S and chage -l; distinguish locked password, password expiration and account expiration.
Check the service’s authentication and account policy and the relevant logs. Do not reveal stored verifiers.
Use an authorized recovery process and retest the same login path. An administrator password reset is a credential change; protect the new secret and verify the user can use it.

Repeated failed attempts can trigger a configured lockout or alert. Avoid guessing credentials. Preserve the existing administrator session and documented console recovery route before changing authentication policy.

title: Passwords, Credential Storage and Policy
text:
Recall card

Verifiers, even salted hashes, require protection.
Password locking, password aging and account expiration are separate controls.
A successful local login test proves only that specific authentication flow.
Inspect status and service policy without exposing secrets.

title: PAM Stacks and Diagnosing Login Failures
text:
What PAM coordinates
Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) provide a framework through which a participating application asks configured modules to perform authentication-related work. A PAM service name selects its configuration, usually a file under /etc/pam.d/. The caller and configured modules determine the actual behavior.
Four common management groups are:







Group
Question




auth
Can the presented authentication method establish the claimed identity?


account
Is this account permitted under applicable account policy now?


password
How is an authentication token changed?


session
What setup and cleanup apply to a session?



The names describe module responsibilities; they do not imply that all applications invoke every group in the same way. Identity lookup can use NSS, and a service can also have non-PAM authorization rules. The PAM configuration manual defines service files, module types and control syntax.
A stack is ordered policy, not just a list of installed modules. Control fields determine how results affect evaluation; required, requisite, sufficient, optional and bracketed controls have different behavior. include and distribution-specific include syntax can refer to other files. Do not infer an entire login result from one matching line.



A login has several diagnostic boundaries.

title: PAM Stacks and Diagnosing Login Failures
text:
Inspect the relevant service
For the lab’s su path, inspect the installed files:
ls -l /etc/pam.d/su /etc/pam.d/common-*
sudo cat /etc/pam.d/su
sudo cat /etc/pam.d/common-auth
sudo cat /etc/pam.d/common-account
Files and includes can differ by installed provider and version. The actual su command may come from a different package on another system; inspect it with command -v su and dpkg -S "$(command -v su)" where applicable. A package lookup may not resolve a symlink in the way you expect; inspect the actual path before drawing conclusions.
Ubuntu’s pam-auth-update manages packaged profiles and the common configuration files. Its manual explains how it treats local modifications. We do not invoke it here: changing a common stack can affect multiple login and privilege paths, and --force can overwrite local policy. A known-good console session and recovery method are essential before a real PAM change.

title: PAM Stacks and Diagnosing Login Failures
section: Lab: observe a bounded failure and recovery
text:
Lab: observe a bounded failure and recovery
First confirm the test account’s known-good login from the ordinary learner shell:
getent passwd blpass
sudo passwd -S blpass
su - blpass
Authenticate with the test password, run id, then exit back to learner. Stop if the baseline login does not work. Do not use sudo su for the test: root’s invocation follows different privilege and authentication circumstances.
Record the current time, then lock only the test password:
date -Is
sudo passwd -l blpass
sudo passwd -S blpass
Confirm the locked status. From the non-root learner shell, attempt su - blpass once with the known password. Expect failure under this local lab’s policy. If it succeeds or behaves unexpectedly, exit the test session if one opened and investigate; do not keep trying passwords. Existing sessions and other authentication mechanisms can behave differently.
Inspect recent evidence without exposing credentials:
sudo journalctl -b --since '-5 minutes' --no-pager
Search the relevant time and service messages in the displayed output. Logging details and identifiers depend on the installed su, PAM modules and journal configuration. A message may be absent, and the journal can contain unrelated sensitive data; do not publish it unredacted. A failed attempt, local password status and PAM configuration are complementary observations, not a complete causal proof on their own.
Unlock this test account’s previously working password and verify recovery:
sudo passwd -u blpass
sudo passwd -S blpass
su - blpass
Authenticate once, run id, and exit. Unlocking is justified because this exercise locked a known usable password. If the original status was unknown, do not blindly unlock it. The test demonstrates this service’s behavior; it does not prove that SSH, a graphical login or another service has the same policy.

title: PAM Stacks and Diagnosing Login Failures
section: Follow a failure through the boundaries
text:
Follow a failure through the boundaries
For a real report, record the service, user, client, timestamp and exact failure without collecting the secret. Then distinguish:

Identity: does getent passwd USER resolve the intended account from the intended source?
Authentication: was the applicable credential accepted by the configured method?
Account: is the account locked, expired or restricted by policy?
Session: can the service establish the requested session, home and shell?
Authorization: is the resulting identity permitted to perform the requested operation?

Substitute the actual user in the lookup. A password prompt is not proof that the correct identity source was used; a successful password check is not proof that a session or later authorization succeeded. If the failure affects the administrator path, retain any working privileged console and use the documented recovery plan before editing configuration. Never comment out all PAM checks or paste an unreviewed stack from another distribution.
Leave blpass available for the following privilege exercise if needed, or retire it on the disposable clone using the account-lifecycle procedure after all relevant sessions end. Keep its UID and retained files in the record.

title: PAM Stacks and Diagnosing Login Failures
text:
Recall card

PAM policy is selected by service and evaluated as a stack.
Authentication, account checks, session setup and authorization are distinct.
Ubuntu common PAM configuration can affect multiple services.
Test a reversible failure on a separate account and verify the same path after recovery.

title: Administrative Privilege and Bounded Delegation
section: Identify the privilege provider and policy
text:
Identify the privilege provider and policy
sudo runs a command under a target identity subject to its policy and authentication rules. su switches identity using a different flow. Neither a locked root password nor a noninteractive root shell prevents a properly authorized administrator from obtaining root through another mechanism; actual policy matters.
Ubuntu 26.04 uses sudo-rs as the default provider, while the traditional implementation remains available. Existing installations can differ. Ubuntu’s system utility reference explains provider differences. Inspect the current clone:
command -v sudo
readlink -f "$(command -v sudo)"
sudo --version
sudo -l
sudo id -u
The final command should print 0. sudo -l describes policy for the current user; an administrator group is only one possible source of permission. Check the installed provider’s sudo --help and man sudoers-rs or corresponding manual before using provider-specific features. Do not switch providers as part of this lab.
The policy may use /etc/sudoers, included files, and in sudo-rs an optional /etc/sudoers-rs that takes precedence when present. Inspect the actual configuration and whether it includes /etc/sudoers.d:
sudo ls -l /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers-rs /etc/sudoers.d
sudo grep -nE '^[[:space:]]*(@includedir|#includedir)' /etc/sudoers
An absent optional file can produce an error. If /etc/sudoers-rs exists, inspect its include directives too. Do not assume a drop-in is active merely because its file exists. A later matching rule or group membership can broaden a grant, so review the effective policy. The sudo-rs policy manual documents includes and matching.



Test both the permitted operation and the boundary.

title: Administrative Privilege and Bounded Delegation
text:
Create a dedicated test operator
Before creating bloperator, check the account, same-named group and home path independently:
getent passwd bloperator
getent group bloperator
test ! -e /home/bloperator
Require both lookups to return no record with status 2 and the path test to succeed. Stop for an existing name, path or lookup error. Create a local account with a unique disposable password:
sudo useradd -m -U -s /bin/bash bloperator && sudo passwd bloperator
If a command fails, inspect partial state before retrying. Verify id bloperator shows no administrator group, and inspect existing grants for this user from the administrator session:
id bloperator
sudo -l -U bloperator
A denial or absence of grants is expected before the lab rule. If the user already has broad effective privileges, stop and identify their source. Keep the learner session available separately throughout.

title: Administrative Privilege and Bounded Delegation
text:
Delegate one diagnostic
The example permits only /usr/bin/id without arguments as root. It demonstrates a policy boundary; running id is not a privileged operational task in itself. Confirm the executable is the expected, root-owned system program and that untrusted users cannot modify it or its parent directories:
command -v id
ls -l /usr/bin/id
ls -ld /usr /usr/bin
Confirm that the active policy includes /etc/sudoers.d. If it does not, stop; do not modify a different policy file by guesswork. Ensure the lab drop-in is absent:
sudo test ! -e /etc/sudoers.d/bl04-observe
Only after that test succeeds, open it using the provider’s checked editor:
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/bl04-observe
Enter this single line and save:
bloperator ALL=(root) /usr/bin/id ""
The empty quoted argument specification means no command-line arguments; omitting it would allow arbitrary arguments to this executable under sudo-rs policy. ALL in the host position matches the host, while (root) is the target identity. The sudoers-rs manual describes the rule and no-argument syntax. This rule retains the default authentication requirement; NOPASSWD is not needed.
Inspect the installed file and validate the complete active policy:
sudo ls -l /etc/sudoers.d/bl04-observe
sudo visudo -c
sudo -l -U bloperator
The file should be owned by root and not writable by the test user or other untrusted users; use the installed provider’s documented ownership and mode requirements. A syntax check is necessary but does not prove the intended permissions or resolve every semantic conflict. If validation fails or the rule is not active, stop and repair from the still-open administrator session or the documented recovery route. Do not close that session and do not use an unchecked editor to bypass a policy error.

title: Administrative Privilege and Bounded Delegation
text:
Test allow, deny and rollback
From the ordinary learner shell, start su - bloperator and authenticate as the test user. In that shell:
sudo /usr/bin/id
sudo /usr/bin/id -u
sudo /usr/bin/touch /tmp/bl04-should-not-exist
Authenticate to sudo with the operator’s password if prompted. The first command should report root’s identity. The second must be denied because it has an argument; the third must be denied because it is a different executable. Stop if either denied test succeeds: another policy rule or group grants more authority than intended. Do not execute additional privileged commands to explore the grant.
A sudo timestamp can allow a later permitted invocation without another prompt; absence of a prompt alone is not proof of NOPASSWD. Exit the operator session. From the retained administrator console, remove only this verified lab drop-in and validate:
sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/bl04-observe && sudo visudo -c
sudo -l -U bloperator
Reopen a fresh bloperator session and verify sudo /usr/bin/id is denied. If it is still allowed, inspect effective rules and group membership; do not declare the rollback complete. End the test sessions. Retire the test account using the earlier lifecycle procedure or keep it only on the powered-off disposable clone with its UID and home recorded.
For a real delegation, assess what the executable can do with its inputs, environment, configuration and child processes. Editors, shells and commands that execute arbitrary programs can make an apparently narrow rule equivalent to broad root access. Use a controlled, root-owned diagnostic interface and test the negative cases; syntax validation alone cannot establish safety.

title: Administrative Privilege and Bounded Delegation
text:
Recall card

Confirm the actual sudo provider and effective policy before editing.
A policy specifies caller, host, target identity, executable and arguments.
visudo validation, an allowed test and denied tests provide different evidence.
Keep a separate administrator and recovery route until rollback is verified.

title: Service Accounts and Runtime Credentials
section: A process identity is not a human session
text:
A process identity is not a human session
A service account is an identity assigned to a workload. It can own files and be selected by a service manager without being used for interactive login. A locked password and a nologin shell reduce ordinary password/shell login paths, but neither prevents an authorized manager or root from starting a process with that UID. They do not revoke SSH keys or other access mechanisms automatically.
A persistent service identity has a stable numeric UID/GID and can own persistent state. A dynamically allocated identity can reduce account management for suitable services, but numeric identity and ownership across restarts, backups and migrations require careful design. Do not copy an ephemeral UID into a different host and assume it represents the same principal. Systemd’s execution environment reference documents User=, Group= and DynamicUser=.
A process can still have supplementary groups or capabilities. Verify the effective process context and the actual allowed operation, not just the account’s shell. Service supervision, restart behavior and unit hardening receive their own treatment later.



A service identity is one part of the workload boundary.

title: Service Accounts and Runtime Credentials
section: Establish a bounded identity and state directory
text:
Establish a bounded identity and state directory
Check the proposed user, group and state path individually:
getent passwd blsvc
getent group blsvc
test ! -e /var/lib/bl04-service-lab
Both lookups should return no record with status 2; the path test must succeed. Stop on any collision or lookup error. Confirm the actual noninteractive shell exists:
command -v nologin
ls -l /usr/sbin/nologin
For this lab use /usr/sbin/nologin only if that path exists on the clone. Create a system account with a private group and no home directory:
sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home \
  --home-dir /nonexistent --shell /usr/sbin/nologin blsvc
Inspect the resulting identity and password status:
getent passwd blsvc
id blsvc
sudo passwd -S blsvc
Do not set a password or grant sudo membership. An account with no usable password is still a valid process identity. The recorded home path /nonexistent is an account-field value; this command does not create that directory. Do not create a home merely to make it resemble a human account.
Create only the new lab state directory, owned by this identity:
sudo install -d -o blsvc -g blsvc -m 0750 /var/lib/bl04-service-lab
sudo ls -ldn /var/lib/bl04-service-lab
Run this only after the earlier absence check succeeds. The mode grants owner access and group read/traversal; other access depends on parent directories and any additional policy. Record the numeric UID/GID, path and intended owner. A separate identity is useful only if the files and operations are scoped to it.

title: Service Accounts and Runtime Credentials
section: Run a transient workload and verify ownership
text:
Run a transient workload and verify ownership
First ask systemd to run id as the service identity:
sudo systemd-run --collect --pipe --uid=blsvc --gid=blsvc /usr/bin/id
The output should show the blsvc numeric identity and group. --pipe connects the command’s output and waits for it; --collect allows the transient unit to be cleaned up after it finishes. The systemd-run manual documents these options. This is an administrative test of service execution, not an interactive login as blsvc.
Now create a harmless file under the permitted state directory:
sudo systemd-run --collect --pipe --uid=blsvc --gid=blsvc \
  /usr/bin/touch /var/lib/bl04-service-lab/probe
sudo ls -ln /var/lib/bl04-service-lab/probe
Require a successful command and compare the file’s numeric owner and group with id blsvc. If it fails, inspect the exact error, account lookup and directory traversal/ownership. Do not make the directory world-writable or run the workload as root to hide a permission failure. Check the manager’s journal for the transient unit name printed by systemd-run if output does not explain the failure.
This test demonstrates creation of one file under one identity. It does not establish isolation from every other path or prove that a future service has correct dependencies, restart policy, resource limits or security configuration.

title: Service Accounts and Runtime Credentials
text:
Handle credentials as runtime data
A workload may need a database password, private key or API token that is distinct from its UNIX identity. Treat the service account and that credential as separate assets with separate rotation, access, audit and revocation plans. Avoid putting secrets in a unit’s command line, publicly readable configuration, logs or a shared environment dump.
Systemd supports service credentials such as LoadCredential= and encrypted credential mechanisms; the systemd-creds reference describes their role. The source file’s protection, the service’s ability to read the delivered credential, backup handling, rotation and revocation still need design. Passing a credential to a process does not protect it from that process or from a sufficiently privileged administrator. This chapter does not create or print a secret.

title: Service Accounts and Runtime Credentials
text:
Retirement and diagnosis
Before retiring a real service identity, stop and disable the workload through its owner, verify no processes or timers still use it, inventory files and external credentials, retain or transfer state according to policy, revoke credentials, and only then remove the identity. A numeric UID can outlive its name on disk and later be reused.
For this lab, the transient commands have ended. Record the UID and /var/lib/bl04-service-lab ownership; leave the account and directory on the disposable clone until an explicit cleanup decision.
