Shut down the clone before restarting bl02. Do not delete a service account while a real workload is running.
If a service cannot start, distinguish: identity lookup failed; its configured user lacks path traversal; the required state mount is missing; a credential was not delivered; or the program itself exited. Inspect the unit’s effective configuration and journal and repeat the intended operation after the narrow fix. Changing its user to root is not a diagnosis.

title: Service Accounts and Runtime Credentials
text:
Recall card

A noninteractive account can still run a service process.
Stable ownership, supplementary groups and privileges determine the practical boundary.
A successful transient test proves only the operation it performed.
Runtime credentials have a lifecycle separate from the UNIX identity.
Stop workloads and account for retained state before removing an identity.

title: Sessions, logind and Authorization Beyond the Terminal
text:
User, process, session and seat
A user account is an identity record. A process has current numeric credentials. A session is a grouping of activity associated with a login or similar interaction. One user can have more than one session, and a service can run under an account without being an interactive login session. A seat represents a set of local interaction devices; a remote session need not have a local seat.
On a system using systemd-logind, the login manager tracks sessions and user activity and coordinates some operations such as power and device access. It does not replace all process credential checks or service-specific authorization. The loginctl manual describes the management interface.
Inspect the current host:
hostnamectl
id
printf 'Session ID: %s\n' "${XDG_SESSION_ID:-not supplied}"
loginctl list-sessions --no-pager
loginctl list-users --no-pager
The environment variable is a hint supplied to some sessions, not a universal session detector. su, service processes, containers or an installation without an appropriate PAM/logind integration may not yield a distinct registered session. An empty list or inaccessible manager is an observation to explain, not proof that no process exists.
If list-sessions shows a session for the console, use its observed session ID in the following command, replacing SESSION_ID:
loginctl show-session SESSION_ID \
  -p Id -p User -p Name -p Type -p Class \
  -p Remote -p Active -p State
Do not substitute a username for a session ID. Values can be empty or unavailable, and Active is a session property, not proof that every process or service belonging to that user is healthy. The session ID is local runtime state; it can change after logout or reboot. Avoid terminate-session, kill-session and lock-session during this inspection.



A service can request an authorization decision about a session’s process.

title: Sessions, logind and Authorization Beyond the Terminal
section: How a polkit request is evaluated
text:
How a polkit request is evaluated
polkit supplies an authorization interface for participating privileged services. In a common arrangement, an unprivileged subject asks a privileged mechanism to perform an action. The mechanism asks the polkit authority for a decision about that subject and named action. A policy can allow, deny or require authentication. When interaction is permitted, an authentication agent may prompt the user or an administrator.
The polkit reference describes subjects, mechanisms, actions, rules and agents. A policy decision depends on the installed rules, the specific action and subject, and potentially session context. The identity used for authentication can differ from the original requesting subject. Authentication demonstrates a credential check; authorization determines whether the operation is permitted.
sudo and polkit are distinct paths. A sudo rule for one command does not automatically authorize a polkit action, and a polkit authorization does not generally grant a root shell. Both can involve PAM or an administrator credential, but their callers, policies and audit evidence differ.

title: Sessions, logind and Authorization Beyond the Terminal
text:
Inspect actions without exercising one
If the tools and service are present:
command -v pkaction
systemctl status polkit.service --no-pager
pkaction
The unit may be absent, inactive or started on demand; status can return nonzero. If pkaction or the authority is unavailable, record that limitation and complete the conceptual exercise below. Do not install a desktop or change service policy merely to match an example.
Choose a harmless registered action identifier from the output. Assign its exact observed name to ACTION in your shell, then inspect its declaration:
test -n "${ACTION:-}" && pkaction --action-id "$ACTION" --verbose
Stop if ACTION is empty or the action does not exist. The pkaction manual describes the listing. The displayed implicit defaults for active, inactive or other subjects are not a complete prediction of the effective decision: installed authorization rules, subject details, authentication agents and the mechanism’s request can alter the result. Listing an action does not execute it.
A server console may have no graphical agent. A denied request, a request requiring authentication without an agent, and a failed credential check are different situations. Do not make an action universally allowed or run a privileged operation simply to see a prompt. Action definitions and local rules can reveal system details; review before sharing.

title: Sessions, logind and Authorization Beyond the Terminal
section: Worked diagnosis: a request cannot be authorized
text:
Worked diagnosis: a request cannot be authorized
Suppose a user reports “authorization failed” when requesting a device operation:

Identify the exact application, action, user, session, time and message. Do not collect the password or token.
Confirm the process’s current UID and groups and, if tracked, its session’s local/remote and active properties.
Check that the mechanism and authority are available and identify the requested action from the application or logs.
Inspect that action’s declaration and the site’s applicable rules; distinguish an explicit denial from an authentication challenge or an unavailable agent.
Test the same operation through an authorized, controlled workflow after a narrowly scoped correction. Verify the actual result and relevant logs.

A successful sudo -l is not a substitute for this evidence. Conversely, a polkit authorization does not prove the requested service successfully completed its operation. Do not terminate the user’s session or edit rules until the effect and recovery path are understood.

title: Sessions, logind and Authorization Beyond the Terminal
text:
Practice and recall
Record the current account, any observed session ID and properties, the presence or absence of polkit tools, and one registered action’s stated defaults if available. Explain why those defaults cannot alone predict an effective request. On a text-only host with no polkit, use the worked example to identify the missing evidence instead of fabricating a result.

An account, process, session and seat are distinct objects.
polkit evaluates a named action for a subject through a participating mechanism.
Session context and an authentication agent can affect a request.
Authentication, authorization and successful completion of the operation are separate observations.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
text:
What central identity changes
A local account database is maintained on one host. A central identity service can provide user and group information, authentication or access policy to multiple hosts. The exact architecture varies: a directory may store identities, an authentication service may issue credentials, and a Linux client may cache and translate results.








Component
Typical role
Distinguish from




LDAP directory
Search and manage structured directory entries and attributes
A guarantee that a particular login is authorized


Kerberos realm and KDC
Authenticate principals and issue time-limited tickets
A complete POSIX UID/GID database or filesystem permission policy


SSSD on a Linux client
Integrate supported identity, authentication and access providers with local interfaces
The remote directory or KDC itself


NSS and PAM
Expose identity lookup and authentication/account interfaces to applications
The remote source’s availability and the application’s own policy



LDAP is a directory access protocol; it can be used in several configurations and is not synonymous with Kerberos. The LDAP protocol specification describes its directory operations. Protect directory communication with the deployment’s verified TLS and trust configuration; an encrypted connection to an unverified endpoint does not establish the intended server’s identity.



Central identity introduces several independent dependencies.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
section: Kerberos in the minimum useful model
text:
Kerberos in the minimum useful model
A principal is a named identity in a Kerberos realm. A key distribution center (KDC) provides authentication and ticket-granting services. A client can obtain a ticket-granting ticket and use it to request a ticket for a particular service. The service must have the appropriate identity and key material to validate its ticket. A keytab holds long-term principal keys and must be protected like other credentials.
A ticket has a lifetime and is not a replacement for local authorization. DNS and time are operational dependencies: clients must locate the intended service, and unacceptable clock skew can prevent authentication. Realm naming conventions and discovery rules depend on the deployment. Ubuntu’s Kerberos introduction provides the terminology; its server guide identifies DNS and time as prerequisites.
If a client already has the Kerberos utility and a legitimate credential cache, klist can display ticket metadata:
if command -v klist >/dev/null; then
  klist
else
  printf 'klist is not installed; no ticket inspection performed\n'
fi
An empty cache or a nonzero result is expected on a local-only lab host. Ticket names, addresses and timestamps can be sensitive; redact before sharing. klist does not create a ticket. Do not use options that display key material or run kinit with an unknown principal simply to produce output. The MIT klist reference distinguishes ticket-cache and keytab inspection.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
text:
Where SSSD fits
SSSD can provide NSS and PAM integration with supported remote identity and authentication sources. It can also cache information and, when configured and permitted, support some offline logins. What is cached, for whom, for how long and under which policy are deployment-specific. A successful cached lookup or offline login does not prove that the directory or KDC is currently reachable. Canonical’s SSSD overview describes these interfaces and common provider combinations.
On a configured host, /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and optional snippets describe domains and providers; their ownership and restricted access matter. The Ubuntu SSSD configuration manual documents file permissions and snippet precedence. Configuration may contain sensitive topology or credential references. Do not publish it, clear caches, change providers or restart SSSD during the introductory inspection.
Numeric identity is an operational dependency. If two hosts map one central user to different UIDs, shared files can appear to belong to the wrong principal. If a local and central account collide by name or number, source order can change which record an application sees. Choose and verify a consistent mapping policy before migrating ownership or enabling shared storage.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
text:
Read-only local inventory
On bl02, establish the existing local baseline:
hostnamectl
id
getent passwd "$(id -un)"
grep -E '^(passwd|group|shadow):' /etc/nsswitch.conf
timedatectl status
systemctl status sssd.service --no-pager
SSSD may not be installed or active; status can return nonzero. A source named sss in NSS configuration is not by itself proof that an SSSD domain is configured or reachable. The clock display is evidence about local time and reported synchronization, not a guarantee that a particular KDC agrees with it. The current user’s successful local lookup does not prove remote identity works.
If this host has no central identity configured, record “not configured or not established by this inspection” and continue with the synthetic exercise. Do not install packages, join a realm, alter the local administrator or expose the guest to a real directory to manufacture a result.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
section: Worked diagnosis: central lookup works but login fails
text:
Worked diagnosis: central lookup works but login fails
Consider a fictional user alex@example.test on a host configured for a directory and Kerberos. The name is illustrative; do not query a real environment without authorization.

getent passwd 'alex@example.test' returns a UID and home. This supports a lookup result, potentially from cache; it does not prove a live directory connection.
A login attempt fails. Record the actual service, error and time. Check account policy and its PAM path, and distinguish authentication from session/home failure.
Inspect configured DNS names and reachability, time synchronization and SSSD status using the site’s approved procedure. Compare the actual provider and current state rather than guessing from package names.
If Kerberos is in use, inspect ticket metadata for the affected authorized session where appropriate; absence of a ticket, an expired ticket, a KDC error and a service authorization denial require different follow-up.
After the targeted correction, repeat the same login and intended operation from the same client context. Verify UID/GID, home access and service authorization, and document whether the result was online or cached.

Do not clear all identity caches as a first diagnostic step. It can discard useful state and affect offline access. Do not create a same-named local user as a shortcut: a collision can change identity resolution and file ownership. For a planned deployment, retain a tested local administrative recovery path that does not depend on the central service, while protecting that path and auditing its use.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
text:
Design exercise and acceptance
Without creating infrastructure, write a one-page dependency plan for two future Linux hosts:

Identify the authority for user/group records, authentication and access policy; state whether they are the same service.
Define how names and numeric IDs remain consistent, and how homes and file ownership are provisioned.
Record DNS, network, time and certificate/trust dependencies and who maintains them.
State offline-login policy, cache limits, credential/keytab protection and a tested local recovery route.
Specify a positive login and client-operation test, a denied-access test, and evidence to collect if directory or KDC access fails.

Success for this chapter is a coherent plan and an honest local inventory, not a simulated claim that a central login has been tested. The integrated implementation belongs after its networking and trust prerequisites are available.

title: Central Identity: LDAP, Kerberos and SSSD Foundations
text:
Recall card

Directory lookup, ticket authentication, account policy and application authorization are separate functions.
SSSD is a client integration component; cached success may not mean the provider is online.
DNS, time, trust and consistent numeric IDs are operational dependencies.
Preserve a protected local recovery path and test the actual login and service operation.

title: Package Metadata, File Ownership and Installed State
section: From software to a running process
text:
From software to a running process
A package is a distribution artifact containing files and metadata used to install and maintain software. Its metadata can name a version, architecture, dependencies and configuration files. Ubuntu’s Debian package system records local package state in dpkg’s database. APT uses repository metadata and local state to plan transactions.



Software has several layers of ownership and evidence.


An upstream release number and the distribution package version need not be identical. A distribution can backport fixes while retaining an upstream-looking version. A version string alone does not prove whether a specific fix is present; consult the package changelog and the distribution’s security information for the exact release and package.
An installed package is not necessarily running, and a running process can continue executing an older mapped executable after files are upgraded. A repository candidate is a proposed available version, not proof that this host installed it.

title: Package Metadata, File Ownership and Installed State
text:
Query the installed database
On bl02, confirm the host and package architecture:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
dpkg --print-architecture
dpkg --print-foreign-architectures
A package’s architecture may be all, the native architecture or another configured architecture. An empty foreign-architecture list is normal.
Use the installed apt package as a stable example:
dpkg-query -l apt
dpkg-query -W -f='${binary:Package} ${Version} ${Architecture} ${db:Status-Abbrev}\n' apt
dpkg-query -s apt
In dpkg-query -l, the columns represent desired action, current status and error flag. The commonly seen ii means selected for installation and currently installed; a package can instead be unpacked, half-configured or have configuration files left after removal. The dpkg-query manual defines the states. The formatted query is easier to compare than assuming that every listed package is fully installed.
Inspect a package’s recorded files and dependencies:
dpkg-query -L apt
apt-cache depends apt
apt-cache policy apt
-L lists paths registered to the package, not necessarily every file created later by a maintainer script or an alternatives mechanism. apt-cache depends reads available metadata; apt-cache policy compares installed and candidate versions using the current APT cache. That cache can be stale or incomplete. A package may have several architecture-qualified names or multiple packages contributing to a working program.

title: Package Metadata, File Ownership and Installed State
section: Map an executable to its package
text:
Map an executable to its package
Ask the shell what it would execute, then inspect the path and package ownership:
command -v apt
readlink -f "$(command -v apt)"
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/apt
The query path is the conventional Ubuntu lab path; first confirm that it exists and is the actual path on this host. If it differs, query the observed path instead. Symlinks, alternatives, diversions and the merged /usr layout can make the invoked path and the package-recorded path differ. dpkg-query -S searches package database records; it is not a full filesystem scan or a proof that the current file contents are authentic. A generated file, local installation, container image or Snap application may have no matching dpkg owner.
For a package file, inspect its installed metadata separately from the file’s current bytes. Package verification tools have limits: not all files have recorded checksums, and local configuration is expected to differ. Do not overwrite a suspected file until you know its owner, expected configuration and recovery plan.

title: Package Metadata, File Ownership and Installed State
section: Worked diagnosis: “the package owns the wrong version”
text:
Worked diagnosis: “the package owns the wrong version”
Suppose apt-cache policy apt shows installed version A and candidate B, while the command’s --version reports A. This may simply mean B is available but not installed. Check dpkg status, the active executable path and the cache timestamp. If a daemon reports an older version after a successful upgrade, check when its process started and plan the service restart or reboot required by its owner; do not infer that package installation failed from a long-running process alone.
If dpkg-query -S cannot find a path, inspect whether it is a symlink, an alternative, generated state or software installed outside dpkg. Do not delete the file as “unmanaged” without understanding its role.

title: Package Metadata, File Ownership and Installed State
text:
Practice and recall
Record the host, architecture, installed apt package version and state, candidate version, executable path and package ownership result. Identify one observation that would require a separate runtime check. Redact internal repository details before sharing.

Package state, candidate version, filesystem path and running process are separate observations.
dpkg-query reports recorded ownership and state, not a complete history of every file.
APT metadata reflects the most recent successful refresh, not necessarily current remote state.
Use the distribution’s package and security information to interpret versions and fixes.

title: dpkg, APT and Dependency Resolution
text:
What each tool knows
A .deb package carries files and control metadata. dpkg records selections, unpacked files and configuration state. APT reads enabled sources and cached package indexes, considers dependency relationships and proposes a set of packages to install, upgrade or remove; it then invokes package installation machinery. The Ubuntu package-management guide describes this division.



APT’s plan, dpkg state and runtime verification are distinct stages.


Depends expresses a required relationship for package configuration; alternatives and virtual packages can provide multiple ways to satisfy it. Pre-Depends, conflicts and version constraints can affect ordering or feasibility. A package manager reasons about declared relationships, not every site-specific application dependency or service health condition.

title: dpkg, APT and Dependency Resolution
section: Refresh and preview on the clone
text:
Refresh and preview on the clone
Check the clone, console, disk space and network before changing package state:
hostnamectl
sudo id -u
df -h / /var
ip -brief address
ip route
sudo dpkg --audit
An empty audit normally means no reported partially installed package state, not that every application is healthy. Address and route output do not prove repository access. Review the configured sources using the first-boot procedure, then refresh:
sudo apt update
Require a clean result; a partial refresh is not a clean baseline. Preserve errors instead of bypassing signature checks. APT’s manual distinguishes refreshing package indexes from installing upgrades.
Check whether tree is already installed or held:
dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${binary:Package} ${Version}\n' tree
apt-mark showhold
apt-cache policy tree
dpkg-query can report no matching package and return nonzero. Proceed only if tree is not installed, is not held, and a candidate is available. If it is already installed or held, record the difference and use a newly prepared clone instead of removing or unholding an existing package. Confirm the clone has no production data or service dependency on this test package.
Preview:
sudo apt-get -s install tree
-s simulates a transaction and does not apply package changes. Read the complete proposal: new packages, upgrades, removals and errors. A simulation is not a reservation; another package job or a metadata change can alter the eventual transaction. If the proposal is unexpectedly broad or removes packages, stop and investigate. Do not accept a destructive change just because a simulation returned output.

title: dpkg, APT and Dependency Resolution
section: Install, verify and keep the test package
text:
Install, verify and keep the test package
After reviewing the simulation, run the interactive transaction:
sudo apt install tree
Review the actual confirmation before accepting. If a package manager is already running, identify it and wait; do not delete lock files. Keep the transaction output and investigate any error before proceeding. Installation scripts may run as part of configuration and can have effects outside the package’s file list.
Verify the result:
dpkg-query -l tree
dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Version}\n' tree
command -v tree
tree --version
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/tree
sudo dpkg --audit
Expect a fully installed package, a command that runs and a recorded package owner for the observed executable. Confirm the actual path before using the conventional /usr/bin/tree query. An empty audit and successful --version are useful but do not prove every feature or external dependency.
APT distinguishes upgrade from full-upgrade: the latter may remove packages to resolve the transaction, while the former does not remove installed packages. The APT manual documents the distinction. Do not switch to a more disruptive command simply to eliminate a pending count.

title: dpkg, APT and Dependency Resolution
text:
Diagnose an incomplete transaction
If installation stops, record the exact operation, package state and logs before retrying:
sudo dpkg --audit
dpkg-query -l tree
sudo tail -n 80 /var/log/apt/history.log
sudo tail -n 80 /var/log/apt/term.log
An unpacked or half-configured status differs from fully installed. Disk capacity, an interrupted maintainer script, dependency problems and another active package job need different responses. Do not delete lock files, remove package database files or force-install unrelated packages. A later chapter practices recovery of an interrupted transaction with a deliberately bounded fault.
Keep tree and the clone for the version and hold exercise. Record the pre-install absence, proposed and actual transaction, installed version, command result and cleanup obligation. A clone on the same host is not an independent backup.

title: dpkg, APT and Dependency Resolution
text:
Recall card

APT proposes dependency-aware transactions; dpkg records and configures package state.
Refreshing indexes, simulating, installing and verifying are separate operations.
A simulation can become stale before the actual transaction.
A package can be unpacked but not fully configured.
Preserve errors and inspect state before attempting repair.

title: Repositories, Signatures and Source Configuration
text:
The authenticated repository chain
A repository publishes release metadata describing package indexes; those indexes describe package files and their checksums. APT verifies repository authentication using the configured trust material and then uses the authenticated metadata chain when retrieving packages. The APT secure manual describes the archive-authentication model.



Trust attaches to metadata, indexes and package files.


A signature establishes that metadata was signed by a key accepted by the configured policy; it does not prove that the software is safe, that a key was obtained from the right publisher, or that the running application is uncompromised. A compromised trusted signing key or repository remains a risk. HTTPS protects transport to a validated endpoint, while repository signatures provide a separate metadata-authentication mechanism; neither replaces choosing a trustworthy source and key.

title: Repositories, Signatures and Source Configuration
text:
Read configured sources
APT can read a traditional one-line .list file and deb822-style .sources files. On a fresh Ubuntu 26.04 installation, ubuntu.sources is common, but imported or upgraded systems can differ. Inspect the actual files:
ls -l /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d
sudo cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources
An absent optional file produces an error; list and inspect the files that actually exist. Source entries can contain private mirror names or credentials; restrict and redact before sharing. The sources.list manual defines source formats and options.
A deb822 entry can describe Types, URIs, Suites, Components, architectures, an enabled state and Signed-By. For this lab, record the observed release suites, components, mirror and any scoped keyring. A source configuration is intent. apt-cache policy and apt update provide additional evidence about loaded indexes and refresh results.
A Signed-By value can restrict which keyring or key may authenticate that source. Keyrings, permissions and their contents must be checked according to the installed APT version and publisher instructions; do not assume every source uses the same key. A third-party signing key should be independently verified through a trusted channel and scoped to the intended source. Avoid adding an unverified key to a broad global trust store.

title: Repositories, Signatures and Source Configuration
section: Connect a package candidate to sources
text:
Connect a package candidate to sources
After the clean metadata refresh in the prior chapter:
apt-cache policy tree
apt-cache policy
apt-config dump | grep -E 'Dir::Etc::(sourcelist|sourceparts|trusted)'
The first command reports the package’s installed version, candidate, priorities and available origins as known to APT. The second summarizes configured package origins and priorities. apt-config dump exposes selected configuration paths; the filter can return no lines. Interpret all results as the local cache and configuration, not an independent attestation of a remote server’s current content.
Origin, Label, Suite, Codename and a repository URI answer different questions. An authenticated Release file contains publisher-provided labels; a familiar label alone is not a fingerprint. A candidate can be the same version available from more than one source, and this policy display is not definitive historical proof of which source supplied an already installed package.

title: Repositories, Signatures and Source Configuration
text:
Diagnose a failed refresh
Suppose apt update reports a missing key, expired metadata or a failed signature. Preserve the exact error and source. Then:

Confirm the guest’s time with timedatectl status and the intended source definition.
Check whether the configured keyring and its access permissions match the trusted publisher’s current instructions and your change record.
Distinguish a network or mirror failure from a signature or metadata-validity failure; read the complete APT result.
Apply a verified, authorized source or key correction using the distribution’s documented process, then run apt update again and require a clean result.

Do not disable authentication, accept an unknown key, or add an unrelated repository to make an update finish. A key rotation requires a trusted verification channel and an operational plan, not a fingerprint copied from the failing mirror itself. A stale cached candidate can still appear after a failed refresh; record the failure and do not treat that candidate as freshly verified.

title: Repositories, Signatures and Source Configuration
text:
Practice and recall
Record the enabled source files, observed suites and components, any Signed-By scope, last clean refresh result, and the tree candidate and origins. Explain why a matching package name, reachable mirror and signed metadata each support different claims. Keep private source URLs and credentials out of shared evidence.

A repository signature authenticates metadata under a configured trust policy.
Source configuration, cached metadata and installed package history are distinct.
Scope and independently verify third-party keys.
Resolve trust errors rather than bypassing them.

title: Version Selection, Holds, Pinning and Dependency Conflicts
text:
Installed, candidate and available
dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Version}\n' tree
apt-cache policy tree
apt-mark showhold
sudo apt-get -s upgrade
The installed version is local package state. The candidate is APT’s current preferred version under its available metadata and policy. A simulated upgrade shows a proposed transaction, including packages that may be deferred. Read the complete result; a hold can affect automatic upgrade behavior even when a newer candidate exists. Other causes include dependency changes, pin priorities, phased updates or a policy that requires a different transaction type.
A simulation does not reserve packages or prevent another job from changing the state. apt-cache policy does not prove that a candidate was installed, tested or supplied by a particular repository in an earlier transaction.

title: Version Selection, Holds, Pinning and Dependency Conflicts
text:
Priorities and pins
APT preferences assign priorities to versions. Default priorities vary with installed state, target release and archive metadata; phased updates can also affect eligibility. APT normally avoids downgrades unless a sufficiently high priority or explicit choice changes that behavior. When priorities tie, version ordering matters. The APT preferences manual documents the complete algorithm and warns that careless preferences can make packages uninstallable.
Inspect existing preferences without editing them:
ls -l /etc/apt/preferences /etc/apt/preferences.d
apt-cache policy tree
An absent optional file is normal. Review actual .pref files only if present, and protect private repository details. A pin is a selection rule, not a guarantee that the resulting combination is supported or secure. Mixing unrelated release suites can select incompatible libraries; do not copy a pin from another host or assign an extreme priority just to force a desired answer.
A hold is a package selection state that suppresses certain automatic package changes. It is not a security update plan, a dependency lockfile or an absolute barrier to every explicit administrative operation. Record why it exists, who owns it, when to review it, and which security fixes are deferred. The apt-mark manual describes hold and unhold.

title: Version Selection, Holds, Pinning and Dependency Conflicts
section: Lab: hold and release the disposable package
text:
Lab: hold and release the disposable package
First reconfirm the exact target and preconditions:
hostnamectl
dpkg-query -l tree
apt-mark showhold
Proceed only on the identified package clone, with tree fully installed and absent from the hold list. If it was already held, do not overwrite another operator’s policy. Record the installed version and pre-existing hold list.
sudo apt-mark hold tree
apt-mark showhold
apt-cache policy tree
Confirm tree appears in the hold list. The candidate output may remain unchanged: a hold and candidate selection are different views. You need not have a newer version available to demonstrate the hold state; do not fabricate an upgrade result.
Restore the original state:
sudo apt-mark unhold tree
apt-mark showhold
dpkg-query -l tree
Verify that tree is no longer held and is still installed. If unhold fails, preserve the output and leave the clone’s record open; do not report rollback complete. No package version was changed by these hold commands.

title: Version Selection, Holds, Pinning and Dependency Conflicts
text:
Investigate a dependency conflict
For a reported package, inspect its installed state, candidate and declared relationships:
apt-cache policy tree
apt-cache depends tree
apt-cache rdepends tree
sudo apt-get -s install tree
A Depends line can include alternatives and version constraints; reverse dependencies show metadata relationships, not proof that every listed package is installed or in active use. Review the full simulated proposal and its error. A request for an explicit package=version is still subject to available metadata and dependency constraints, and a real installation can change or remove other packages. Do not force a version or downgrade the lab’s core libraries to make the simulation succeed.
For a real conflict, record the enabled sources, installed and candidate versions, holds, preferences and the exact resolver message. Determine a supported set of packages, service impact and recovery path before changing policy. A version rollback can leave newer data formats or configuration incompatible with the older program; a package downgrade is not a complete application rollback.
Keep tree on the clone for the next configuration chapter, then remove it as directed there. Keep the original guest unchanged.

title: Version Selection, Holds, Pinning and Dependency Conflicts
text:
Recall card

Installed version, APT candidate and hold state answer different questions.
Pins affect selection; they do not prove compatibility or safety.
A hold needs an owner, expiry/review decision and security-update plan.
Read the whole resolver proposal and preserve a recovery path before changing versions.

title: Configuration Files, Alternatives and Package Hooks
section: A conffile is a package-managed configuration file
text:
A conffile is a package-managed configuration file
A Debian package can mark selected files as conffiles. dpkg tracks the installed package version and can ask what to do when both the administrator and a new package version changed a conffile. Not every file under /etc is a dpkg conffile: packages and applications also generate or manage configuration by other mechanisms.
Inspect the package’s recorded conffile information:
dpkg-query -W -f='${binary:Package}\n${Conffiles}\n' apt
The output can contain paths and recorded checksums; it does not show an intelligible three-way diff or prove that a service accepts its current configuration. If the field is empty, choose another installed package known to have conffiles rather than fabricating a path. The dpkg manual describes conffile handling and package states.
Before a real upgrade, record the service’s current configuration, package version, dependencies, validation command and recovery path. During a conffile prompt, inspect the displayed difference and consult the package’s instructions. Common choices can keep the local file, install the maintainer’s file, or inspect differences; available prompts and defaults depend on the operation and options. Keep a protected backup and test the resulting service behavior. Blindly accepting either side is not a merge strategy.
Files with suffixes such as .dpkg-dist, .dpkg-old or .dpkg-new can be evidence of a package operation, but their presence and exact meaning depend on the operation. Review the actual files before deleting or merging them. Configuration can contain secrets; restrict access and redact differences before sharing.

title: Configuration Files, Alternatives and Package Hooks
text:
Maintainer scripts and triggers
Packages can run maintainer scripts during installation, configuration, upgrade and removal. Triggers allow one package to request deferred work from another; package state can remain pending while that work is incomplete. These scripts can affect generated files or services that are not listed as ordinary package payload paths.
Inspect the available control files for the installed apt package:
dpkg-query --control-list apt
If postinst appears in the list, inspect it without executing it:
dpkg-query --control-show apt postinst
A missing script is normal for some packages. The dpkg-query manual documents these read-only control-file queries. A script’s content is not a transaction preview; its execution depends on package state, arguments, dependencies and environment. Never run a maintainer script manually just to see what it does.
When a transaction fails, capture the package state and exact script error. A partially configured package and a fully configured package with a broken application are different conditions. The later interrupted-transaction chapter covers controlled recovery; do not force a package state or remove scripts from the database to silence an error.

title: Configuration Files, Alternatives and Package Hooks
text:
Alternatives select an implementation
The alternatives system can present a common name that points through managed symbolic links to one of several implementations. Automatic mode generally follows configured priorities; manual mode retains a selected choice until an administrator changes it. Inspect the editor group if present:
update-alternatives --display editor
ls -l /usr/bin/editor /etc/alternatives/editor
readlink -f /usr/bin/editor
An unavailable alternatives group or path is a result to investigate, not a reason to create one. The update-alternatives manual describes link groups and modes. Package ownership of the final executable, an alternatives selection, and a user’s EDITOR environment variable can all affect what is actually invoked. Inspect the relevant caller before changing the system default.
This operation is read-only. A real alternatives change should identify the owner and consumers, record the previous mode and selection, test the affected application and provide a rollback. Not every Ubuntu command is managed by alternatives; for example, distribution provider selection may use other packaging mechanisms.

title: Configuration Files, Alternatives and Package Hooks
section: Lab: finish and remove the test package
text:
Lab: finish and remove the test package
The earlier chapters installed tree only after confirming it was absent, then removed its temporary hold. Reconfirm those assumptions on the clone:
hostnamectl
dpkg-query -l tree
apt-mark showhold
Proceed only if the manager identifies bl05-packages-lab, tree is the test package installed during this lab and it is no longer held. If the original state is uncertain, stop; do not remove a package merely because it is named tree.
Preview removal:
sudo apt-get -s remove tree
Read the whole proposed transaction. If it removes anything other than the intended test package or reports unexpected dependency consequences, stop and investigate. When the actual proposal is understood:
sudo apt remove tree
Review the real confirmation before accepting. Do not run autoremove or purge as part of this exercise: dependencies or configuration can have other owners and retention requirements. Verify the package state and command result:
dpkg-query -l tree
command -v tree
sudo dpkg --audit
command -v tree may return no output and nonzero if no other executable with that name is on PATH; that is expected for this clean lab. A removed package can leave configuration records, and another installation mechanism could provide a command with the same name. Record the actual state and investigate any discrepancy. End with the clone powered off before restarting bl02.

title: Configuration Files, Alternatives and Package Hooks
section: Worked diagnosis: a service changed after upgrade
text:
Worked diagnosis: a service changed after upgrade
Suppose a service fails after its package upgraded. Compare the transaction time, package version, service logs and configuration validation. Check whether a conffile was kept, replaced or left with an alternate version, and whether a maintainer script or trigger failed. Restore or merge only after understanding which configuration belongs to the new version. Then restart through the service’s documented procedure and repeat a client-side acceptance test.
Replacing all of /etc from an old backup or downgrading a package without accounting for data-format changes can create further failures. Preserve the evidence and use the service’s supported recovery plan.

title: Configuration Files, Alternatives and Package Hooks
text:
Practice and recall
Record one package’s conffile field, one available control-file name, the editor alternatives state if present, and the test package’s before/after removal state. Explain why none of those alone proves the application is working.

A conffile is one package-management mechanism, not every configuration file.
Maintainer scripts and triggers can change state beyond a file list.
Alternatives, package ownership and an environment override are different selection layers.
Preview removal and verify the actual resulting state; do not assume purge or autoremove is harmless.

title: Security Updates and Maintenance Windows
text:
Decide what must change
A distribution often backports security fixes without changing the upstream-looking version to the latest upstream release. Compare the installed package version and its Ubuntu security notice or changelog; an upstream version string alone does not establish exposure. Check the release, enabled repositories, support status and whether the affected component is actually used. Ubuntu’s security-update documentation describes its archive and extended security coverage.
A maintenance window is an agreed period for a change and its verification. Establish a responsible operator, expected disruption, dependencies, a restorable backup, access through a console if networking fails, and a stop condition. For a fleet, update a representative canary first and measure results before proceeding. A backup is only a recovery plan if its restore has been tested and the application data is consistent.

title: Security Updates and Maintenance Windows
text:
Observe policy and evidence
On bl05-packages-lab, start the previously prepared clone with the original bl02 powered off. The two share an identity and must not be online together. Confirm the lab identity and inspect:
hostnamectl
cat /etc/os-release
apt-cache policy
apt-mark showhold
systemctl list-timers 'apt-*'
apt-config dump | grep -E 'APT::Periodic|Unattended-Upgrade'
A missing timer or an empty match is evidence to investigate, not proof that no other automation exists. Configuration may be spread across files and list options can accumulate. Review the effective settings and their source files; a later scalar assignment can override an earlier one, while list entries may be added. Avoid placing credentials in shared logs.
dpkg-query -W unattended-upgrades
systemctl status apt-daily.timer apt-daily-upgrade.timer --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u apt-daily-upgrade.service --since '7 days ago' --no-pager
sudo ls -l /var/log/unattended-upgrades/
Some images omit these packages, timers or logs. A timer’s next activation does not prove the previous run succeeded, nor that it covered a particular repository. If present, inspect the unattended-upgrades log and compare its timestamp and actual package changes with the security policy. APT periodic downloads, unattended installation, Snap refreshes and reboot scheduling are distinct controls. The Ubuntu documentation recommends local drop-ins instead of editing the packaged 50unattended-upgrades file; review the active origins and reboot policy rather than assuming defaults apply to every image or third-party source.

title: Security Updates and Maintenance Windows
section: Perform a controlled update on the clone
text:
Perform a controlled update on the clone
The clone needs working DNS and access to its configured, trusted repositories. Record its installed versions and running kernel; ensure the virtual console works and a recovery copy exists. apt update changes the local package indexes and requires network access:
uname -r
sudo apt update
apt list --upgradable
sudo apt-get -s upgrade
Read the complete simulation, including held-back packages, conffile implications and any service or kernel changes. A simulation is not a reservation: repository state, other package operations or local policy can change before execution. upgrade and full-upgrade have different removal behavior; do not substitute the latter merely to make the list empty.
If the lab’s proposed changes are understood and a maintenance window is available, run sudo apt upgrade on the clone, read the actual proposal and confirmation, and decline if it differs unexpectedly. Do not interrupt a running package transaction. Record the result and investigate errors before attempting another operation:
sudo dpkg --audit
apt list --upgradable
journalctl -b -p warning --no-pager
Some updates may remain phased, held or unavailable through the configured sources. Check apt-cache policy PACKAGE for a specific package; do not assume an empty audit proves every workload healthy. Test the service or command affected by each update and record versions, timings and any required restart or reboot. The next chapter handles the kernel decision. Leave the clone available for the next lab.

title: Security Updates and Maintenance Windows
text:
Diagnose a missed update
If an advisory’s fix is absent, first establish the distribution release, architecture, installed version and advisory’s fixed version. Then inspect sources, apt-cache policy, hold state, timer/service logs and network or signature errors. A fresh index cannot fix an untrusted or unreachable repository, and an installed library does not automatically replace code already mapped into every running process. Decide on a service restart or reboot with the workload owner, then verify the running service and client-visible behavior.

title: Security Updates and Maintenance Windows
text:
Practice and recall
Write a one-page maintenance record with preconditions, the simulated proposal, actual result, restart decision and acceptance check. Explain why automatic installation does not guarantee automatic remediation and why a clean package database is only one success signal.

title: Kernel Updates, Reboots and Livepatch
section: Inspect the running and installed kernels
text:
Inspect the running and installed kernels
On bl05-packages-lab, inspect without changing boot selection:
uname -r
dpkg-query -W 'linux-image-*' 2>/dev/null
ls -l /boot/vmlinuz-* /boot/initrd.img-* 2>/dev/null
ls -l /var/run/reboot-required* 2>/dev/null
The package query may include records for packages that are not installed. Inspect their status with dpkg-query -l PACKAGE. The reboot-required files are useful signals when present, not a complete list of all reasons to restart and not proof of which change triggered them. Missing files or unmatched globs may produce errors on a particular image. /boot can be separate and can fill independently of the root filesystem:
findmnt /boot
findmnt /boot/efi
df -h /boot /boot/efi
An absent separate mount is not necessarily an error; verify the actual layout before changing it. Meta-packages track a kernel series and flavor, while versioned image, modules and headers packages serve different roles. Out-of-tree modules, including DKMS-built drivers, must be compatible with the target kernel and the host’s Secure Boot policy. See the earlier boot chapters for initramfs and boot-entry evidence.

title: Kernel Updates, Reboots and Livepatch
text:
Plan the transition
Before applying updates, record the current kernel, the intended target, storage space, bootloader entry and fallback console. A fallback requires an installed, bootable previous kernel with its matching modules and initramfs; an old filename alone is not a tested fallback. Preserve access to any encrypted root unlock mechanism and confirm a recovery environment is available. Review package proposals before removing old kernels: keeping every version indefinitely can fill /boot, while deleting the only tested fallback can make recovery harder.
After the controlled update in the preceding chapter, compare installed versioned images with uname -r. If the next boot should use a newer kernel, arrange a reboot within the window:
sudo systemctl reboot
Run this only on the lab clone after confirming its identity and access through the VM console. A reboot ends sessions and interrupts workloads. Reconnect after startup and verify:
uname -r
systemctl is-system-running
journalctl -b -p warning --no-pager
sudo dpkg --audit
A degraded state warrants investigation; unrelated warnings require context. Verify the actual workload, network and any external kernel modules, not just the version. If the new kernel fails, use the known bootloader fallback through the console, capture its failure evidence and repair the cause before trying again. Do not blindly restore an older kernel indefinitely or disable boot security to make an unsigned driver work.

title: Kernel Updates, Reboots and Livepatch
section: Livepatch changes the timing, not the lifecycle
text:
Livepatch changes the timing, not the lifecycle
Canonical Livepatch can apply selected security fixes to a supported running Ubuntu kernel. Coverage, kernel support and subscription availability vary; it does not cover all kernel fixes or eliminate normal package updates and planned reboots. Check the service’s actual status and advisory coverage, not merely the presence of a client package. Ubuntu’s security-update documentation describes the service and its limits. Other Linux systems have different live-patching implementations and support policies.

title: Kernel Updates, Reboots and Livepatch
section: Worked diagnosis: package updated, vulnerability remains
text:
Worked diagnosis: package updated, vulnerability remains
An administrator installs a fixed kernel image but the scanner still sees the old running release. Compare uname -r with the installed version, inspect the planned boot entry and determine whether the relevant issue is covered by an active live patch. If a reboot is required, schedule one, then verify the running release and service acceptance. If the booted version remains old, investigate the actual boot selection and boot logs rather than repeatedly reinstalling the image.

title: Kernel Updates, Reboots and Livepatch
text:
Practice and recall
Record running and installed kernels before and after the lab reboot. Identify one reason a version string is insufficient to establish security status and one reason a fallback kernel is not a substitute for a tested restore.

title: Snaps, Flatpak and Other Software Formats
section: Identify the owner and update path
text:
Identify the owner and update path
APT and dpkg manage Debian packages and their dependencies. Snap packages are managed by snapd, with revisions, channels, interfaces and a separate refresh mechanism. Flatpak applications and shared runtimes are managed per system or per user through configured remotes. Standalone binaries, language-specific environments and container images have still other owners and update paths. A container image is not a replacement for updating the host kernel or runtime.
Start by identifying a particular command instead of guessing its format:
type -a firefox
command -v firefox
readlink -f "$(command -v firefox)"
If the command is missing, command -v returns nonzero and there is no resolved path to inspect. A launcher or wrapper may hand off to another manager; a Debian-owned launcher does not prove the application payload is a Debian package. Follow the actual execution path and compare inventories:
dpkg-query -S /usr/bin/firefox
snap list
flatpak list
The example path may be absent or unowned; the snap or flatpak commands may not be installed. Run the relevant query only when its manager exists, and inspect the path actually found. Manager inventory and application behavior both matter.

title: Snaps, Flatpak and Other Software Formats
text:
Snap: revisions, confinement and refresh
Where snapd is installed, inspect without installing or changing anything:
snap list --all
snap refresh --time
snap changes
A Snap has a publisher, channel and revision; snap list --all may show retained disabled revisions. Snaps normally refresh automatically. Strict confinement uses interfaces to mediate access, whereas classic confinement grants broader host access; confinement is not a guarantee that an application is safe. A refresh can affect running services or application sessions. Snap’s update documentation explains schedules, holds and their scope.
A targeted refresh can bypass a hold on that specific snap; do not treat a hold as an immutable freeze. Reverting to a retained revision can restore some revision-specific data, but common application data and external databases can remain changed. Test the application’s own recovery procedure and compatibility before relying on a revert. See Snap revisions for data behavior.

title: Snaps, Flatpak and Other Software Formats
text:
Flatpak: applications, runtimes and remotes
If Flatpak is installed, inventory both applications and runtimes, and distinguish the user and system installations:
flatpak remotes --show-details
flatpak list --app
flatpak list --runtime
A remote is a software source with its own trust and lifecycle. An application can depend on a runtime maintained separately from the host’s Debian libraries. Permissions and desktop portals mediate access, but available grants and overrides change the effective boundary. Inspect an installed application’s declared permissions with flatpak info --show-permissions APP_ID; use an actual application ID from the inventory. See Flatpak’s concepts and command reference.
No installation or permission change is required for this exercise. On a server, avoid installing an additional manager simply to run these queries. Missing tools and empty lists are legitimate inventory results.

title: Snaps, Flatpak and Other Software Formats
text:
Make one maintenance inventory
For each application record its executable or launch method, manager, publisher/source, version or revision, automatic update policy, data location, privileges, restart needs and removal/restore method. Do not assume apt remove removes a Snap or that removing an application removes its data. A script in /usr/local, a language virtual environment or a vendor tarball may have no central update service at all; assign an owner and patch process explicitly.

title: Snaps, Flatpak and Other Software Formats
text:
Worked diagnosis and practice
A desktop application is reported vulnerable after apt upgrade succeeds. Determine which application is actually launched, inspect its manager and source, and compare its installed revision against the publisher’s advisory. Check whether a pending refresh requires the application to exit. Update using that manager’s documented process in a maintenance window, then verify the running application. On the lab clone, create a two-column inventory of installed managers and sources; explain what each manager does not update.

title: Source Builds, Local Packages and Reproducibility
text:
Record the supply chain
Record the project’s identity, release or commit, source URL, verified signature or hash from an independently authenticated channel, license, target architecture, compiler, dependency versions and build instructions. Build in an isolated disposable environment with no production credentials and limited network access. Build scripts are executable code: an untrusted source tree must not be run with administrator privileges. Inspect the build system and use the upstream project’s documented tests.
A reproducible build means independent builds from equivalent declared inputs produce bit-identical artifacts. It does not establish that the source is benign. Timestamps, generated file order, toolchain versions, paths and network-fetched dependencies can make outputs differ. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH supplies a deterministic timestamp to tools that support it; it does not make an arbitrary build reproducible by itself. See the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH specification.

title: Source Builds, Local Packages and Reproducibility
section: Stage instead of installing into the host
text:
Stage instead of installing into the host
Many build systems support a staging directory (often DESTDIR) that receives files under their intended final paths without writing into /usr on the build host. Check the project’s documentation: support and syntax vary. Avoid sudo make install as an untracked shortcut, especially when a distribution package already owns the same paths. Build artifacts for deployment should have a documented owner, version, dependencies, upgrade path and removal procedure.
A Debian package records ownership and metadata in the package database. Creating one does not automatically solve dependency selection, signatures, upgrades, triggers or service policy. Debian source packaging and a clean build environment are the appropriate next step for a maintained application. The dpkg-deb manual documents the archive format and inspection commands.

title: Source Builds, Local Packages and Reproducibility
section: Lab: build and inspect a tiny local package
text:
Lab: build and inspect a tiny local package
On the disposable bl05-packages-lab clone, create an isolated working directory owned by the current user. This example packages a text file and has no maintainer scripts; it does not install anything. dpkg-deb must already be available.
labdir=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'Working directory: %s\n' "$labdir"
mkdir -p "$labdir/pkg/DEBIAN" "$labdir/pkg/usr/share/bl05-demo"
cat > "$labdir/pkg/DEBIAN/control" <<'CONTROL'
Package: bl05-demo
Version: 1.0-1
Architecture: all
Maintainer: Lab Operator <lab@example.invalid>
Description: Disposable local packaging example
 A small file for inspecting a package without installing it.
CONTROL
printf 'Package ownership demonstration\n' > "$labdir/pkg/usr/share/bl05-demo/readme"
dpkg-deb --root-owner-group --build "$labdir/pkg" "$labdir/bl05-demo_1.0-1_all.deb"
dpkg-deb --info "$labdir/bl05-demo_1.0-1_all.deb"
dpkg-deb --contents "$labdir/bl05-demo_1.0-1_all.deb"
sha256sum "$labdir/bl05-demo_1.0-1_all.deb"
Examine the package name, version, architecture and file paths. all means the package is architecture-independent, not that every dependency or interpreter would work on all hosts. The hash identifies these bytes; it is not a signature or evidence of trust. Rebuilding and comparing hashes is an experiment, not proof of independently reproducible builds unless inputs and environments are controlled independently.
Record the printed working directory. Remove it only after checking that it is the disposable directory just created:
printf '%s\n' "$labdir"
# After checking the path is the disposable directory:
rm -r -- "$labdir"
Do not reuse this removal command in a later shell where labdir is missing or has a different value. A real deployment would use a reviewed package with appropriate dependency metadata, authenticated distribution, an upgrade policy and acceptance tests. Installing a local .deb can execute its maintainer scripts as root; inspect and trust the whole package before installation.

title: Source Builds, Local Packages and Reproducibility
text:
Diagnose and practice
If an application works on the build host but fails elsewhere, compare architecture, interpreter, shared-library requirements, build flags, paths and runtime dependencies. A successful build may have used undeclared libraries already present on the builder. Rebuild in a clean environment and verify on a separate test host before changing dependency metadata. Explain the differences between file ownership, source authenticity and artifact reproducibility.

title: Offline Repositories, Mirrors and Disconnected Installation
text:
Design the supply route
Record the target release and architecture, enabled components, installed packages, storage capacity and update cadence. Decide who approves sources and signing keys, how metadata and packages cross the boundary, who verifies them, and how old snapshots are retained for recovery. A mirror can carry signed upstream metadata unchanged; an internally assembled repository needs its own signed release metadata and an independently provisioned, scoped trust key. Protect the signing key separately from the distribution server.
APT authenticates repository release metadata, which identifies index hashes; indexes in turn identify package hashes. Transport encryption can protect the connection but does not replace repository authentication. Conversely, valid signatures do not establish that software is appropriate for the target or that its metadata is fresh. A release’s expiry can make an old snapshot unusable; handle freshness through an explicit policy rather than disabling verification to get past an error. The APT authentication manual explains this trust chain.
A cache saves bandwidth only for objects it has retained and may need network access on a miss. A mirror needs sufficient space for all selected architectures, components and versions; incomplete synchronization can temporarily mix metadata with missing packages. Publish a completed, verified snapshot atomically and test it before clients consume it. Preserve source packages and required licenses when your policy requires them.

title: Offline Repositories, Mirrors and Disconnected Installation
section: Inventory a target without changing it
text:
Inventory a target without changing it
Use the bl05-packages-lab clone. Keep its network configured for this observation; no sources will be added or disabled. Record release and architecture along with current sources and package state:
cat /etc/os-release
dpkg --print-architecture
dpkg --print-foreign-architectures
apt-cache policy
dpkg-query -W -f='${binary:Package}\t${Version}\t${db:Status-Status}\n' \
  > "$HOME/bl05-package-inventory.tsv"
The inventory file is written in the lab user’s home and may disclose installed software. It is not a complete list of repository configuration, package selections, dependencies or application data. Keep it with the target’s change record and restrict distribution as appropriate. Review enabled source files and scoped signing keys as described earlier in this part. Inspect the package candidates required by a proposed change:
apt-cache policy tree
sudo apt-get -s install tree
This simulation uses the target’s current local indexes and state. It neither downloads packages nor guarantees that another host will resolve the same transaction. tree is only an example; the preceding lab removed it. Do not install it during this inspection.

title: Offline Repositories, Mirrors and Disconnected Installation
text:
Prepare and verify a transfer
A connected staging system must use a repository snapshot and target-compatible release, architectures, source configuration and package state. Resolve the whole transaction, including dependencies, on a representative target or controlled equivalent. Export the required signed metadata, indexes and package files using your chosen mirror or bundle tooling. Authenticate the portable media or transfer manifest independently; then verify repository signatures and hashes at the receiving side. A checksum copied beside a file on the same untrusted medium cannot by itself authenticate either file.
Test the procedure on a disposable host with its external network disconnected. Configure the approved local source using a scoped Signed-By key that was provisioned through a separate trusted channel; do not use trusted=yes to bypass a signature failure. Run apt update, inspect apt-cache policy and simulate the planned installation. If resolution wants a missing dependency or another repository, stop and rebuild the bundle or snapshot; do not silently reconnect the supposedly isolated host. Apply only a reviewed proposal, then validate package state and the workload. Record the snapshot identity, transfer date, signatures, versions, results and next update deadline.
The exact source stanza depends on how the repository is published. The Ubuntu sources.list manual describes deb822 sources and Signed-By. A directory of .deb files alone is not a signed APT repository. For a full implementation, also plan key rotation, revocation, repository expiry, storage monitoring, audit trails and emergency transport.

title: Offline Repositories, Mirrors and Disconnected Installation
text:
Diagnose and practice
If apt update reports a signature error, preserve the exact message and check the source URL, key identity, release metadata, clock and snapshot completeness. An expired release, wrong key and corrupted metadata require different fixes. If installation fails with an unavailable dependency, compare the candidate versions and architecture with the snapshot manifest; copying only the requested package rarely captures the full dependency closure.
Draw a supply route from upstream to the isolated host and mark the trust check and responsible owner at each crossing. Describe how you would test a stale or incomplete snapshot without changing a production host.

title: Interrupted Package Transactions and Recovery
text:
Establish the failure boundary
If another package process is working, let it finish; identify it and the associated service instead of deleting lock files. Check space on both the filesystem holding /var and any separate /boot. Capture the failing command, the error, package status, recent APT and dpkg logs, source configuration and any relevant service logs before retrying:
sudo dpkg --audit
sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/dpkg.log
sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/apt/term.log
df -h / /var /boot
systemctl list-jobs
Logs may be absent or rotated; protect them if they contain sensitive information. Inspect the specific package using dpkg-query -l PACKAGE and apt-cache policy PACKAGE, replacing PACKAGE with the actual name. The dpkg manual explains package states and configuration. A failed network download, a full filesystem, a dependency conflict and a maintainer-script failure require different repairs.
Fix the identified cause first. For a reviewed, interrupted configuration, sudo dpkg --configure PACKAGE can retry that package’s configuration; sudo dpkg --configure -a may configure all pending packages and run their scripts. sudo apt-get -s -f install previews APT’s proposal to fix broken dependencies. The actual apt-get -f install can change or remove packages and run scripts, so review its full proposal and stop if it is unexpected. Neither command repairs the underlying storage fault or makes an unsafe script safe. Do not use force options or edit package database files as a routine fix.

title: Interrupted Package Transactions and Recovery
section: Lab: recover a deliberately failed configuration
text:
Lab: recover a deliberately failed configuration
Use the disposable bl05-packages-lab clone, not a production host. Keep bl02 off, confirm the clone in the VM manager and have its console and a tested recovery copy available. This exercise creates and installs a tiny package whose post-install script intentionally fails until a marker exists. It will modify the clone’s package database and /run. dpkg-deb and dpkg must be present.
First ensure sudo dpkg --audit is empty, no package operation is running, bl05-recovery-demo has no existing installed or residual record, and /run/bl05-recovery-ready does not exist. If any condition fails, stop and investigate instead of overwriting another owner’s state:
sudo dpkg --audit
dpkg-query -l bl05-recovery-demo
ls -l /run/bl05-recovery-ready
The last two queries are expected to report no match. A package in rc or any other recorded state is not a clean baseline. Build the known lab package as the unprivileged user:
labdir=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'Lab directory: %s\n' "$labdir"
mkdir -p "$labdir/pkg/DEBIAN" "$labdir/pkg/usr/share/bl05-recovery-demo"
cat > "$labdir/pkg/DEBIAN/control" <<'CONTROL'
Package: bl05-recovery-demo
Version: 1.0-1
Architecture: all
Maintainer: Lab Operator <lab@example.invalid>
Description: Disposable package recovery exercise
 A deliberately failing post-install script for a lab clone.
CONTROL
cat > "$labdir/pkg/DEBIAN/postinst" <<'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/sh
set -e
if [ "$1" = configure ] && [ ! -f /run/bl05-recovery-ready ]; then
    echo 'Lab prerequisite is missing' >&2
    exit 1
fi
SCRIPT
chmod 755 "$labdir/pkg/DEBIAN/postinst"
printf 'Recovery exercise\n' > "$labdir/pkg/usr/share/bl05-recovery-demo/readme"
dpkg-deb --root-owner-group --build "$labdir/pkg" "$labdir/demo.deb"
dpkg-deb --info "$labdir/demo.deb"
dpkg-deb --contents "$labdir/demo.deb"
Review the package and script above before installing: package scripts execute as root. If the build failed or the contents differ, stop. The next command intentionally returns an error and leaves this package in an incomplete state:
sudo dpkg -i "$labdir/demo.deb"
sudo dpkg --audit
dpkg-query -l bl05-recovery-demo
Confirm the failure mentions the lab prerequisite and the audit names the lab package. If anything else failed, stop and investigate. Supply the deliberately missing prerequisite, then retry only this package:
sudo touch /run/bl05-recovery-ready
sudo dpkg --configure bl05-recovery-demo
dpkg-query -l bl05-recovery-demo
sudo dpkg --audit
A successful retry should show the package fully installed and no audit issues. If it does not, preserve the output and do not continue to cleanup until the cause is understood. Remove only the lab package and marker, then inspect the result:
sudo dpkg -r bl05-recovery-demo
sudo rm -- /run/bl05-recovery-ready
sudo dpkg --audit
dpkg-query -l bl05-recovery-demo
printf 'Remove this disposable directory only after checking: %s\n' "$labdir"
Remove the printed temporary build directory after confirming it is the one created for this exercise. If the shell session is lost, recover the recorded path; do not guess. Power off the clone before starting bl02.

title: Interrupted Package Transactions and Recovery
text:
Rollback has boundaries
Removing or downgrading a package does not necessarily reverse database migrations, external side effects, generated files or a changed configuration. An older package may not be available or compatible with newer data. Recovery may require a coordinated restore of software, configuration and application data from a tested, consistent backup; a same-host VM clone is not an independent backup. Verify both package state and the application through a client after recovery.

title: Interrupted Package Transactions and Recovery
text:
Practice and recall
Record the intentional error, status before and after configuration, the exact prerequisite and final audit. Explain why the targeted retry was appropriate here and why it must not be generalized into running arbitrary maintainer scripts by hand. Compare the package-state repair with an application-data restore.

title: Service Supervision, Units and Managers
section: Unit state is not application health
text:
Unit state is not application health
On a systemd host, a unit describes an object managed by systemd. Service units supervise processes; other unit types represent sockets, timers, mounts, devices and targets. The system manager handles system units, while a user’s manager handles that user’s units. systemctl --user addresses the current user’s manager when a user session and bus are available; it is not the same manager as sudo systemctl.
Inspect the system without making changes:
ps -p 1 -o pid,comm,args
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service
systemctl --failed
Loaded units and installed unit files are different inventories. A unit’s active state, its enabled state and its client-visible health are separate facts. enabled generally describes links for future activation, not a promise that the service is running now; a disabled unit can still be started manually or by another unit. A static unit may be activated by a dependency despite lacking direct enablement. systemctl’s manual documents these states.

title: Service Supervision, Units and Managers
text:
Prepare a separate service lab
Create bl06-service-lab as a full clone of powered-off bl02, following the same single-disk, no-shared-disk, no-backing-chain and no-TPM precautions used for bl05-packages-lab. Confirm sufficient space and that the destination name and disk path do not already exist:
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domstate bl02
sudo virsh --connect qemu:///system domblklist bl02 --details
sudo virt-clone --connect qemu:///system \
  --original bl02 --name bl06-service-lab \
  --file /var/lib/libvirt/images/bl06-service-lab.qcow2
Run the clone command only after checking that the original is shut off and has the expected disk layout. Inspect both domains for distinct disks and NVRAM; keep bl02 and other clones off when this clone runs, because the copied guest has the same identity. The guest hostname may still be bl02: identify it through the VM manager and console, not the hostname alone. Keep a recovery copy and console access. The clone needs Python 3; check command -v python3 and /usr/bin/python3 --version. Do not install tools solely to hide an unexpected baseline.

title: Service Supervision, Units and Managers
text:
Create a bounded example service
The example serves existing documentation on loopback port 18765, only inside the VM. Python’s demonstration HTTP server is not a production web server. Verify that port is unused and the name is not already owned before proceeding:
sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :18765'
systemctl cat bl06-demo.service
ls -ld /usr/share/doc
An empty listener result and a unit-not-found result are expected. If the port, unit, or /etc/systemd/system/bl06-demo.service already exists, stop and choose a fresh clone. Create the local unit:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/bl06-demo.service > /dev/null <<'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=BL06 loopback documentation demonstration

[Service]
Type=exec
DynamicUser=yes
WorkingDirectory=/usr/share/doc
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 18765 --bind 127.0.0.1
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
UNIT
sudo systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/bl06-demo.service
If verification reports errors, fix them before loading. DynamicUser=yes uses a transient service identity; this service needs only read access to the documentation directory. It is deliberately not enabled at boot. Load the definition and start it:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start bl06-demo.service
systemctl status bl06-demo.service --no-pager
systemctl is-enabled bl06-demo.service
sudo journalctl -u bl06-demo.service -b --no-pager
is-enabled returns a nonzero status for a disabled unit; that is expected here. Test from inside the same guest:
python3 - <<'PYCODE'
import urllib.request
response = urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:18765/", timeout=5)
print(response.status)
PYCODE
Expect HTTP 200 for the directory listing. If it fails, inspect the unit status, log, listener address and permissions. Do not expose this example to an untrusted network. Keep the unit for the next chapters; later exercises will remove it.

title: Service Supervision, Units and Managers
text:
Practice and recall
Record the manager, unit file, main PID, active and enabled states, listener and client response. Explain why starting a process and obtaining a successful HTTP response answer different questions. Compare systemctl list-units with systemctl list-unit-files and describe why their counts differ.

title: Execution Environment, Identity and Exit Status
section: Inspect what the manager will run
text:
Inspect what the manager will run
On bl06-service-lab, inspect the example created in the previous chapter:
systemctl cat bl06-demo.service
systemctl show bl06-demo.service \
  -p Type -p ExecStart -p User -p DynamicUser -p WorkingDirectory \
  -p MainPID -p Result -p ExecMainCode -p ExecMainStatus
systemctl status bl06-demo.service --no-pager
systemctl cat shows the fragment and drop-ins; show exposes effective properties and runtime results. The dynamic user’s actual identity can be allocated at runtime and is not a persistent human account. A PID is a point-in-time observation and can change on restart. If access is denied or the service is absent, resolve the lab setup before continuing.
ExecStart= is parsed by systemd, not automatically by an interactive shell.
