Shell features such as redirection, pipelines and command substitution do not work as they do in a shell unless a shell is explicitly invoked; avoid constructing shell strings from untrusted input. Use absolute executable paths, and understand the unit’s WorkingDirectory= and User=. The systemd execution manual describes execution context and environment.

title: Execution Environment, Identity and Exit Status
text:
Environment and privileges
Environment= and EnvironmentFile= can provide configuration. They are not a safe secret store: environment values can be exposed through manager interfaces or inherited by child processes. Prefer service credential mechanisms and appropriate file permissions for secrets. A user session’s PATH, home directory and shell initialization files should not be assumed to exist in a system service. WorkingDirectory= failure can prevent execution entirely; permissions must allow the selected service identity to traverse every parent directory and read the needed files.
Run the application with the least privilege it needs. A service account, a dynamic identity and a human user’s identity have different persistence and access properties. Dynamic identities are convenient for this stateless read-only example; persistent state requires explicitly managed directories and ownership. Do not use root merely because a permission error disappeared.

title: Execution Environment, Identity and Exit Status
text:
Read exit evidence
systemctl show bl06-demo.service \
  -p ActiveState -p SubState -p Result -p ExecMainCode -p ExecMainStatus
sudo journalctl -u bl06-demo.service -b -n 40 --no-pager
ExecMainCode and ExecMainStatus describe how the main process exited when that information is available; the unit’s Result describes the manager’s outcome. A service that never executed because setup failed has different evidence from one that executed and returned an error. A successful process exit can still be wrong for a long-running service, and active alone is not a functional check.
For the lab server, compare the process context with the unit properties and repeat the HTTP request from the previous chapter. Do not change the service identity or write to /usr/share/doc; that directory is package-managed. Later chapters address persistent service data and sandboxing.

title: Execution Environment, Identity and Exit Status
text:
Worked diagnosis and practice
Suppose a service reports status=200/CHDIR. Inspect the effective working directory and journal, determine whether the path exists and is accessible to the service’s identity, and fix the documented path or permissions at their owning layer. Re-run a client test after restart. If the status instead indicates an executable or permission failure, follow that evidence rather than changing unrelated paths. Record the lab unit’s effective execution context and explain why an environment variable is unsuitable for a password.

title: Startup Types, Readiness, Watchdogs and Restarts
text:
How a service reports startup
Systemd’s Type= selects a startup protocol. With simple, the manager considers the service started after the process is forked, before confirming that the executable ran. exec waits until the executable has been invoked successfully, but does not prove that it has bound a port or can answer a request. oneshot waits for its start command to exit; it is appropriate for bounded work, not a daemon that stays in the foreground. notify expects an application that implements the notification protocol to send READY=1 when it considers itself ready. Legacy daemons may use forking, with their own process-identification considerations.
The precise semantics, timeouts and other types are in the systemd.service manual. Do not switch a program to Type=notify unless it actually sends the required notification. A readiness signal is the application’s assertion; an independent client check can still reveal a broken dependency or wrong response.

title: Startup Types, Readiness, Watchdogs and Restarts
text:
Examine the lab service
The bl06-demo Python HTTP server uses Type=exec. On the lab clone:
systemctl show bl06-demo.service \
  -p Type -p ActiveState -p SubState -p MainPID -p Restart -p NRestarts
sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :18765'
python3 - <<'PYCODE'
import urllib.request
response = urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:18765/", timeout=5)
print(response.status)
PYCODE
The service state and listener are useful evidence; the HTTP response tests an actual request. They are snapshots and can change between commands. Python’s basic server does not send systemd readiness notifications. For a real service, choose a documented startup protocol and test the required dependency and response semantics, including failure and timeouts.

title: Startup Types, Readiness, Watchdogs and Restarts
text:
Restart policy and watchdogs
Restart=on-failure requests a restart after qualifying failures; it does not make a failed dependency healthy and does not guarantee an endless retry loop. Start-rate limiting can suppress repeated starts. RestartSec= spaces attempts. Choose a policy with the service’s data integrity and failure mode in mind, and inspect both the service logs and the manager’s restart counters. A deliberately stopped service should not be used as a test of failure recovery.
A watchdog is a deadline for periodic notifications from a cooperating application. WatchdogSec= alone cannot teach an application to send watchdog messages. A process may send heartbeats while a dependent network service or client path is broken, so supplement the watchdog with meaningful health checks. Do not add watchdog settings to the Python lab server.
To inspect restart evidence without injecting a fault:
systemctl show bl06-demo.service -p Restart -p RestartUSec -p NRestarts
sudo journalctl -u bl06-demo.service -b -n 50 --no-pager
A high restart count suggests examining the first failure, not merely resetting the counter. If the unit reaches its start limit, diagnose and correct the cause before reset-failed or another start. The reset clears manager failure/rate-limit state; it does not fix the underlying application.

title: Startup Types, Readiness, Watchdogs and Restarts
text:
Worked diagnosis and practice
A dependent unit starts after a web service but its first request fails. Inspect the web unit’s type and startup logs, listener and client response; After= on a Type=exec service provides ordering through execution, not proof that the web server is ready. Use the application’s supported readiness protocol or design retries with bounded timeouts. Record the lab service’s type, restart policy and HTTP response, and explain what each tells you and what it cannot establish.

title: Requirements, Ordering and Failure Propagation
text:
Build the dependency model
Wants= pulls another unit into the transaction but is weak: its failure does not by itself prevent the requesting unit from starting. Requires= pulls in a stronger requirement; combined with After=, failure to activate the required unit prevents the ordered dependent from starting. After= and Before= specify ordering only and do not themselves pull another unit in. Shutdown order reverses the start order. BindsTo= with After= expresses a stronger ongoing association, but even an active unit is not necessarily an available remote endpoint. Conditions and unexpected deactivation have subtleties; use the systemd.unit manual when designing a real unit.
network.target does not guarantee an assigned address or remote connectivity. network-online.target is an optional synchronization point with meaning determined by the installed network stack and wait service; it cannot promise a remote database or DNS server will stay reachable. Applications need timeouts, retry and failure handling as well as unit dependencies.
Inspect the demo’s actual relationships:
systemctl list-dependencies bl06-demo.service
systemctl show bl06-demo.service -p Wants -p Requires -p After -p Before
Implicit dependencies and defaults can add relationships absent from the unit file. The listing describes manager relationships, not the complete application dependency graph.

title: Requirements, Ordering and Failure Propagation
text:
Lab: observe a failed prerequisite
On bl06-service-lab, create two temporary system units under /run/systemd/system; they disappear at reboot and are not enabled. The prerequisite exits unsuccessfully, and the dependent requires it and is ordered after it. First check both names and files are unused:
systemctl cat bl06-prereq.service bl06-dependent.service
ls -l /run/systemd/system/bl06-prereq.service \
  /run/systemd/system/bl06-dependent.service
Unit-not-found and missing-file messages are expected. If either unit or file exists, stop rather than overwrite it. Confirm /usr/bin/false and /usr/bin/true exist, then write the units:
sudo tee /run/systemd/system/bl06-prereq.service > /dev/null <<'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=BL06 intentionally failing prerequisite
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/false
UNIT
sudo tee /run/systemd/system/bl06-dependent.service > /dev/null <<'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=BL06 ordered dependent
Requires=bl06-prereq.service
After=bl06-prereq.service
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/true
RemainAfterExit=yes
UNIT
sudo systemd-analyze verify /run/systemd/system/bl06-prereq.service \
  /run/systemd/system/bl06-dependent.service
Resolve verification errors before continuing. Reload and start the dependent:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start bl06-dependent.service
systemctl status bl06-prereq.service bl06-dependent.service --no-pager
sudo journalctl -b -u bl06-prereq.service -u bl06-dependent.service --no-pager
The start is expected to fail: the ordered requirement fails before the dependent can run. Compare unit result and journal messages. The dependent’s own program has not demonstrated a failure; it was prevented from running by the dependency transaction. If the result differs, inspect the effective unit files and manager state before changing them.
After recording evidence, remove only the two units created in this exercise and clear their failure state:
sudo systemctl stop bl06-dependent.service bl06-prereq.service
sudo systemctl reset-failed bl06-dependent.service bl06-prereq.service
sudo rm -- /run/systemd/system/bl06-dependent.service \
  /run/systemd/system/bl06-prereq.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
Keep bl06-demo.service for subsequent chapters. No real system prerequisite was modified. In a production incident, preserve failure evidence before resetting status and check the implications of stopping a unit and its dependents.

title: Requirements, Ordering and Failure Propagation
text:
Practice and recall
Draw two arrows: one for pulling in a prerequisite and one for ordering it. Explain what changes if Requires= becomes Wants=, and why After= alone would not start the prerequisite. State what this lab does and does not prove about a continuously running remote dependency.
